📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that around four years ago, humanity intentionally hit an asteroid. The Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) was by pretty much all measures a resounding success when it struck the asteroid moonlet Dimorphos going more than 22,000 kilometers per hour. However, we still donât know just how much of a success it actually was - DART was a one-way mission with no real way to track the results of the impact close up. Enter Hera, the European Space Agency (ESA) mission that recently arrived in the binary asteroid system. Now, in a press release, ESA has provided some of the best pictures of the binary system since that fateful day four years ago.

Sources indicate that the lack of accurate measurement isnât for lack of trying. Ground-based observatories have been watching 151m wide Dimorphos and its parent asteroid, 780m wide Didymos very closely over the last four years. They could tell that Dimorphos slowed its orbit around its larger companion by about 33 minutes. But some scientists were surprised by the magnitude of the change in orbit, based on the theoretical math done before the mission.

To help clear up any ambiguity about the math underlying this planetary defense mission, Hera is equipped with three main imaging tools. Its standard âeyesâ are the Asteroid Framing cameras, which handle both black-and-white photography and navigation. The press release showcases an image from this system showing Didymos from roughly 28.5km away, with features down to roughly 2.7m per pixel.

Fraser talks about Hera's final insertion into the binary asteroid system.

It has been revealed that in the image, you can clearly see the âspinning topâ shape of the larger asteroid in the pair. Didymos spins at a relatively rapid speed for its size, completing a rotation every 2.2 hours. That energy is strong enough to pull boulders and gravel towards the middle of the asteroid, causing a build-up of material that makes it look fatter in the middle than at its poles.

According to recent reports, however, seeing an asteroid in black in white isnât as scientifically useful as seeing it in âcolorâ. That is what Heraâs second imaging system, the HyperScout H instrument, is designed to do. It monitors the asteroid over 25 different color bands. With that information, HyperScout H can absorb and reflect light with different unique patterns - essentially it can spectroscopy. Comparing the results to lab experiments on meteorite samples on Earth will help determine what Didymos and its smaller companion are actually made up of.

But why stop at simple hyperspectral imaging when you can also have heat vision? The Thermal Infrared Imager (TIRI), supplied to ESA by Japanâs Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) gives Hera âSuperman-likeâ heat vision according to the press release. TIRI maps the temperature of the surface of the asteroids, and since solid rock dissipates heat much more slowly than porous or fragmented rock, it will also give a good indication of how solid Didymos really is.

Fraser talks about some of the results of the DART test.

It has been revealed that crucially, Dimorphos itself, the actual subject of the original DART test, is surprisingly absent from many of the pictures in this first round of releases. In the visible light images, Dimorphos is tucked almost entirely into the shadow of Didymos, appearing as a tiny sunlit spec beneath Didymos in one of the images. But with TIRIâs âSupermanâ view, the entire 151m wide asteroid is clearly in focus, glowing a shade of cool purple in the infrared. Cameras arenât the only thing Hera is carrying either. It will eventually launch two CubeSats, Juventus and Milan, to study the asteroid binary very closely. They will use ground-penetrating radar and even touch down on the surface of Dimorphos in an effort to understand what itstruly made of.

But ultimately the overarching purpose of the mission is to get a better idea of how effectively we can move an asteroid out of the way if we need to. DART appeared to be a success on the surface. Understanding what really happened to Dimorphos is what Hera, with all its cameras and companion spacecraft, was literally designed for. And weâre just at the earliest phases of that process. The next step is a major release of even sharper images planned for a live event at the Berlin Museum of Natural History on November 25th. Asteroid watchers, and space enthusiasts more generally, should mark their calendars for our first high-resolution view of one of the biggest impacts weâve had on another body in the solar system to date.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Upcoming England is the ancestral home of moderate Republicans, from the Saltonstalls to the Bushes, whose fiscal conservatism and social moderation defined the national GOP for decades.
  • Sources indicate that last week, Yankee Republicans suffered a near-total wipeout.
  • Sources indicate that one Republican operative sees a path out of the wilderness in a post-Trump era.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Upcoming England is the ancestral home of moderate Republicans, from the Saltonstalls to the Bushes, whose fiscal conservatism and social moderation defined the national GOP for decades.

Sources indicate that last week, Yankee Republicans suffered a near-total wipeout. Maine’s Susan Collins, Fresh England's last GOP senator, lost her seat to Democrat Troy Jackson, leaving former Maine Gov. Paul LePage, who just won a House seat, as the lone Republican headed to Congress from the region. (The picture was a bit brighter at the state level, where GOP Govs. Phil Scott of Vermont and Kelly Ayotte of New Hampshire were both reelected.).

Sources indicate that one Republican operative sees a path out of the wilderness in a post-Trump era. In an opinion piece in The Boston Globe, consultant Kristin Tate urged Latest England Republicans to focus on fiscal discipline and recognize that “independence from national party leadership can be a political asset, not an act of betrayal.”.

After all, as the midterm election results remind us, no political realignment lasts forever.

Industry observers note that three decades ago, there were plenty of moderate Democrats from Southern states serving in Congress, governor’s mansions and even the White House. But in the years since Bill Clinton's exit from the political stage, Democrats have largely written off the South.

Which is partly why last week’s Democratic wins in the Carolinas, Georgia and, perhaps most notably, Mississippi were so stunning. All the elements that powered the party to victory nationally – disillusionment with Donald Trump, a rise in economic populism and hunger for change – played a role in the South as well.

But other factors were unique to a region that has seen renewed attempts to dilute Black political power with the redrawing of House districts to favor the GOP.

The Republican redistricting gambit in Southern states did not fully yield the desired results and seems to have helped galvanize Black voters and their allies, powering Democrats to unlikely victories.

It’s too soon to say whether the GOP’s reduced hold on the South represents a temporary blip or an enduring shift.

But Joe Trippi, a longtime Democratic strategist who advised candidates in Alabama and Florida this year, has a message for his party: “We need to invest in the South.”.

#MSSEN: Democrat Scott Colom defeated GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith to become Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction and the first in his party to win a Senate seat in the Magnolia State since 1982.

According to recent reports, tar Heel tidal wave: Democrats in North Carolina have picked up at least five House seats, a striking development given the steep structural disadvantages the party faced. Prior to last week, no House Republican incumbent had lost a general election in the state since Republicans won control of the redistricting process more than a decade ago. And the Democratic gains could grow: In the 5th District, former journalist Chuck Hubbard narrowly leads 11-term Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx, and in the 3rd District, former state Rep. Raymond Smith holds a razor-thin edge over Republican Rep. Greg Murphy. The Associated Press had not called either race at publication time, though Murphy has conceded.

Republicans pick campaign chairs: Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno and Georgia Rep. Brian Jack will be the chairs of Republicans’ respective campaign committees for the 2028 cycle. GOP lawmakers held their leadership elections Tuesday, as our colleagues Savannah Behrmann and John T. Bennett reported. Senate Republicans are sticking with South Dakota’s John Thune to lead them in the next Congress, while House Republicans picked former Freedom Caucus Chair Jim Jordan as their leader.

Redistricting doubts: Maryland could be getting a new congressional map after voters approved a constitutional amendment that would clear the way for new lines in 2028. Our colleague Victor Feldman has more on the result and other election-related ballot measures across the country. But it’s not clear how many other states may look to redistrict next cycle after Republican efforts over the past 18 months largely didn’t pay off in last week’s elections.

According to recent reports, run the table: With Rep. Darren Soto winning a sixth term in Florida, no Democratic incumbent lost reelection to a Republican this year. Soto’s win in a redrawn district also meant that Florida Democrats defended all four seats the GOP had targeted under a fresh congressional map.

In a recent development, california contest: Rep. Ken Calvert defeated fellow Republican Rep. Young Kim in a rare member-versus-member contest for a redrawn Southern California seat that turned acrimonious. Republicans are poised to hold just four House seats in the Golden State after Democrats made good on five pickup opportunities under a new congressional map.

Cheesecake Factory caucus: The latest episode of the Political Theater podcast, hosted by Roll Call editor-in-chief Jason Dick, breaks down how candidates in both parties fared in counties where The Cheesecake Factory operates, after the popular chain restaurant became something of a side character in the closing weeks of the midterm campaign.

Back to school: Newly elected members of Congress are on Capitol Hill this week for freshman orientation, an experience Massachusetts Rep.-elect Dan Koh told our colleague Nina Heller is “like high school – but it’s fun high school.” The incoming lawmakers took their class photo Thursday morning and will get to pick their Capitol Hill offices after next week’s famed lottery, Nina writes.

Recent findings suggest that tracking the count: As of 4:30 p.m. Eastern time Thursday, House Democrats had flipped 44 seats, while Republicans had picked up three. Twelve races remain uncalled, including a pair in Louisiana that will be decided by December runoffs. On the Senate side, Democrats have flipped eight seats, with only Alaska’s race still undecided.

Sources indicate that guv upgrade: Democrats flipped at least five governorships last week and will hold a majority of governor’s mansions next year. Two gubernatorial races remain uncalled by the AP: Kansas, where Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher is narrowly ahead of Republican state Senate President Ty Masterson, and Alaska, where Democratic former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins is just below the 50 percent threshold to win the election outright. In territorial elections, Republicans flipped the governor’s office in Guam while voters in the Northern Mariana Islands will pick their next governor in a Nov. 20 runoff.

In a recent development, #TNSEN: Republican Sen. Marsha Blackburn, who was elected Tennessee governor last week, is poised to pick her Senate successor. According to the Nashville Banner, the short list includes Knox County Mayor Glenn Jacobs, a former professional wrestler, Reps. Tim Burchett and Chuck Fleischmann, and Tennessee Deputy Gov. Stuart McWhorter.

2028 on the brain: A handful of House Democrats are already considering 2028 Senate bids, according to Axios, including Kansas’ Sharice Davids, North Carolina’s Don Davis and Pennsylvania’s Chris DeLuzio.

Senator Morrison? Minnesota Rep. Kelly Morrison is earning buzz as a potential appointee to fill the Senate seat that Democrat Amy Klobuchar is vacating to become governor, Semafor reports. House Democrats aren’t likely to be as concerned about open seats as their Republican counterparts were in recent years, given the size of the incoming Democratic majority.

AOC’s future: Progressive activists have introduced a fresh organization to encourage New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to run for president in 2028. Meanwhile, Axios reports that Ocasio-Cortez has parted ways with the digital fundraising firm she’s worked with for several years and has brought on the same firm that Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders used during his two presidential campaigns.

It has been revealed that women lead: Shirley Emehelu is Newly introduced Jersey’s new lieutenant governor after Democratic Gov. Mikie Sherrill picked her to succeed Dale Caldwell, who resigned in September amid sexual harassment allegations and other ethical lapses. New Jersey is now one of five states to have women in both the governor’s and lieutenant governor’s offices, along with Massachusetts, Arkansas, Iowa and Virginia. Iowa will come off the list next year after an all-male Democratic ticket swept this year’s gubernatorial race, though five other states elected women to both offices last week.

Congress will once again be filled with losers – i.e, latest members who have lost previous bids for elected office. Roll Call elections analyst Nathan L. Gonzales of Inside Elections returns to his biennial tradition as he runs down the latest list of “losers.”.

In a recent development, ducking the wave: Democrats notched big wins in unexpected places, but one state grew redder after last week’s elections. The New York Times checks in with voters in South Dakota, where the GOP won all nine statewide elections.

Industry observers note that here come the MBAs: Democrats with corporate connections were among the winners in last week’s elections, countering the idea that candidates with serious business credentials have struggled within the party, The Wall Street Journal reports. The field of 19 winners with M.B.A. degrees includes Costco board member Helena Buonanno Foulkes, who won the Rhode Island governor’s race, and Paige Cognetti, a Goldman Sachs alum who flipped a House seat in Pennsylvania.

In a recent development, how Ricketts did it: Nebraska Sen. Pete Ricketts’ election night success was one of the few bright spots for the GOP. Ricketts fended off a challenge from independent Dan Osborn by painting him as a Democrat, questioning his authenticity and highlighting leaked audio of his comments denigrating Trump voters, writes the Nebraska Examiner.

According to recent reports, was it necessary? California redrew its congressional map to favor Democrats in response to Texas taking a similar step to boost the GOP. But some are questioning whether the state needed to cast aside its independent redistricting commission to rejigger the lines, given the scale of Democrats’ wins. “What they were literally saying is, ‘Let’s undo democracy to protect democracy,’” Lincoln Project co-founder Mike Madrid told CalMatters. “There’s something very Orwellian about it.”.

Song of the cycle: The Latest York Times reviews “Talafreako,” an unlikely viral anthem celebrating the newly elected Democratic senator from Texas.

History does rhyme: An opinion piece in The (Charleston) Post & Courier argues that the win by Democratic Sen.-elect Annie Andrews is the latest in a long line of cases in which South Carolina voters bucked the idea of party bosses picking their leaders.

The man behind the grill: The Latest York Times profiles Russ Hudson, the Mississippi man in Colom’s now-legendary “Pick another protein” ad.

That was the last time Democrats won 11 House seats in North Carolina.

As of Thursday afternoon, they appear on track to match that number. They’ve already won nine seats – a mark they last cleared in the 1982 midterms – and they’re narrowly ahead in two more races.

If those leads hold, Democrats' 11-member delegation would look much different than the one sworn in some 66 years ago in 1961. Tar Heel Democrats taking office in January would include four women, six Black members and one Hispanic member.

Their 11 representatives (out of 12) in the 87th Congress were all white men who consistently voted to uphold racial segregation and oppose major federal civil rights legislation.

Industry observers note that vote counting in Alaska is expected to conclude by Wednesday, Nov. 18, the targeted date for ranked choice tabulations in races in which no candidate took more than 50 percent of the vote. As of Thursday, Democratic former Rep. Mary Peltola narrowly leads Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan in the Senate race, though she’s below the 50 percent threshold.

Meanwhile, Democrats are gathering in Denver beginning Thursday to celebrate their historic wins and plot their next steps.

Industry News: Earth's Atmosphere Took Three Deep Breaths of Oxygen Before the Oceans Caught Up

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1461 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that earth formed about 4.5 billion years ago, along with the rest of the planets.
  • The atmosphere, the oceans, and life itself are all parts of the system.
  • In a recent development, cyanobacteria used sunlight to split water molecules apart.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that earth formed about 4.5 billion years ago, along with the rest of the planets. Life appeared somewhere between about 4.28 and 3.8 billion years ago; it's difficult to determine clearly. An oxygen atmosphere is a more recent development for Earth, in geological timescales, and understanding how that happened is a significant part of understanding the present-day Earth.

Earth is one big system. The atmosphere, the oceans, and life itself are all parts of the system. In some respects, they can be studied in isolation. But when trying to understand Earth and its long history, they need to be understood together. The system changed significantly when life changed. Somewhere around 2.4 billion years ago, cyanobacteria appeared, and they brought a new trick with them: photosynthesis.

In a recent development, cyanobacteria used sunlight to split water molecules apart. That did two things: it generated their chemical energy, and it released free oxygen into water, which eventually found its way into the atmosphere. That was a monumental stage of Earth's development that eventually led to an ozone layer, letting life flourish on the surface. The oxygenation of the atmosphere also led to complex life like us.

Recent findings suggest that but this all happened a long time ago. At first, the oxygen didn't accumulate in the atmosphere, and figuring out how it all played out isn't simple. Scientists know that the oxygenation history of the ocean and the atmosphere are coupled, but there are many questions. Some researchers argue that the atmosphere's oxygenation took place in different stages, one of which was the Great Oxygenation Event (GOE), while others have argued that the process was smoother. The debate continues.

Sources indicate that newly introduced research in The Innovation shows how Earth's atmosphere was oxygenated in three distinct steps, and that the deep ocean lagged behind in each case. In the last of the steps, deep ocean oxygenation lagged behind by 600 million years.

The research is titled "Stagewise oxygenation of the Earthâs atmosphere and oceans," and the authors are Haiyang Wang and Chao Li, geochemists at the Chengdu University of Technology.

"Earthâs surface oxygenation was a protracted, multi-step process," the authors write. "It is widely accepted that atmospheric O2 rose through three major steps, each closely linked to key evolutionary innovations.".

Recent findings suggest that the oceans and the atmosphere are linked, and during the quest to understand Earth's oxygenated atmosphere, researchers used the geological rock record to understand ocean chemistry. The well-known banded iron formations are a part of this. They record the ocean's oxygen levels. The atmosphere doesn't hold an ancient record, so the ocean's geological record was used as a proxy for the atmosphere's evolution and oxygenation, too.

So scientists largely think that three stages of rising oxygen created the modern atmosphere: the GOE about 2.4 billion years ago, the Neoproterozoic Oxygenation Event about 800 to 540 million years ago, and the Paleozoic Oxygenation Event about 400 million years ago.

Sources indicate that the researchers reiterate the understanding that ocean and atmospheric oxygenation are coupled. Research shows that on billion year timescales, episodes of rising atmospheric oxygen precede the same episodic rise in ocean oxygenation, "whereas on shorter, million-year timescales, their redox states could diverge, exhibiting negative coupling," they write.

"Here, we synthesize geochemical, sedimentological, and palaeobiological evidence to reconstruct this coupled and dynamic atmosphere-ocean oxygenation history and to reassess its timing, mechanisms, and ecological consequences," the authors explain.

This work hinges on newly introduced geochemical proxies that give researchers a clearer picture of what happened so long ago.

"Recent advances in geochemical proxies, most notably sulfate triple-oxygen isotopes (Îâ²17O), provide upcoming constraints on atmospheric oxygenation, complementing and in some cases revising interpretations from traditional ocean redox proxies," the authors explain.

In a recent development, the researchers say that this sulfate (SO4)offers a cleaner way to understand the oxygenation of the atmosphere. That's because of the isotopic composition of atmospheric oxygen, which is recorded when sulfate forms. It has a deficit of the isotope oxygen-17. So the sulfate can be used to track the rise of atmospheric O2, putting dates on each rise in atmospheric oxygen.

Recent findings suggest that they found that the GOE is unchanged, sitting between 2.4â2.1 billion years ago. But this work changes the dates of the second and third oxygen rises.

In a recent development, the second, the Neoproterozoic Oxygenation Event was 1.3â1.0 billion years ago instead of 800 to 540 million years ago. The Paleozoic Oxygenation Event was 0.42â0.36 billion years instead of 0.44â0.41 billion.

Industry observers note that the researchers found something else, too. The previous dates for the Neoproterozoic and Paleozoic events still record something. But instead of dating atmospheric oxygen, they date the delayed oxygenation of the deep ocean. They lagged behind the oxygenation of the atmosphere by about 200 and 30 million years, respectively.

According to recent reports, this graphic illustrates the results from new research into the oxygenation of Earth's atmosphere that reveals how Earth's O2 rose unevenly: shallow seas first, then the atmosphere, and much later the deep ocean. During a 2-billion-year transition, atmosphere and ocean O2 sometimes diverged despite long-term rise. Ocean oxygenation was highly variable, with extreme spatial heterogeneity over time. Image Credit: Stagewise oxygenation of the Earth's atmosphere and oceans. Wang and Li 2026, The Innovation.

On shorter timescales, the link between ocean and atmospheric oxygen is still the defining feature in this work. But it indicates that a change in one could've pushed the other in the opposite direction. The researchers think that what seems like a signal of rising oxygen levels is actually a drop. When a pulse of oxygen enters the ocean, it oxidized organic carbon and sulfide in the oceans. The organic carbon becomes CO2, and the sulfide becomes sulfate. The more organic carbon and sulfide there was in the ocean, the more it depleted atmospheric oxygen.

In a recent development, over longer, billion year timescales, the atmophere is oxygenated as photosynthesis continues. But on shorter timescales, it can't keep up.

Industry observers note that "Earthâs surface oxygenation history reflects a dynamic and nonlinear interplay among atmospheric O2 evolution, land and ocean redox buffering, and ecological innovation," the authors write. "Overall, the trajectory from localized Archean oxygen oases to the globally well-oxygenated surface environments of today underscores how atmosphere-ocean oxygenation both governsâand is reciprocally shaped byâthe evolution of life.".

According to recent reports, this figure demonstrates the evolution of Earth's atmosphere-ocean redox states through time and space. (A) Before 2.4 Ga: atmosphere and oceans were largely anoxic, with oxygen restricted to localized, shallow-water oxygen oases. (B) From 2.4 to 1.0 Ga: atmospheric O2 remained low; oxygenated waters were confined to the ocean surface, and oxygen oases developed primarily along continental shelves. (C) Between 1.0 and 0.41 Ga: atmospheric O2 increased but fluctuated, while oxygenated waters progressively penetrated to greater depths, with shelf environments continuing to host oxygen oases. (D) Since â¼0.41 Ga: atmospheric O2 approached near-modern levels; deep oceans became pervasively oxygenated, whereas mid-depth waters developed oxygen minimum zones (OMZs) that waxed and waned (solid curves) in response to high organic matter export and oxygen consumption. DOC, dissolved organic carbon. Image Credit: Wang and Li 2026, The Innovation.

According to recent reports, it all happened in stages, as the different elements fed back on one another. This work shows that during Earth's long path to an oxygenated atmosphere, the ocean and atmosphere didn't change in lockstep on shorter timescales. "Throughout the 2-billion-year oxygenation transition, atmospheric and oceanic oxygen levels were episodically decoupled on shorter timescales, superimposed on a long-term trajectory toward global oxidation," they write.

Recent findings suggest that the pair of researchers acknowledge some of the weakness in the evidence that paints this picture. The record of oxygen isotopes in sulfate is coarse, not exquisitely detailed. Beyond one billion years ago, the levels aren't well-constrained. So it's still more open to interpretation. There may be other steps in the path to oxygenation that aren't clear yet.

Sources indicate that understanding how life and the planet co-evolved together is a monumental task. Scientists know it happened, but all of the details are difficult to detect. But if it happened here, it almost certainly happened on any other habitable worlds.

"These deep-time perspectives illuminate the co-evolution of life and Earthâs surface environments and provide a conceptual framework for evaluating planetary habitability," the authors write.

Then I remembered the puff pastry. For some reason, I attached a moral imperative to the idea of making the whole pie from scratch, and spent the next two weeks poring over puff pastry recipes that felt like casual guides to wizard-tier alchemy. I loved to cook, but I simply wasn’t a big baker. (I also didn’t own a food processor, unless you counted my Magic Bullet.) My mother eventually brought me down to Earth. “Just buy it,” she told me over the phone, undoubtedly rolling her eyes. “Everyone knows it’s a pain in the butt.” Even the Barefoot Contessa herself, she reminded me, famously avoids the time-consuming task (“Nobody wants to make puff pastry!”).

Sources indicate that those words set me free. Once I realized that I could outsource my puff pastry, and the source of my Thanksgiving stress, I was finally able to relax and enjoy the holiday. Folks take pride in their Turkey Day dishes, as they should, but there’s nothing wrong with accepting a little help.

In the hopes of encouraging you to lighten your load, my colleague Bettina Makalintal and I asked some of the coolest people we know in the food industry what they prefer to outsource for Thanksgiving, from smoked hams to appetizers, in order to keep their holiday stress-free.

It has been revealed that “There is a single premade item that I purchase for Thanksgiving: a smallish in-house smoked ham from The Meat Hook. It’s a sort of whatever part of the Thursday meal — I make a banging turkey, which commands most of the attention. But! The ham has become a key player during what my family calls Leftover Sandwich Weekend. Having an extra piece of protein mitigates any concerns about not having enough turkey left over. “I outsource pies because I don’t especially enjoy making them… or eating them!”— Laila Gohar, food-based conceptual designer, artist, and co-founder of Gohar World.

So while I have a couple really simple apps I’ll put out if there are no volunteers, I much prefer having a friend or family member bring their favorite wedge of cheese and crackers, or [crossing fingers] bacon-wrapped dates. Here is one of my simple go-tos (it’s also in my Smitten Kitchen Every Day cookbook): herb-and-garlic baked Camembert. I’d still prefer if someone else can prep it; I don’t mind heating it up.” — Deb Perelman, cookbook author and recipe developer behind Smitten Kitchen.

Tiny Grains of Sand Act as Cosmic Speedometers for Alien Winds

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1001 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Weâve managed to take high-resolution orbital images of many worlds across our solar system, and many of them with an atmosphere have one feature in common - sand dunes.
  • According to recent reports, earth and Mars, the two most commonly thought of planets with sand dunes, arenât the only ones.
  • Understanding why this is important requires looking at how wind actually moves sand in the first place.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Weâve managed to take high-resolution orbital images of many worlds across our solar system, and many of them with an atmosphere have one feature in common - sand dunes. Scientists have been using the size and orientation of these dunes for decades to act like a weather vane, figuring out which way the wind blows on these other worlds. Unfortunately, weather vanes arenât good at telling the full windy story - they canât tell you how fast the wind is going. However, according to a newly introduced paper published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences by researchers at Stanford, sand dunes can.

According to recent reports, earth and Mars, the two most commonly thought of planets with sand dunes, arenât the only ones. Weâve also seen them on Venus, Titan, and, surprisingly, Comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko. Each is made up of different materials, but all share a crucial characteristic - their âsandâ consists of small grains of similar particles, which could be blown around by wind.

Understanding why this is important requires looking at how wind actually moves sand in the first place. When air is moving across a dune, individual grains stay stationary until the wind itself reaches a critical speed known as the transport threshold. Once it rises above that, the grains begin bouncing across the ground in a movement known as saltation. Each time a grain crashes back to the surface, it kicks up other surrounding grains into the air, creating a self-sustaining cascade of moving sand.

Fraser talks about whether Martian dust storms are dangerous.

Sources indicate that what was unclear to scientists was whether these motions were primarily driven by violent dust storms that were relatively rare, or moderate winds which are much more common on the other worlds where dunes have been seen. It might seem counter-intuitive that a comet would have âwindâ, but a 2017 study showed that the âripplesâ ESAâs Rosetta probe found on the comet's surface were created by localized vapor flows caused by extreme day-night temperature cycling.

Recent findings suggest that solving the mystery of what type of wind causes these shifting sands was the focus of the paper. Lead author M. Colin Marvin, a PhD student in the Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences at Stanford, collected wind speed data and detailed grain-size measurements from twenty-four different dune fields spread all over the world. From the Coral Pink Sand Dunes State Park in Utah to the ancient, hundred-meter-tall dunes in the Namib Sand Sea in Namibia, the researchers found a remarkable similarity.

Across every terrestrial site, the most sand was moved when the wind was slightly above the speed required to start moving it. And, crucially, the same relationship also held on a Maritan sand dune. The process didnât require the odd violent gale to get sand moving, just every day wind speeds common throughout the globe. For example, a dune made of sand 0.2 mm across (about the width of two pieces of paper) is mostly moved by winds blowing at only 26 kilometers per hour 10 meters above the ground.

Fraser talks about the Dragonfly mission, which will land next to dunes on Titan.

With that data set in hand, the researchers then turned to simulations. Using a tool called ReSCAL, they grew virtual dunes from flat sand beds using different wind speeds. As part of that process, the team confirmed that, as long as a world has plenty of loosely bound grains of sand and winds that grow rarer as they grow stronger, dunes will largely be formed by the wind speeds that correspond directly to the grain sizes that compose them.

Despite the challenges of finding individual sand grain size from orbit, this technique is useful on more than just Earth. Curiosity has already drilled into the Stimson formation, a layer of sandstone that used to be a windblown dune billions of years ago. Another upcoming interplanetary mission â Dragonfly â is expected to touch down on the surface of Titan, where there are dunes of hydrocarbons, sometime in the 2030s.

In a recent development, combining the grain size measurements from these missions with the math laid out in the new paper will provide scientists with a rough indication of the history of wind speed in the area. There will also undoubtedly be other missions to other dune-ridden planets - Venus comes to mind as a potential target. And from now on, scientists will be able to read a major part of a worldâs geological history directly written into its sand.

Stanford - Scientists discover sand dunes can reveal wind speeds on Earth and beyond.

#65822. This is the First Time Astronomers Have Seen One of These Stellar Mergers

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1854 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Universetoday ↗ Open Full Page

This is the First Time Astronomers Have Seen One of These Stellar Mergers

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1854 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Binary stars are common in the Milky Way.
  • Astronomers know that in some situations, binary stars share common envelopes (CEs).
  • It all begins with common envelope evolution (CEE), a critical stage in the evolution of binary stars.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Binary stars are common in the Milky Way. Up to 40% Milky Way stars are binaries, though there's a lack of absolute certainty. Sirius, which is the brightest star in the night sky, is actually a binary star.

Astronomers know that in some situations, binary stars share common envelopes (CEs). It means that a body of gas surrounds both stars, but the gas doesn't move with either one separately. These envelopes are transitory; the CE creates drag that slowly draws the planets together, sometimes ending in an explosion. But it's difficult to predict when that will happen, and when astronomers should observe a particular binary star to learn more about it.

It all begins with common envelope evolution (CEE), a critical stage in the evolution of binary stars. No two stars in a binary system are the same. One evolves and puffs up, overflowing its Roche lobe. Mass begins to pile up on its companion. That process becomes unstable, and the two stars become engulfed in a common envelope of gas.

It has been revealed that the common envelope exerts a powerful drag on both stars, and they're drawn closer together. After that, the CE is ejected and the two stars are left behind in a compact binary. The pair of tightly-bound stars can remain as a compact binary, or they can merge and cause an explosion, called a luminous red nova(LRN). Whether they merge and explode, or whether they remain as a compact binary, depends on how soon the CE is ejected. If the CE isn't dissipated soon enough, the continued drag forces the stars closer together until they merge and erupt.

Sources indicate that this simple graphic reveals how common envelopes evolve. At first, on star fills its Roche lobe. Then, the companion is engulfed and both stars orbit one another inside the common envelope. Then, either the common envelope is ejected and the stars remain as a binary, or the common envelope isn't ejected, and the stars are forced to merge. Image Credit: By Philip D. Hall - Own work, CC BY-SA 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/page/55287112.

According to recent reports, this is a coarse overview of the process. Astronomers know it can happen, and they'd like to learn more about it. But they need to observe them, and that's tough to do. Not only are they difficult to predict, but they're also relatively rare.

Observations with the JWST and other telescopes have found one CE situation where a main sequence star a little less massive than the Sun spiralled into its CE partner, a puffy supergiant star, and erupted as a LRN. This happened in our neighbouring galaxy, Andromeda. The observations and details are in new research in Nature titled "An inspiral of a star inside a common envelope with its giant companion." The first author is Viraj Karambelkar, a NASA Hubble Fellow at Columbia University in New York.

"The formation of compact stellar binaries requires rapid orbital tightening of their progenitor binary stars," the authors write. "This is theorized to happen via Common Envelope Evolution, when the stars orbit in a loosely bound, shared convective envelope, triggering an inspiral due to frictional drag.".

In a recent development, that much is known by astrophysical theory. But nobody's observed the end of the inspiral and the eruption yet. "Here, we present observations of ATâ2025abao, a transient eruption in the Andromeda Galaxy," the researchers write.

Astronomers have lots of observations of ATâ2025abao with multiple telescopes because it's been experiencing brightness changes for several years and has attracted their attention. They've become familiar with ATâ2025abao and now simply refer to it as 'Bao'.

Recent findings suggest that âStellar mergers are very, very difficult to observe in real time because they are hard to predict,â remarked first author Karambelkar. âHowever, we noticed something unusual was going on in 2023 and continued to monitor the system to see what it would do. Then, in 2025, it erupted! Webb observed Bao only 47 days after the starsâ eruption peaked, the earliest ever follow-up of an event like this. The telescopeâs data helped us characterize what the system looked like before, during, and immediately after the merger, which is absolutely mind-blowing.â.

Recent findings suggest that stars in these situations orbit each other for thousands of years with little change, and that was true of ATâ2025abao. But once they contacted each other, things changed. Other stars in CEs take thousands of orbits before they merge. But this one was different from other CE binaries. The pair merged after only 7 orbits (about 7 years.).

Observations go back as far as 2018, and between then and early 2025, the star gradually brightened in optical light. After that, it gradually faded in optical light, but its infrared light continued to brighten. Then, in October 2025, it erupted. It brightened by 100 times in the r-band over a period 25 days, and its temperature jumped to about 8000 Kelvin. Then, for about 80 days it plateaued and cooled down to about 3000 Kelvin. The JWST observed it during this period, only 47 days after its peak.

âWe thought an outburst from a such an extended star would take years,â said co-author Nadia Blagorodnova, an associate professor at the University of Barcelona in Spain. âOne day, its brightness started rising and within a week, it peaked!â.

In a recent development, âWhen a companion star begins to interact with the outer surface of the primary star, it produces a subtle effect â a slow brightening, which we clearly saw in Baoâs data,â mentioned co-author Kishalay De, an assistant professor at Columbia University in New York. âAs the companion continues its orbit, it keeps peeling off the primary starâs outer layers, and that gas flows away into the surrounding space.â.

This was when the CEE began. The primary star engulfed the companion star in a common envelope, and drag stole its momentum, forcing it to spiral inward. This is when the JWST saw the destructive merger.

Recent findings suggest that this is the finding chart for AT 2025abao. It was captured by the Asiago 67/92cm Schmidt telescope on 7 November 2025, when the light was at is maximum. M 31's (Andromeda) spiral disk is just visible on the left of the image. The zoomed-in panel reveals the transient. Image Credit: Reguitti et al. A&A, 709, A25 (2026).

Industry observers note that since the transient has been in the watchful eyes of astronomers for so long, they have detailed spectroscopy from it. The SPHEREx near-infrared space observatory played an key role, catching the star in its survey. "In July 2025, the source was serendipitously observed during its rapid optical fading by the first sky survey of the SPHEREx mission, providing a precise glimpse of the stellar photosphere during this phase," the researchers state. That let them determine the masses of the stars, but only with some help from simulations.

Recent findings suggest that as in a lot of astronomy research, simulations played an key role here. In this research, the authors worked with different models of CEE until the outcome of one matched the JWST's detailed observations of the star and its surrounding dust, shed by the primary star over hundreds of years.

That work revealed that the primary was seven times more massive than the Sun, with a radius 350 times larger. It was also 18,000 times brighter than our star. âIt was an absolute beast of a star, completely outshining its companion in the data,â noted co-author Karel Temmink, a Ph.D. student at Radboud University in Nijmegen, Netherlands, who led the simulations.

The modelling also revealed the smaller star's true nature. It had only about 0.7 solar masses, one-tenth as massive as the other star. Its radius was much smaller and it was also much dimmer.

In a recent development, the astronomers called the pair Major Bao and Little Bao, and when Little Bao was engulfed, there was a massive explosion. Only more observations will reveal what the resulting star, now simply called Bao, looks like.

Industry observers note that these artist's illustrations help explain what happened with ATâ2025abao and its common envelope evolution. The first panel shows the quiescent phase, when the stars are surrounded by a common envelope. The brightness was consistent during this phase. The second panel shows the stars brightening in the precursor stage. The companion star experiences drag and begins to spiral toward the primary star. In the third panel, there's a sudden bright eruption, as the companion spiralled and the common envelope is ejected. The JWST observed this. Then, in the final panel, months after the eruption, gas from the starâs ejected envelope freely expanded at the poles, but not at the equator, where previous ejecta from the more massive star was concentrated. Image Credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Leah Hustak (STScI); Science: Viraj Karambelkar (Columbia).

"The 2025 eruption of ATâ2025abao displays the defining hallmarks of Luminous Red Novae, a class of transients established to arise from impulsive energy injection into a common envelope during the merger of a star with its companion," the authors write. But it's different from all other known LRN. It's progenitor is unambiguously an evolved AGB star with an extended convective envelope.

"In contrast, all known LRN progenitors have primary stars on the main sequence," the researchers explain. But classical CEE theory notes that the primary star should be an AGB star.

"Thus, ATâ2025abao provides the first view of a classical CEE progenitor system continuously monitored from its onset through its culmination," the authors explain.

Watching a common envelope evolution in real time like this is a first in astronomy. Astronomers have had to perform a sort of forensic astrophysical study of transients like this in other cases, trying to reconstruct what happened thousands or even millions of years ago. Even with powerful telescopes and computer simulations, and with detailed theoretical frameworks to guide their work, that's tough to do.

But this work opens a newly introduced window into CEE and how efficient it can be. And it's just in time to help with a potential flood of upcoming transient detections. Only a few dozen luminous red novae have been detected, but the Vera Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time will detect hundreds of them, possibly thousands. The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will also detect some LRN and CEE, but probably far fewer.

This work lays the foundation for understanding some of what those surveys will find. In a few years time, astronomers should have a much clearer understanding of common envelope evolution and luminous red novae.

"This end-to-end characterization using multi-survey observations demonstrates a path towards mapping the landscape of CEE outcomes with upcoming surveys," the authors write.

Industry News: Sound Waves From Sunspots Launch Fiery Plasma Jets Across the Sun

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1059 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It feels like every week for the past few months weâve been reporting on more research regarding the temperature difference between the Sunâs surface and its corona.
  • Industry observers note that the key to understanding this discrepancy, as weâve stated before, is energy transfer.
  • Dynamic fibrils are one such potential mechanism.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It feels like every week for the past few months weâve been reporting on more research regarding the temperature difference between the Sunâs surface and its corona. This week is no exception, with a new paper in The Astrophysical Journal detailing the formation and tracking of around two hundred jet-like bursts of plasma from the surface known as âdynamic fibrils.â They serve as another piece of the puzzle of why the Sunâs outer atmosphere is hundreds of times hotter than its surface.

Industry observers note that the key to understanding this discrepancy, as weâve stated before, is energy transfer. How does the pathway work for energy to come from the Sunâs interior to its upper atmosphere? At this point, the accepted answer seems to be through massive magnetic fields pushing plasma outwards and heating it intensely, but the nuances of the exact mechanism remain hazy.

Dynamic fibrils are one such potential mechanism. They are rhythmic jets erupting from the outer haloâknown as the penumbraâsurrounding a sunspot. But up until now we have had difficulty tracking where exactly they go, largely because the Sun is so bright it's hard to isolate individual tendrils from the overall burning mass of plasma.

Fraser attempts to answer why the Sun's corona is hotter than its surface.

To do so, Guotang Wu and Xiaoli Yan of the Yunnan Observatories at the Chinese Academy of Sciences combined data sources. They used the Upcoming Vacuum Solar Telescope, located in southwestern China, to monitor a sunspot in an active region of the Sun known as NOAA 13182. Crucially, they did so for just over an hour on January 10th, 2023, and took snapshots of the chromosphere â the middle layer between the Sunâs surface and its outer atmosphere â every 45 seconds. They then combined these ground observations with data from Chinaâs CHASE solar satellite and NASAâs Solar Dynamics Observatory, providing a multi-layered and multi-spectral view of this active sunspot.

Sources indicate that over that hour of observations, they catalogued 176 individual dynamic fibrils â jets of plasma that rise off the surface and into the Sunâs atmosphere. On average, they do so at a speed of 16 km/s, faster than the speed of sound in the surrounding plasma medium of the chromosphere. But eventually they slow down, falling back to the surface after an average lifespan of about 4.5 minutes. Even during that time, they manage to stretch on average 1,130 kilometers â roughly the distance from New York to Chicago.

So where do those jets come from in the first place? Sunspots are already famous for creating features known as ârunning penumbral wavesâ of compressed gas that move across the halo surrounding the sunspotâs core. According to math described in the paper, the rhythmic pulsing of the fibrils almost matches the five-minute cadence of the running penumbral waves in the sunspot. This, in turn, points to another underlying phenomena â magnetoacoustic waves.

Fraser talks about the highest resolution image ever taken of the Sun.

Sources indicate that under the surface of the Sun, hot convection cells of plasma constantly vibrate features known as âmagnetic flux tubesâ, creating low-frequency sound waves that leak upwards into the chromosphere. As the gas they are traversing gets thinner and thinner, they grow steeper and stronger until they âbreakâ in a similar manner to waves on a beach. However, these breaking waves are not like those of water â each breaking wave is accompanied by a miniature sonic boom known as a magnetoacoustic shock. These push the plasma residing in the chromosphere where they break, pushing chromospheric plasma upward to form dynamic fibrils.

Buried in the data there was a clear pattern of how much the orientation of these magnetic fields matters for the creation of fibrils. When the magnetic field lines point straight up, the plasma jets experience stronger deceleration and pulse at shorter intervals. Whereas when the fields lean more horizontally across the Sunâs surface, the fibrils decelerate more gently and pulse over longer periods. This confirmed a long-standing theory about how magnetic tilt affects solar sound waves.

Sources indicate that to tie all this back to the original theme â extreme coronal heating â observations from SDO revealed corresponding signatures in gas heated to hundreds of thousands or even millions of degrees. So, the plasma pushed up by those shockwaves doesnât just appear to fizzle out - it directly transfers energy into the corona itself, which aligns with what many of the recent papers on this topic have been proving in various ways.

According to recent reports, but weâre still not 100% sure of some of the nuances of how this complex magnetic dance actually works. That might have to wait for even bigger ground-based telescopes such as the Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope, which can resolve the magnetic threads inside these massive jets. But until then, we have an even clearer picture of how an acoustic hum plays a role in stoking the inferno of the Sunâs outer atmosphere.

CAS - Researchers Link Sunspot Dynamic Fibrils to Slow Magnetoacoustic Waves.

Industry observers note that G. Wu et al. - High-resolution Observations of Physical Properties of Dynamic Fibrils around a Sunspot.

UT - Tiny Solar Whirlpools May Hold the Secret to the Sunâs Blistering Corona.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sometimes astronomers search for one thing and find something completely different.
  • Their unexpected discovery is presented in a paper titled "WelopÅâai: A peculiar triple system 8 pc from the Sun," and it's published in Astronomy and Astrophysics.
  • âThe system should not exist.â - Professor Patrick Dufour, UniversitÃ© de MontrÃ©al.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sometimes astronomers search for one thing and find something completely different. There are many examples of that, from the Cosmic Microwave Background to Pulsars to Gamma-Ray Bursts. The same thing happened recently to researchers who were hunting for exoplanets. Instead of distant planets orbiting a distant star, they found an unusual triple star system in our stellar neighbourhood.

Their unexpected discovery is presented in a paper titled "WelopÅâai: A peculiar triple system 8 pc from the Sun," and it's published in Astronomy and Astrophysics. An international team of researchers made the discovery, and the lead author is Ãtienne Artigau. Artigau is from the Trottier Institute for Research on Exoplanets (IREx) at the UniversitÃ© de MontrÃ©al.

âThe system should not exist.â - Professor Patrick Dufour, UniversitÃ© de MontrÃ©al.

Recent findings suggest that âWe were actually looking for planets,â lead author Artigau mentioned in a press release. âInstead, we found something much more surprising.â.

IREx is the group behind Canada's contribution to the JWST, the FGS/NIRISS instrument. IREx's other instrumentation projects include the SPIRou and NIRPS high-precision infrared spectrographs, installed in Hawaiâi and Chile respectively, and the GPI imager on the Gemini-South telescope. This discovery began with the SPIRou (SpectroPolarimeter Infrared) instrument, which uses the radial velocity method to detect exoplanets tugging on their stars.

But in this case, instead of finding an exoplanet tugging on a star, they found another star tugging on a star.

"Serendipity has long played a key role in astronomy, offering insights into new phenomena," the researchers point out. "We report the serendipitous discovery of a white dwarf companion to the M4 V dwarf WelopÅâai Aa (IRAS 21500+5903) during a radial-velocity search for exoplanets with SPIRou," the authors write in their paper. "The system is located at 8.46 pc and forms a hierarchical triple with a more distant white dwarf, which has no known analogue within 30 pc.".

Astronomers have watched the M dwarf, named IRAS 21500+5903 (also called TYC 3980-1081-1 A), and known about its unusual radial velocity (RV) signal since 2019. In this work, the researchers used SPIRou to gather almost five years of RV data on the red dwarf. That data showed that the RV signal had a large amplitude, which was inconsistent with an exoplanet signal. Exoplanets produce small wobbles as they tug on their stars.

"The mid-M dwarf revealed a near-constant acceleration of approximately 5 m sâ1 dâ1 (â¼1800 m sâ1 yrâ1), a level inconsistent with a planetary companion: on a few-year orbit around a 0.42 Mâ star, even a Jupiter-mass planet would induce an acceleration of at most â¼40â130 m sâ1 yrâ1," the authors write.

That's math-speak for saying that the RV signal is up to 45 times stronger than a planet the mass of Jupiter could produce.

Industry observers note that this figure indicates the RV curve of WelopÅâai Aa from SPIRou observations spanning 4.8 yr, with the best-fit Keplerian model overplotted. The inset shows one week of observations, and shows how precise the measurements were. Image Credit: Artigau et al. A&A Volume 715, November 2026 A321.

Astronomers already knew that the M dwarf had a binary companion. It's a white dwarf, the massive dead core of a star that was once a main sequence star like our Sun. But that star is too far away to be responsible for the RV signal. Instead, another massive white dwarf was most likely close to the M dwarf.

According to recent reports, âThe objectâs unusual combination of high mass and dim light left only one plausible explanation: it was the remains of a dead star,â said co-author Charles-Antoine Parent, a Mastersâ student at the University of Montreal. âThe most likely explanation was a white dwarf, although a neutron star or even a black hole couldnât be ruled out.â.

To narrow it down, the researchers turned to the Gemini North Telescope and its âAlopeke instument. âAlopeke is a high-resolution imager that can eliminate distortion caused by Earth's atmosphere.

It has been revealed that âAlopeke revealed the nature of the third star in the system, showing that it was a second white dwarf that forms an inner pair. "This inner pair lies at a projected separation of 123.9 au (Pâ>â1000 yr) from a previously known white dwarf," the authors write.

Industry observers note that these panels show Alopeke observations in three different epochs, with yellow arrows showing the new white dwarf's position in December 2023 and 2024. It's more visible in some channels than others. The M dwarf is the central bright spot or region, it's shape distorted in the effort to highlight the white dwarf. Image Credit: Artigau et al. A&A Volume 715, November 2026 A321.

Determining the mass of a solitary white dwarf is challenging. There are billions of them in the galaxy, but precise mass measurements of them are very rare. Only a handful of masses have been determined for nearby white dwarfs. Determining their masses in binary stars is easier, and because the latest white dwarf interacts gravitationally with the red dwarf, the researchers could determine its mass dynamically, rather then depending on its brightness or its spectrum.

Recent findings suggest that they found that the newly introduced white dwarf companion has about 0.62 solar masses. "The dynamically determined mass of the inner white dwarf is one of only a handful of such measurements for white dwarfs within 20 pc, and the most precise, at the sub-percent (0.7%) level," the researchers explain.

The system has been named WelopÅâai, a Hawaiian word that combines welo (an inherited or family trait) and pÅâai (an orbit or encircling path), together evoking a âpath of family traits.â The primary red dwarf is designated WelopÅâai Aa, its newly discovered close white dwarf partner is WelopÅâai Ab, and the outer white dwarf is WelopÅâai B.

It has been revealed that this graphic indicates observations of the WelopÅÊ»ai triple-star system, located only 28 light-years from Earth. The image on the left shows the two components of the system: WelopÅÊ»ai A, a closely orbiting red dwarf and white dwarf pair, and WelopÅÊ»ai B, a second white dwarf much farther away. The image on the right is a close-up view of the inner pair, and it shows the faint white dwarf companion (Ab) that was detected with the Gemini North telescopeâs âAlopeke instrument. The overlaid curves illustrate the starsâ orbital paths. Image Credit: Pan-STARRS1/STScI/MAST (left); International Gemini Observatory/NSF.

Recent findings suggest that this system is very unusual, and rare. By determining its mass so accurately, the discovery will inform models of stellar evolution, something astrophysicists are always keen to improve.

âDiscoveries like this remind us that our own cosmic neighborhood still contains remarkable surprises.â - Ãtienne Artigau, IREx, University of Montreal.

The new white dwarf was once a main sequence star like our Sun. But since it's so close to the red dwarf, the pair most likely interacted gravitationally at earlier stages of the white dwarf's evolution. It's possible that the two were inside a common envelope at one point, a situation where an envelope of gas surrounds both stars. That often forces the stars to spiral inward and merge. That should have destroyed WelopÅÊ»ai A, the red dwarf. But it appears to be intact, which is surprising. Somehow it survived that disruptive, turbulent scenario and follows a stable orbit.

Sources indicate that âThe system should not exist,â indicates Prof. Patrick Dufour, white dwarf specialist at UniversitÃ© de MontrÃ©al and co-author of the study. âWe have no clean explanation for how it got here. That is the question driving our next observations.â.

It has been revealed that there are still some unexplained things about this system. The red dwarf is between 9 and 11 billion years old, yet is suprisingly metal-rich. Stars this old aren't expected to have such high metallicity. "Reproducing the metallicity would require the M dwarf to have captured roughly two-thirds of the metals, and almost none of the hydrogen or helium, ejected by the inner WDâs progenitor," the authors write, and there's no known mechanism that could do this.

"These puzzles, together with the still-open question of how the inner binary avoided a classical common-envelope in-spiral, identify WelopÅâai as a valuable benchmark for future work on binary-star pollution and tidal evolution," the authors write.

âDiscoveries like this remind us that our own cosmic neighborhood still contains remarkable surprises,â said Artigau. âEven when weâre searching for planets, our Universe often has something completely unexpected waiting for us!â.

Democrats mulling Iran war funding cutoff strategy

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tim Kaine, D-Va., talks with reporters in the Capitol on Sept.
  • A group of prominent Senate Democrats is pushing to use a must-pass spending bill to cut off funding for the Iran war, complicating the path toward a bipartisan deal for averting a partial government shutdown next month.
  • Tim Kaine, D-Va., remarked Thursday he is working on legislative language ending the war that he wants attached to the next continuing resolution that is needed by Dec.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., talks with reporters in the Capitol on Sept. 30. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

A group of prominent Senate Democrats is pushing to use a must-pass spending bill to cut off funding for the Iran war, complicating the path toward a bipartisan deal for averting a partial government shutdown next month.

Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., remarked Thursday he is working on legislative language ending the war that he wants attached to the next continuing resolution that is needed by Dec. 11, when current funding runs out.

It has been revealed that “I know it’s going to be my main push,” he remarked. “I have to work with colleagues to try to find some language that works. And I’m not there yet, but I’ve told everybody that’s an opportunity.”.

In a recent development, democratic Sens. Michael Bennet of Colorado, Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, Tammy Duckworth of Illinois and independent Bernie Sanders of Vermont released a statement Thursday that they would oppose any deal that does not include “language that restricts the Trump Administration from using appropriated funds to continue his war against Iran.”.

“When we vote on appropriations, we intend to fund the government and stop funds for this war,” the senators noted. “It is what the American people demand, and what they deserve.”.

It is unlikely that Republicans, who are in control of both chambers of Congress until January, not to mention the Oval Office beyond that, would agree to such a deal.

House Appropriations Chairman Tom Cole, R-Okla., remarked earlier this week that “a Republican Congress is not going to send bills to a Republican president that he's going to veto.”.

While ending the war is a top priority of Democrats as they take back power in the new Congress, insisting on doing so this year could lead to a Christmas-time partial government shutdown. If a shutdown starts after Dec. 11, it’s possible it would still be ongoing when Democrats take control of both chambers in January.

But some Democrats appeared to still be weighing how quickly to push for a cutoff of war funding.

Senate Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray, D-Wash, noted that whether or not Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth remains in his job, “we’re still going to have language stopping this war.”.

She was coy on whether that fight would take place on the anticipated continuing resolution in December or wait until next year when Democrats take back power, saying that lawmakers are “looking at all options.”.

Sources indicate that democrats are committed to ending the "reckless and costly war of choice in Iran," House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., stated Thursday. He deferred to House Appropriations ranking member Rosa DeLauro, D-Conn., "to see what’s possible in advance of Dec. 11" in talks with the other top appropriators.

"I don’t want to get out ahead of Congresswoman DeLauro, but House Democrats have uniformly opposed providing any additional money to Donald Trump’s war machine. to Pete Hegseth’s war machine, over in the Middle East," Jeffries noted.

It’s not clear how long a potential continuing resolution would last, and DeLauro stated earlier this week that she wants it to be as short as possible.

The Office of Management and Budget has not yet submitted “anomalies” — changes to the current spending levels to be included in the continuing resolution — to Congress.

It has been revealed that the administration is considering options including a stopgap bill that would run through March, sources familiar with the talks noted. But no decision on the timing covered by the anomalies has been made.

Aris Folley, Jacob Fulton and Michael Macagnone contributed to this report.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By the 1970s, scientists largely accepted the theory that the Universe was permeated by a dark, invisible mass that prevented galaxies from flying apart. While scientists had speculated about the existence of "Dark Matter" for years, it was the work of Vera C. Rubin that made it official. By the 1990s, deep field observations made by the venerable Hubble Space Telescope led scientists to theorize that there was a powerful cosmic force driving expansion, what would come to be known as "Dark Energy.".

Sources indicate that these two theories have become part of the predominantly accepted model of the Universe, known as the Lambda Cold Dark Matter (ÎCDM) model. However, alternative theories, like the Covarying Coupling Constants plus Tired Light (CCC+TL), still endure. Between 2025 and 2026, researchers at the University of Ottawa (go GeeGees!) tested the CCC+TL model against a range of important astronomical observations. The model passed these tests, challenging what we think we know about the Universe.

Recent findings suggest that the research was conducted by Rajendra Gupta, an Adjunct Professor in uOttawa's Department of Physics, and postdoctoral researcher Dr. Nikolaos Samaras. As they described, they tested the CCC+TL model against the predicted abundance of certain elements (hydrogen, helium, and other light elements) shortly after the Significant Bang, using cosmic-chronometer measurements. Their results are detailed in a paper published in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society.

Industry observers note that the cosmic Dark Ages refer to the first one billion years after the Significant Bang and before the formation of the first stars and galaxies. Credit: NASA.

While scientists have observed considerable indirect evidence for Dark Matter and Dark Energy (DM and DE), no direct detections have been made, despite decades of research. In addition, the ÎCDM model has faced challenges in recent years, as observations by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) revealed an abundance of mature galaxies in the early Universe. This has led to renewed interest in alternative theories such as Modified Newtonian Dynamics (MOND) and CCC+TL.

Sources indicate that the latter model suggests that what is usually attributed to DM and DE could instead come from evolving fundamental constants that govern how forces and particles interact. In particular, CCC+TL changes Einstein's field equations for General Relativity (which describes gravity) and the FriedmannâLemaÃ®tre (FL) equations that describe cosmic expansion (aka. the Hubble-LemaÃ®tre Constant). Moreover, it uses the ages of galaxies to estimate how fast the Universe has expanded over time. As Gupta summarized:.

According to recent reports, most emerging models explain only a limited set of observations. A new model must not conflict with the pillars of cosmology and astrophysics, and our findings meet that challenge, including the yet-to-be-published Cosmic Microwave Background challenge.

According to recent reports, for their simulations, Gupta and Samaras couldn't simply modify standard computer models; they had to develop CCC+TL-compliant equations and code. As they describe in their paper, the model's results agreed with several major observations. They further applied the model to the 175 galaxies in the SPARC database and found that it reproduced their rotational curves without dark matter. They also applied it to the famous Bullet Cluster, a pair of merging galaxy clusters from which Rubin derived much of the evidence for DM.

In this case, the extra gravitational effect predicted by the CCC+TL model was consistent with observations of the clusters, which the researchers consider an early proof of concept. Alongside Utkarsh Kumar, a postdoctoral researcher in observational cosmology at uOttawa, Gupta and Samara applied the model to observations of time dilation in supernovae. Their results are described in a separate study that is still pending review. In another study, Gupta proposes that observations attributed to DM and DE likely originated from covarying coupling constants.

According to recent reports, age comparison against redshift in CCC+TL and ÎCDM models. Credit: uOttawa/Gupta et al. (2026).

It has been revealed that in the standard model, the Universe was only about 300 million years old when the first stars and galaxies began forming, a period known as Cosmic Dawn. Under CCC+TL, the Universe would have been about 4.6 billion years old during this period, which would be long enough for the early galaxies observed by Webb to have formed and matured. In summary, the CCC+TL model suggests that we live in a Universe much older than 13.8 billion years, placing its age at around 26.7 billion years.

In a recent development, upcoming observations will offer additional opportunities to test this newly introduced model. For example, there's the General Observations (GO) GO 3293 GLIMPSE program, or the Gravitational Lensing and NIRCam IMaging Program to probe Early galaxy formation and Sources of reionization. This ultra-deep observation program will use the JWST's Near-Infrared Camera (NIRCam) and gravitational lensing from the Abell S1063 galaxy cluster to study early galaxy formation and cosmic reionization. Stated Gupta:.

In a recent development, impossible early galaxies become predictable galaxies. We predict that galaxies exist well beyond the distances the James Webb Space Telescope has reached. The success should encourage astronomers to take the new model seriously. It is challenging to understand and apply, but we believe it extends the physics of the Universe beyond ÎCDM limits.

Further Reading: University of Ottawa.

#65811. Complex Life on Earth May Not Have Appeared Without Tall Mountains
