Complex Life on Earth May Not Have Appeared Without Tall Mountains

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1291 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The more scientists learn about Earth, the more habitability appears to involve an almost kaleidoscopic array of variables and interactions.
  • New research suggests that another factor may come into play: mountains.
  • Their main claim is that mountains are critical because they increase the surface area exposed to weathering, and that makes crucial chemicals and nutrients available, as well as changing the chemistry of the oceans and the atmosphere.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The more scientists learn about Earth, the more habitability appears to involve an almost kaleidoscopic array of variables and interactions. Though our current search for potentially habitable worlds is mostly restricted to finding rocky planets with liquid water and atmospheres, it will have to advance well beyond that to bear fruit. Things like exoplanet plate tectonics to keep climates moderate, and stars with long, stable lifetimes that let life fluorish and evolve are factors in habitability.

New research suggests that another factor may come into play: mountains. The research is titled "Raising mountains for a habitable Earth," and it's published in Science Advances. The lead author is Dr. Matthijs Smit of the University of British Columbiaâs Department of Earth, Ocean and Atmospheric Sciences.

Their main claim is that mountains are critical because they increase the surface area exposed to weathering, and that makes crucial chemicals and nutrients available, as well as changing the chemistry of the oceans and the atmosphere. That, in turn, led to the eventual appearance of complex life.

"The formation of mountain belts (orogens) elevates rocks above sea level, making them available for chemical weathering and altering the composition of the atmosphere and oceans, which in turn control habitability," the authors write.

It has been revealed that K2 is the second tallest mountain in the world. The crust underneath it is some of the thickest in the world. Research shows that in Earth's past, the crust thickened in some places, leading to the growth of very tall mountains. Increased weathering from those mountains preceded the planet's episodes of oxygenation, and researchers hypothesize that episodic spurts of mountain growth enabled Earth's habitability, and the eventual appearance of complex life. Image Credit: By Zacharie Grossen - Own work, CC BY-SA 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/page/42469860.

According to recent reports, "Continental silicate weathering controls the oceanward flux of carbon and bioactive nutrients that limit marine primary productivity, thus exerting control on atmospheric chemistry, climate, and marine biomass and biodiversity," they explain. "The majority of the global terrigenous runoff derives from mountainous regions.".

The researchers focused on the last three billion years of Earth's history. They examined metamorphic rocks that were pushed deep underground by overlying tectonic plates. When mountains formed where plates collided, the mountains were able to reach much greater heights. That raised nutrient levels in the oceans, which helped photosynthesizing lifeforms oxygenate Earth's atmosphere.

In a recent development, âChanges that occurred deep in the Earth ultimately gave rise to much taller mountains over time, which may have made our planet habitable by providing the nutrients needed for life to form and flourish,â lead author Smit noted. âNutrients such as phosphorous are essential ingredients for life on our planet, but prior to three billion years ago, these elements were locked in the Earthâs crust and the oceans were quite nutrient-starved. All this changed when tall mountains started to develop.â.

According to recent reports, the research indicates that two periods of peak metamorphic pressure inside the planet, between 2.7 to 2.2 and 0.8 to 0.7 billion years ago, led to thicker crusts in mountain-forming regions, and that let taller mountains form. The growth of Earth's mountains spiked, and those orogenic growth spurts were synchronous with other notable changes on the planet.

Sources indicate that âThe first growth spurt may have led to the emergence of land on a large scale for the first time, while the second growth spurt thrust mountain ranges to enormous heights,â said co-author Dr. Douwe van Hinsbergen of Utrecht University, The Netherlands. âGiven such profound effects, mountains may well have played a far greater role in the creation of a habitable planet than previously assumed.â.

In a recent development, earth's atmospheric oxygen rose in distinct periods, and the most well-known and consequential one was the Great Oxygenation Event (GOE) from about 2.4 to 2.0 billion years ago. The researchers say that by the time the GOE occurred, Earth's mountains had grown substantially. They rose from near sea-level to about half the height of the modern-day Himalayas. Another distinct period of rising atmospheric oxygen was the Neoproterozoic Oxygen Event (NOE) from around 700 million to 500 million years ago. Mountain growth spiked at that time, too, according to the researchers. Various other atmospheric factors and oceanic factors related to habitability and complex life increased, too.

According to recent reports, this figure shows time on the x-axis and more other information throughout. Blue shows how atmospheric O2 pressure rose compared to modern levels, especially during the GOE and the NOE. Purple shows the rise of sulfur isotope diversity, a measure of biological sulfur metabolism over time, and grey shows the percentage of oceanic strontium that comes from continental mountain erosion. Green shows the rise of organisms capable of oxygenic photosynthesis. The snowflake symbols show Earth's main icehouse stages. Image Credit: Smit et al. Science Advances 13 Nov 2026 Vol 12, Problem 46.

The timing of these spurts of mountain growth coincided with the growth of crustal thickness in mountain belts. In these belts, the thickness of the upper accreted crust grows as plates collide. The first episode increased thickness from 30km to 60 km, and the second episode saw an increase to almost 90 km. âWe suspect that these increases are ultimately linked to the cooling of our planet,â Dr. Smit stated. âAs a result, the process that makes mountains changed, allowing mountains to grow taller.â.

"Causes for environmental upheaval culminating in the GOE and NOE have been sought in various external forcing mechanisms, such as increased runoff resulting from supercontinent breakup, enhanced weathering of basaltic rocks at low latitude, and a dwindling CO2 (carbon dioxide) flux from arc volcanism," the authors write. While the researchers agree that these are valid hypotheses, they also point out that they're transient. That doesn't match the "irreversible nature of global oxygenation," and other changes. They're also not restricted to periods preceding the GOE and NOE.

Recent findings suggest that the two episodes of crustal thickening and resulting spikes in mountain elevation and erosion are a better fit. "In contrast to all of these processes, the orogenic growth associated with tectonic revolutions R1 and R2 broadly coincide with the major periods of environmental upheaval in terms of their approximate timing, paucity, and irreversibility," the authors write.

It has been revealed that the researchers couldn't measure the height of long-gone mountains, but they were able to determine the density and thickness of ancient crust. Since crustal thickness and density correlate with mountain height, they could calculate the height of ancient mountains.

It has been revealed that earth's tallest mountains today, Mount Everest, K2 and Kangchenjunga, are almost certainly some of the tallest ever produced. They approach nine km above sea level, and the crust under them is about 80 km thick. That's twice as thick as other continents. They illustrate how crustal thickness generates tall mountains, and emphasize the hypothesis that mountain growth helped enable Earth's habitability.

Industry observers note that âItâs likely not a coincidence that life on Earth developed and diversified approximately during the same period that the two growth spurts occurred,â stated co-author Dr. Ellen Kooijman of the Swedish Museum of Natural History, Stockholm. âItâs exciting to think that mountain belts were once non-existent and that their development over the past three billion years may have driven the environmental and biological change that shaped our planet.â.

Space Entrepreneurs Should Look To 16th Century Spice Trade For Inspiration

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1096 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Despite all the hype about a new space economy, humanity has yet to reap much benefit offered by the prospect of offworld mining, manufacturing, or space tourism.
  • But historical precedent dictates that ventures into the unknown need to be driven by commerce to achieve profitability.
  • The idea was to circumvent the Silk Road from and drive the spice trade from overland camel caravans to large cargo-holding ships.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Despite all the hype about a new space economy, humanity has yet to reap much benefit offered by the prospect of offworld mining, manufacturing, or space tourism.

But historical precedent dictates that ventures into the unknown need to be driven by commerce to achieve profitability. Such was the case five centuries ago, when most of Western Europe was agog over the importation of precious spices from East Asia.

The idea was to circumvent the Silk Road from and drive the spice trade from overland camel caravans to large cargo-holding ships.

For centuries, camels had enabled trickles of spices such as cloves, nutmeg, and ginger to make their way into the kitchens of the high and mighty, be they landed gentry or royalty.

Cloves originally grew in the volcanic soils of only a handful of small islands in the northern Moluccas archipelago, author Lewis Dartnell notes in his 2019 book âOrigins: How the Earth Shaped Human History.â And the nutmeg tree appeared on only nine pinprick-sized islands --- the Bandas-further south, Dartnell writes.

Dried nutmeg. Credit: Wikipedia.

It has been revealed that but as early as the late 15th century and the Age of Columbus, middlemen had run up the cost of these rare spices to such a degree that Portugal and Spain, in particular, were in competition for a sea route to the Moluccas. That is, the Moluccan archipelago in what is now Indonesia.

The idea was to travel point to point by sea and weed out a multitude of middlemen along the long Silk Road --- mostly stretching overland from the Black Sea and Mediterranean through northern India to China.

Thus, Portuguese explorer Ferdinand Magellan had a novel idea.

Magellan, born into a family of minor nobility and modest possessions, had somehow convinced Spainâs King Charles V that it was possible to reach the eastern riches by traveling west, author Romeu Gaspar writes in his 2026 book âThe Revolution of Magellan: How 500-Year-Old Rocket Science Changed the World.â.

And even though Magellan tragically lost his life en route at least a remainder of his crew did circumnavigate the globe. In the process, they forever changed the course of history, commerce, and human exploration.

Dried spices were a lightweight, high-value, reasonably imperishable product with which to stuff a ship's hold on long voyages, John Keay writes in his 2005 book âThe Spice Route: A History.â The profits were huge; in 1515, the return on such cargo docked at Lisbon was 700 per cent, Keay notes.

Industry observers note that by 1520, the income from Portugalâs spice trade provided 40 percent of the Crownâs total revenue, Dartnell writes in his book. Spices eventually became so prized that in 1677, the Dutch swapped the island of Manhattan for the nutmeg-rich island of Run Palau, he notes.

A 21st century analogy to such commercial exploration might be if by the end of this century, space entrepreneurs were able to extract and then process rare minerals from the Moon or Mars or even accessible Main Belt asteroids. And then in a cost-efficient manner, reap the profits by bringing them back to Earth. Or at least low-Earth orbit.

Sources indicate that to that end, NASA Apollo 17 astronaut and geologist Harrison Jack Schmitt has long argued for Helium-3 mining on the Moon. But until someone fulfills the economics of making cislunar Space profitable human exploration of our solar system is likely to lag. That's because throughout history, scientific innovation usually goes hand in hand with someone's quest for a large profit margin.

A durable commercial reason for people to work in space could give human space science the transportation and infrastructure it needs, Ret. U.S. Brigadier Gen. Pete Worden, an astrophysicist, chairman of the Breakthrough Prize Foundation, and Laureate Professor at the University of Arizona in Tucson, told me via email.

Within the next fifty years at least, the future of scientific space exploration is arguably best served by robotic means rather than astronauts.

Iâd rely heavily on robots for science and give commercial companies a larger role in developing and operating human spaceflight systems, Worden, who directed NASA Ames Research Center from 2006 to 2015, told me via email. NASA should return to its roots in the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics (NACA) by emphasizing research and technology development that industry and scientists can build on, he notes.

Routine human sorties beyond low-earth orbit are key.

If commercial space transportation becomes routine, agencies such as the National Science Foundation (NSF) could support research that uses it, Worden argues.

Meanwhile, we are left with space programs that for decades have been hampered by both politics and economics and as a result, have limped along in fits and starts.

In a recent development, over the past 30 years, NASAâs plans for the Moon and Mars have had to survive changes in administrations, budgets, and priorities, states Worden. When a program needs agreement from too many people, it becomes harder to take sensible risks, he says.

If humanity can ever succeed in making forays beyond low Earth orbit that are commercially viable in the same way the 16th Century spice trade was profitable, then this upcoming ocean of space-time could be ours for the taking.

Industry News: Van Hollen announces bid for majority leader, but Schumer claims he has the votes

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., left, has unveiled a challenge to current Senate Minority Leader Charles Schumer, D-N.Y.
  • Chris Van Hollen revealed Thursday night that he would run for Senate majority leader, launching a challenge to Sen.
  • Recent findings suggest that van Hollen, a Maryland Democrat first elected to the Senate in 2016, served in leadership in the House and has been chairman of both the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., left, has unveiled a challenge to current Senate Minority Leader Charles Schumer, D-N.Y. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo).

Sen. Chris Van Hollen revealed Thursday night that he would run for Senate majority leader, launching a challenge to Sen. Charles E. Schumer of New York, the current Democratic leader.

Recent findings suggest that van Hollen, a Maryland Democrat first elected to the Senate in 2016, served in leadership in the House and has been chairman of both the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee. He has mentioned since the midterm elections he was listening to fellow Senate Democrats about the possibility of a run for the top job.

Sources indicate that “In this election, the American people called for change. They called for a change from Donald Trump’s disastrous policies but even bigger than that, a change from the status quo that isn’t working for working people,” Van Hollen said in a statement. “It’s now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need latest leadership. This is not about any one person – it’s about answering the call of the American people. That is why I’m running for Senate Majority Leader.”.

Schumer has already stated he has the votes needed to continue serving as the leader.

“I welcome any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead. I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished together — 55 seats and counting is an amazing result — and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader. I look forward to leading our new Democratic majority and delivering for the American people,” Schumer noted in a statement.

Schumer's supporters were quick to highlight the success at the ballot box in 2026, with the Democratic caucus potentially growing to 56 seats if former Rep. Mary Peltola prevails in Alaska.

“Chuck has outlined an aggressive strategy for the upcoming Democratic majority which is directly responsive to the message we heard from the voters, and he has the experience and unique mastery of the Senate process to make it happen,” Sen. Angus King, a Maine independent who caucuses with the Democrats, stated in a statement. “Why would you fire the manager when you just won the World Series?”.

In keeping with the World Series theme, Sen. Tammy Baldwin, D-Wis., echoed King with her own statement of support for Schumer.

“The Brewers just had a record season, and next year is not the time to change our management," Baldwin remarked. "The same is true in the Senate.”.

In an interview with MS NOW about his run, Van Hollen conceded that Schumer would be the favorite in the secret-ballot contest, which will take place in December.

It has been revealed that “Am I the underdog? Yes,” Van Hollen mentioned. “You’re talking about an incumbent who uses the power of incumbency to, you know, provide deals to people.”.

Industry observers note that van Hollen outlined legislative priorities including restoring Medicaid funding that Republicans cut in last year's budget reconciliation law and extending Affordable Care Act tax credits. But he suggested Democrats need to go further.

Recent findings suggest that "We need to extend tax credits for the Affordable Care Act, but we can’t stop there, right? We have a completely broken health care system. It’s become profits, not people. And so my view is, we also need in the first 100 days to make health care more affordable for tens of millions of people," Van Hollen said. "We need to immediately make it clear that nobody’s going to pay one penny to subsidize data centers. ... We need to make sure that we have a livable minimum wage.".

He also mentioned he would not take sides in contested Democratic primaries, and he would make sure the DSCC did not take money from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, or AIPAC.

Van Hollen's early backers include progressive Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, who emerged from a hotly contested Democratic primary in Michigan while the Senate Democratic political apparatus was backing Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich.

“In April, I was the first candidate in the country to call on Senator Chris Van Hollen to lead Senate Democrats, and I am proud to stand with him in his bid to become Senate Majority Leader,” El-Sayed mentioned in a statement. “Michiganders demand money out of politics, money in pockets, and Medicare for All. Sen. Chris Van Hollen offers both the courage to go toe-to-toe with the Trump administration to deliver for working people and the experience to maneuver the Senate caucus. It’s why he has my full support to lead our caucus.”.

Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

#65798. Latest Update: The next ice age may have begun 2,000 years ago, but humans cut it short

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1242 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: The next ice age may have begun 2,000 years ago, but humans cut it short

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1242 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Buried plants on Baffin Island reveal when a remnant of the Laurentide Ice Sheet began growing again and how human-caused warming reversed its advance.
  • About 2,000 years ago, the last remnant of the ice sheet that once covered much of Canada began growing again on Baffin Island.
  • It expanded in bursts, then began retreating around 1960 as warmer summers melted more ice than winters added.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Buried plants on Baffin Island reveal when a remnant of the Laurentide Ice Sheet began growing again and how human-caused warming reversed its advance.

About 2,000 years ago, the last remnant of the ice sheet that once covered much of Canada began growing again on Baffin Island.

It expanded in bursts, then began retreating around 1960 as warmer summers melted more ice than winters added.

The researchers argue that the regrowth marked the earliest stage of a newly introduced glaciation in North America, and that human-caused warming cut it short.

At the peak of the last glacial period, the Laurentide Ice Sheet covered much of Canada and reached into the northern United States.

“People always say that it disappeared, but that’s not true,” stated Nicolás Young, a geochemist at Columbia University’s Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory who led the study.

It has been revealed that what’s left of it is the Barnes Ice Cap, on the central plateau of Baffin Island in Nunavut. Its bedrock is low for the Canadian Arctic, only about 1,640 feet (500 meters) above sea level.

The ice has lasted this long because it is roughly 2,300 feet (700 meters) thick, enough to lift its surface to where snow survives the summer.

Young’s team wanted to know whether the ice cap had ever been smaller than it is today and then grown back. Gifford Miller of the University of Colorado Boulder was among the co-authors.

The answer matters beyond one ice cap, because models say glaciations over North America most likely begin on Baffin Island.

Recent findings suggest that the Barnes Ice Cap is frozen to the rock beneath it, so it doesn’t slide the way most glaciers do. Instead of grinding the ground as it spreads, it buries whatever is growing there and preserves it.

When the margin retreats, the moss and small plants it killed centuries ago come out of the ice.

Radiocarbon dating estimates when the plants died, giving researchers a way to date the ice’s advance.

Young’s team collected 88 of those plants at or near the 2022 ice edge. About 70% of them died around the year 1800, give or take 200 years. Those were the coldest summers of the Little Ice Age.

In a recent development, sixteen more came from a half-mile (800-meter) line running out from the ice edge. A drained lake there had let the margin retreat farther than anywhere else.

In an interview with Earth.com, Young said that result surprised the team.

The researchers hadn’t expected the ice cap to have been smaller than it is now at any point in the last several thousand years.

“This unique finding allowed us to unexpectedly use these plants to track the ice cap’s renewed expansion,” Young noted.

Industry observers note that the researchers also dated 35 boulders and bedrock surfaces around the ice cap. Rock that is open to the sky builds up a rare form of beryllium at a known rate.

The amount in a surface tells how long it has been uncovered.

All of the surfaces gave the same answer: the old ice sheet had retreated inside its 2022 position about 3,600 years ago.

The oldest plants along the half-mile line died around the year 1000, so the ice was already advancing by then.

To fill the gap, the team turned to 186 radiocarbon dates from plants under smaller ice caps on the same plateau. Not one of those dates is older than the Common Era.

The authors read that as the moment, roughly 2,000 years ago, when the summer snowline dropped onto the plateau and ice began to build up across it.

So the Laurentide reached its smallest size between about 3,000 and 2,000 years ago and then started to grow. The authors count that reversal as the start of the next glaciation.

The ice advanced in pulses during cold spells and was nearing its largest modern extent by about 1800.

By 1960 the growth had stopped. Aerial photographs show the margin retreating from about 1961, and the ice cap has since given up between 650 and 2,600 feet (200 and 800 meters) of ground.

Snow also survives the summer on less and less of it.

Industry observers note that around 1960, about 35% of its surface was high enough for snow to last through the summer. By the early 2000s only 3% was, and since 2010 none of it has been.

There is no longer any part of the ice cap where snow can pile up and turn into ice.

Recent findings suggest that summer temperatures have been climbing since the late 1700s, and since the early 1960s warmer summers account for almost all of the ice cap’s losses. Those summers track the greenhouse gases people have added to the air.

In a recent development, between 1750 and 1850, the total rose by only about 12 parts per million of carbon dioxide equivalent. By 1960 it had risen another 50, and by 2024 another 138.

“The expansion and retreat of ice sheets has been one of Earth’s most consistent patterns over the last 2.6 million years,” Young told Earth.com.

According to recent reports, about 2,000 years ago, he said, the Laurentide was starting its next phase of expansion, as it should have. Then greenhouse gases ended that expansion in the middle of the 20th century.

In the 1970s, some climate scientists argued that a fresh ice age was coming, and the idea got a famous airing in Newsweek.

Sources indicate that young said those scientists were essentially correct, even if the media twisted the story. “We did just barely start the next glaciation, but they didn’t know it at the time,” he said.

Behind that growth was a slow decline in summer sunlight at high northern latitudes, the orbital rhythm that paces ice ages.

It has been revealed that greenhouse gases did rise over those thousands of years, by about 20 parts per million. The authors found that was too small to overcome the cooling.

According to recent reports, computer models suggest the next glaciation will not begin for thousands of years. But those models usually define its start as the point where upcoming ice sheets hold enough ice to lower the sea by about 10 feet (3 meters) or more.

Young’s team noted that would miss the earlier stage of ice growth that his team considers the start of a glaciation.

A 2025 study built from ocean sediments and Earth’s orbit estimated that the first regrowth of ice in this interglacial would come somewhere in the last 1,800 years or so. The plants on Baffin Island agree.

In a recent development, what the record can’t yet say is exactly when the regrowth began. The plants that would date it are still under the ice, and only continued retreat will bring them out.

The dates so far are archived at the NSF Arctic Data Center.

Young said models of the ice cap’s future have it disappearing completely within the next few hundred years.

Asked what happens once the last piece of the Laurentide is gone, Young said another glaciation is unlikely anytime soon.

“Given the amount of greenhouse gases that are in the atmosphere and that we continue to pump, the next glaciation is a long way off,” he said.

The full study was published in the journal Science.

Calls for Nvidia probes, new chip export limits intensify

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • “The bottom line is we need to understand the magnitude of this with respect to Chinese intelligence, possible chip diversion,” noted Rep.
  • The resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on Thursday did little to quell bipartisan demands from Congress for an accounting of potential national security fallout from his affair with an alleged Chinese spy and talk of adding tougher chip export controls to the annual defense authorization bill.
  • Industry observers note that huang admitted on Sunday to having an affair, and reports say that it was with Alice Huang, an executive at Singaporean tech organization and Nvidia customer Megaspeed, whom the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“The bottom line is we need to understand the magnitude of this with respect to Chinese intelligence, possible chip diversion,” noted Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., seen above. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo).

The resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on Thursday did little to quell bipartisan demands from Congress for an accounting of potential national security fallout from his affair with an alleged Chinese spy and talk of adding tougher chip export controls to the annual defense authorization bill.

Industry observers note that huang admitted on Sunday to having an affair, and reports say that it was with Alice Huang, an executive at Singaporean tech organization and Nvidia customer Megaspeed, whom the U.S. government believes spied for China, according to recent reports. The Newly introduced York Times and Reuters reported he also had affairs with two Nvidia employees.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., told reporters Thursday that he supports the Senate investigating Huang’s potential influence on U.S. artificial intelligence and chip policy.

“I think that it would make sense because of the… nature of the association… and the governments and the national security interests we were talking about here,” Thune said, though he said he thought it would be “wrong” to make assumptions about how close Huang’s relationship with President Donald Trump has been.

Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., echoed the need for lawmakers to delve into the scandal, saying in a post on X that “Congress must demand answers.”.

Recent findings suggest that “The Trump administration must also answer for what it did once it learned about Mr. Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. Were government officials told not to investigate because of Trump’s relationship with Mr. Huang? What did Trump know when he personally invited Mr. Huang aboard Air Force One?” Schumer wrote, referring to the president having invited Huang to accompany him to China in May.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., noted at a press conference that Reps. Gregory W. Meeks, D-N.Y., and Jim Himes, D-Conn., the ranking members of the Foreign Affairs and Intelligence committees, respectively, are leading Democrats’ efforts to “get to the bottom of what has happened.”.

“We need a classified briefing made available to members of Congress as it relates to the Nvidia situation,” Jeffries said. “And to the extent that our national security has been compromised, the American people deserve answers, and we're going to work to make sure that happens.”.

The investigations look likely to begin before control of Congress changes hands in January.

In a recent development, rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., who chairs the House select China committee, told reporters that his panel, along with House Foreign Affairs and Intelligence, are in negotiations with Huang to find a date for his testimony before Congress.

“The bottom line is we need to understand the magnitude of this with respect to Chinese intelligence, possible chip diversion,” Moolenaar stated. “What ways is Chinese intelligence influencing his perspective, his perspective influencing national security policy?”.

Last week, the chairs of the three committees sent a letter to Huang requesting that he appear at a joint closed-door briefing. Moolenaar mentioned that if Huang does not agree to a date, the committees will subpoena him.

Late Thursday, he joined with House Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast, R-Fla., and House Intelligence Chairman Rick Crawford, R-Ark., in sending a new letter to Huang seeking a closed-door transcribed interview on Dec. 1. They also wrote to Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter seeking a similar interview on Dec. 2. Separately, Mast wrote to Jeffrey Kessler, the Commerce Department undersecretary for industry and security, seeking his appearance at a committee hearing on Dec. 3.

Industry observers note that moolenaar also said that Congress needs to understand what privileged information Chinese intelligence may have gained access to through Huang and how they may have tried to influence U.S. policy.

According to recent reports, “We need to have strong safeguards when it comes to our technology and export controls,” Moolenaar mentioned. “And [Huang has] been one of the strongest proponents for not having export controls. This shines a whole new light on that discussion.”.

In a recent development, also late Thursday, Senate Banking Chairman Tim Scott, R-S.C.,  sent a letter to Huang calling on him to appear at a Dec. 3 committee hearing and another letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify at a Dec. 10 hearing "regarding recent public reports about NVIDIA and the Department of Commerce's role that raises national security concerns.".

A proposed manager’s amendment to the Senate's fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act bill (S 4784) contains several possibilities for those safeguards, including requirements for chip security mechanisms that would allow for verification if semiconductors are diverted to countries of concern and a ban on exporting certain very powerful chips to those countries. The House NDAA does not contain similar language.

However, House Armed Services Chair Mike D. Rogers, D-Ala., is open to the restrictions. He told reporters Wednesday that he “would like to see” semiconductor export controls in the NDAA, but that the Huang scandal had not changed his position.

Democratic Caucus Vice Chair Ted Lieu, D-Calif., told reporters on Thursday that after reports that the federal government had been aware of Huang’s affair with the alleged spy, the administration should have shared the information with Congress.

“The administration needs to be investigated for hiding this information from Congress and the American people,” he noted.

Lieu also suggested that Nvidia’s reported donation to the White House ballroom project influenced the Trump administration’s decision to allow the export of some powerful Nvidia chips to China.

Sources indicate that “There is no reason to do that. That hurts our national security, and we have an opportunity right now to fix that in the upcoming National Defense Authorization,” Lieu noted.

Sources indicate that mast said the Huang revelations could give upcoming momentum to including chip export rules in the NDAA. He also said that his “directive” on the issue came “straight from the admin” and informed his objectives on the committee.

“Don't let chips be smuggled to China. Make sure that American companies get to buy them first,” Mast said. “Make sure that the machines that make them don't get sold to them, even though it's the Dutch that make the machines. Make sure that they can't access it remotely.”.

Mast’s committee has advanced many of those priorities, including some of the language included in the NDAA.

In March, the committee on a unanimous vote advanced legislation known as the Chip Security Act, which would require chip security mechanisms to verify that certain semiconductors subject to export controls aren’t diverted to countries of concern, including China and Iran.

The committee also advanced bills to require the Bureau of Industry and Security and the State Department to work with allied suppliers of semiconductor manufacturing equipment to implement export controls to prevent the equipment from going to countries of concern, and to require licenses for the export of certain powerful chips, including banning exporting certain chips to countries of concern.

Versions of all three bills are included in the Senate manager’s amendment to the NDAA.

The scandal has also led to calls for oversight of the Commerce Department, including Secretary Howard Lutnick, for its handling of export policy and actions around Huang.

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., told reporters Thursday that Lutnick and Nvidia should testify “before Democrats can set the narrative.”.

Sources indicate that “If there is some reasonable basis or some way to discount some of the reporting, the best way to do it is request a meeting with us and give us a briefing,” Tillis remarked. “Because otherwise, you're going to get what you get in an oversight hearing in about six weeks.”.

Asked about oversight of the Commerce Department’s role in the Huang scandal, Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, who chairs the Commerce Committee, said his panel “has engaged in vigorous oversight under Republican presidents and Democrat presidents and will continue to be [engaged in it].”.

According to recent reports, on Wednesday, prior to Huang’s resignation, Senate Banking ranking member Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Sen. Chris Coons, D-Del., sent a letter to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller requesting that they “preserve all documents, communications, records, and other materials regarding the export of NVIDIA’s advanced AI chips to China or to entities that may divert such chips to China.”.

“This incident raises significant concerns about the federal government’s ability to effectively enforce our export controls and protect our national security,” the senators wrote.

Recent findings suggest that in a statement Thursday, Warren mentioned that Huang’s resignation did not “absolve” him of the need to answer questions. She also called for the passage of stricter export controls, including the bill to ban the export of certain chips to China.

Sen. Michael Bennet, D-Colo., sent his own letter on Wednesday to Lutnick, Rubio, Attorney General Todd Blanche and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, requesting an update on the Justice Department’s investigation into Megaspeed for possibly diverting U.S. chips to China.

According to recent reports, savannah Behrmann, John M. Donnelly, Jacob Fulton and David Jordan contributed to this report.

Eleven pregnant garter snakes went to a San Francisco zoo, and now 62 of their young are in the wild

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1209 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 62 endangered San Francisco garter snakes born at the San Francisco Zoo were released in San Mateo County this fall, the first head-start release.
  • Geological Survey biologists caught 11 pregnant San Francisco garter snakes on the San Mateo County coast, in a preserve run by the Midpeninsula Regional Open Space District (Midpen).
  • They took them to the San Francisco Zoo, where the snakes gave birth later that year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

62 endangered San Francisco garter snakes born at the San Francisco Zoo were released in San Mateo County this fall, the first head-start release.

In spring 2025, U.S. Geological Survey biologists caught 11 pregnant San Francisco garter snakes on the San Mateo County coast, in a preserve run by the Midpeninsula Regional Open Space District (Midpen).

They took them to the San Francisco Zoo, where the snakes gave birth later that year.

In a recent development, after giving birth, the mothers were returned to the wild, the zoo claims. The zoo’s team raised their young until they were big enough to be released.

On November 10, 2026, the San Francisco Zoo & Gardens said 62 of those zoo-born garter snakes had been released this fall in San Mateo County.

Recent findings suggest that it was the first release under a head-starting program for the endangered subspecies. The announcement does not say how many are still alive.

The San Francisco garter snake (Thamnophis sirtalis tetrataenia) is a subspecies of the common garter snake. The zoo says it lives only in San Mateo County and a small corner of Santa Cruz County.

It has been revealed that the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service describes red on the top of the head, a greenish-blue or blue belly, a wide pale stripe down the back and red and black stripes on the sides.

Sources indicate that A major loss of habitat came after World War II. In the 1940s, the sag ponds along Skyline Boulevard, small ponds in low spots along a fault line, held hundreds of the snakes.

By the 1960s, nearly all of those ponds had been drained and built over, according to the Golden Gate National Parks Conservancy.

It has been revealed that the snake went onto the first federal endangered species list on March 11, 1967, six years before the Endangered Species Act of 1973. The zoo estimates that a couple thousand remain in the wild today.

Federal biologists blame illegal collection, construction, drought and saltwater in coastal ponds. Bullfrogs and largemouth bass are on the list too, because they eat the snakes and their prey.

That prey includes threatened California red-legged frogs, which the snakes rely on for food, the zoo claims.

Since 2004, the conservancy and the National Park Service have restored and enhanced 33 acres (13 hectares) of wetland, grassland and coastal scrub for the snakes, according to Midpen’s 2025 release. The work added newly introduced ponds for breeding habitat.

In a recent development, garter snakes give birth to live young instead of laying eggs. In this subspecies, birth comes in July or August. A litter can hold 6 to 35 babies, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service species profile says.

After the 11 females arrived, the team scanned them with ultrasound. The early scans indicated that a goal of 80 to 120 live babies was feasible, Midpen reported in September 2025.

Later that month, the district estimated that the zoo’s Conservation Team was raising about 120 newborns.

The zoo had practice with the species. Its staff bred San Francisco garter snakes in the 1990s to work out how to keep them.

From 2005, they developed care protocols with the San Diego Zoo on housing, diet, growth tracking and parasite checks, Midpen remarked in 2025.

Rochelle Stiles, the zoo’s director of field conservation, described the goal of the zoo’s snake rearing work.

“By providing these young snakes with a safe environment during their most vulnerable stage of life, we’re giving them a stronger start in the wild,” she noted.

Head-starting works that way. The young are fed and sheltered until they are big enough to handle predators and competition for food, a method that also saved an endangered wallaby population in Australia.

Each snake born at the zoo had a genetic test before it left, and the results set its destination. About one-third went back to the area where its mother had been caught.

The rest went to several other populations that were short on both snakes and genetic variety. Isolated groups slowly lose diversity, the same problem behind a proposed genetic rescue for Lassen red foxes in northern California.

According to recent reports, disease data mattered too. Laura Patterson coordinates amphibian and reptile conservation statewide for the California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW).

She noted a CDFW survey for snake fungal disease, an emerging disease found in many wild snakes, “aided in the selection process.”.

The partners will not name the release sites. The zoo mentioned secrecy protects the snakes from collectors, cars and disease.

Midpen biologist Karine Tokatlian also commented on the release. “Seeing these young snakes returning to the wild represents years of research, collaboration, habitat restoration and careful conservation work,” she noted.

Removal from the endangered list requires at least 10 viable, self-sustaining breeding populations. Each one needs at least 200 snakes.

It has been revealed that U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) ecologists had already tested the idea on a computer. In a 2023 paper in PLOS ONE, a team led by Jonathan Rose of the USGS Western Ecological Research Center simulated upcoming populations started with newborns, juveniles, adults or a mix.

Sources indicate that head-started juveniles gave those populations the best chance of lasting. Releases would have to continue for at least 15 years to keep the risk of near-extinction low, the model noted.

Sources indicate that raising juveniles also takes fewer adults away from the donor site. Justin Sloan, acting deputy field supervisor at the USFWS Sacramento office, credited research, genetic testing, habitat work and specialized care.

Ariel Starr, a Midpen wildlife ecologist, looked beyond this one subspecies.

“The success of this project and the associated research will not only benefit the San Francisco garter snake but will also hopefully inform the recovery of many imperiled reptile species,” she stated.

The November announcement gives no survival rate for the 62. It also does not say how long they had been out when it was posted.

Survival is low even for snakes born in the wild. One study found only 2 percent of females born live to age 5, according to the USFWS.

There is also a gap between the 2025 estimate of about 120 newborns and the 62 released. The zoo did not explain it.

Industry observers note that the 2023 model focused on snake demography. Its authors wrote that the genetics of the donor, captive and released snakes would also be a major concern for any reintroduction blueprint.

Industry observers note that more than 130 garter snakes were born at the zoo in 2026. They are being raised for a second round of releases in 2027. Monitoring of both rounds will show whether the populations at the sites grow.

Rachel Townsend, a National Park Service wildlife biologist, put the first round in proportion. “Releasing these snakes is a significant moment, but it is one step of many in a much larger recovery effort,” she said.

The mothers are back in the wild. This fall, 62 of their young were let go at sites the partners will not name.

The information was obtained from the San Francisco Zoo & Gardens.

At Dior’s First Spa in Venice, Old Glamour Gets the Hi-Tech Treatment

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The buzz of the Venice Film Festival has only just died down, when I step out of a Riva boat that bobs at the berth of the Hotel Cipriani Venice on Giudecca Island.
  • Venice’s links with Dior go back to 1951 when the French couture brand’s eponymous founder fell in love with the city after attending the Ball of the Century costume party at the Palazzo Labia, hosted by art collector Charles de Beistegui.
  • Sophia Loren and Julia Roberts are just a few of the starry names to have stayed at this classic hotel, which rolled out its upcoming spa in July 2026 as part of ongoing renovations led by New York architect Peter Marino.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The buzz of the Venice Film Festival has only just died down, when I step out of a Riva boat that bobs at the berth of the Hotel Cipriani Venice on Giudecca Island. I’m excited but also exhausted after spending the previous ten days on several long-haul flights, and I fear it’s beginning to affect my conversational skills—and my collagen levels. Luckily, I’m not here to attend a premiere or hop between Biennale events. I'm here to experience Cipriani's newly opened Dior Spa, the fashion house's first in Venice.

Venice’s links with Dior go back to 1951 when the French couture brand’s eponymous founder fell in love with the city after attending the Ball of the Century costume party at the Palazzo Labia, hosted by art collector Charles de Beistegui.

The views from my suite's private terrace.

A welcome Dior takeover on Cip's ground floor.

Sophia Loren and Julia Roberts are just a few of the starry names to have stayed at this classic hotel, which rolled out its upcoming spa in July 2026 as part of ongoing renovations led by New York architect Peter Marino. The cream and pastel palette channels an 18th-century Venetian Rococo spirit, with elegant mid-century Italian stucco and terrazzo flooring. Science-driven skincare nerds tend to believe that fashion houses can’t run beauty departments worthy of their approval, but Dior has the potential to persuade them otherwise. Many luxury spas are often either visually stunning temples that offer underwhelming treatments, or medically-driven centers that leave you glowing but feeling as if you’re in a hospital. Dior combines the best of both worlds, recalling an old-school glamour while deploying higher-tech treatments that aren’t geared towards “maxxing” but aim for clients to look and feel their best in a tranquil environment.

The Dior Spa's La Collection Privée island.

One of the Dior Spa's Murano chandeliers.

After spending the morning in Murano watching the world’s most talented glassblowers at work, I head down to the spa’s marbled entrance where a Murano chandelier dangles above a centerpiece table festooned with beautiful bottles of parfums from Dior’s La Collection Privée, including Tobacolore and, my favorite fragrance, La Colle Noire. I’m handed a rose infusion before slipping into cloud-soft Dior slippers and waiting outside my treatment room for one of the signature treatments, which include Le Théâtre Corporal, a four-handed, Ayurvedic-inspired massage (which couples can do together), and the Golden Aura hydrafacial. But I’m here for what feels like the most apt option in a city famed for its masked balls: the Mascarade facial.

Setting up for a canalside Dior masterclass.

Industry observers note that developed by the brand’s global skincare ambassador, Hadda Akrim, the Mascarade aims to regenerate the skin and soothe the mind. I’m in need of it now that my circadian rhythm is disrupted after back-to-back flights, cabin pressure and changing time zones. The treatment is more than just a facial: it involves 90 minutes of drainage, rebalancing, and re-boosting with the help of devices that encourage the nutrients being massaged into your skin to sink deeper. Firstly, I lie on the treatment table to receive an abdominal massage, which rebalances my nervous system (the gut is our second brain, after all) and restores my inner harmony to maximize my radiance.

Next, ultrasound waves are applied across my face to improve the skin’s elasticity and circulation, followed by microcurrent muscle stimulation during which I literally feel my cells awakening. The procedure soothes my mind so much I fall into a contented sleep. It’s all designed to boost my complexion’s glow—and it works. Dior’s global spa director, Olivier Hahn, told me he’s most proud of the sonic component of the spa offering, which does its job by calming me down without me even noticing.

A heavenly breakfast in my top-floor suite.

The best kind of antioxidants at Oro restaurant.

Recent findings suggest that I wake up for the next stage of the treatment, a technical jaw massage, which the facialist carries out to counteract my nighttime teeth-grinding. She then places cryogenic stones over a cooling mask to firm, drain, and reoxygenate my skin. It’s a perfect way to re-enter the world, cognitively and physically. I feel snatched as I sip coffee by the pool after the treatment. The Mascarade facial is great for a morning-after depuffing, but, given the OMGs I receive from fellow spa-goers, I conclude that it’s also perfect for an evening out. I head out into the Venetian night with nothing but a touch of mascara and a post-facial luminosity.

Feeling like a kid on Christmas morning, the staff sent me on my way with a bag of the Dior Prestige products to keep up my skincare routine back home. The ingredients are mainly organic, something I hadn’t expected. In the same way that historic French vineyards downplay their organic practices for fear of alienating clients disdainful of natural wines, Dior also keeps its products' natural roots on the down low. It all comes as a pleasant surprise and further cements this spa’s authority in the world of regenerative beauty therapy.

Breaking: Grand Canyon hotels reopen 81 days after a deadly flood, echoing a 1966 disaster

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Grand Canyon's South Rim hotels reopen November 20 after an August flash flood cut off their water.
  • For the first time since the end of August, visitors can book a hotel room on the South Rim of the Grand Canyon again.
  • On Friday, November 20, the South Rim’s hotels reopened to overnight guests, including El Tovar, which has stood on the edge of the canyon since 1905.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grand Canyon's South Rim hotels reopen November 20 after an August flash flood cut off their water. In 1966, a flood wrecked 40% of the same pipeline project.

For the first time since the end of August, visitors can book a hotel room on the South Rim of the Grand Canyon again.

On Friday, November 20, the South Rim’s hotels reopened to overnight guests, including El Tovar, which has stood on the edge of the canyon since 1905.

It has been revealed that they had been closed for 81 days. A flash flood on August 29 tore through Bright Angel Canyon, killed two hikers and badly damaged the pipeline that carries water to the South Rim.

According to recent reports, it was not the first time. In 1966, while that same pipeline was being built, a flood destroyed or carried off about 40% of the project, according to the National Park Service.

The park announced on November 18 that six South Rim lodges would reopen on November 20: El Tovar Hotel, Thunderbird Lodge, Kachina Lodge, Bright Angel Lodge and Maswik Lodge, along with Yavapai Lodge, which is operated by Delaware North.

On the same day, the park moved from Stage 4 to Stage 3 water conservation measures, which it called an important milestone in the restoration of South Rim water services.

Food and drink services will resume gradually, and the park is asking visitors to check its website for dining hours.

Conserving water is still important. Guests, visitors and residents are asked to take shorter showers, turn off faucets when they are not in use and avoid unnecessary water use.

Recent findings suggest that the flash flood hit Bright Angel Canyon and the Phantom Ranch area at about 2:30 p.m. on August 29. By the next morning, 62 people had been evacuated from Phantom Ranch and the lower North Kaibab Trail.

Nearly all of the footbridges over Bright Angel Creek were destroyed.

It has been revealed that metal structures and debris washed into the Colorado River, which was closed to river traffic. In steep terrain, heavy rain can trigger flash floods in mountain rivers faster than expected.

Two hikers from Granbury, Texas, John Giusti, 46, and Brent Rosenkranz, 42, died in the flood.

A member of their hiking group was reported missing, and the park stated in its September 8 enhancement that one person remained unaccounted for.

The flood badly damaged the Transcanyon Waterline, a 12½-mile pipeline built in the 1960s.

It carries water from Roaring Springs, on the North Rim side, down through the canyon and up to the South Rim, where it supplies drinking water and fire protection for every facility, including more than 800 historic buildings.

The park’s drinking water comes from a single spring connected to more than 6 miles of caves.

About 40% of the old pipeline between the Phantom Ranch area and the North Rim was damaged, and the water intakes at Bright Angel Creek and Roaring Springs were hit hard.

On August 31, the park stopped all overnight stays at its hotels, including Phantom Ranch, and the South Rim began living on stored water.

The park stayed open for day visits. When it announced the closure, it stated South Rim food and drink services, the Grand Canyon Clinic and the post office would remain open, some with reduced hours, while campers could only dry camp.

On September 16, a second flash flood damaged a temporary water intake that crews were building at Bright Angel Creek.

No one was hurt, but crews had to work out what repairs were needed and how the damage would affect the timeline.

On September 19, the park said it expected to start pumping water from the creek to a new treatment plant by November 16, and it was working on an agreement to haul about 200,000 gallons of water a day to keep its tanks from running low.

At the time, the South Rim was using about 137,000 gallons a day.

By November 18, the park said water services to the South Rim were being restored, which allowed the hotels to reopen two days later.

The pipeline itself was born out of a water problem. From 1901 to 1932, the Santa Fe railroad brought drinking water to the South Rim by train every day, and the trains came back as needed until the late 1960s.

In the summer of 1961, a water train of 20 cars carried about 204,000 gallons.

Construction of the Transcanyon Waterline began in January 1965, using 6-inch and 8-inch aluminum pipe. Most of the equipment was designed specifically for the project, and the rest of the work was done by hand.

A year later, the project was nearly finished when what the park calls a 1,000-year flood struck.

Fifteen inches of rain fell on the inner canyon, and the water carried away trees, boulders and sections of new pipe.

A survey after the flood found that about 40% of the project was destroyed or missing. The cost rose from $2 million to $5 million, and construction resumed in late 1967.

The flood’s high-water mark is still recorded on the walls of the Phantom Ranch Ranger Station.

Sources indicate that the old line was built to last about 30 years and has been in service for more than 50. Since 2010, it has suffered over 85 major breaks.

A single repair often costs more than $25,000, and crews can reach the inner canyon only by trail or helicopter.

It has been revealed that breaks had closed the hotels before. In December 2025, after three significant breaks since late October, the park suspended overnight stays on December 6 and reopened the lodges on December 17.

In 2023, the park began a $208 million project to replace the pipeline and modernize the water system.

The upcoming pipeline on the south side of the canyon was not damaged by either flood this year, and before August 29 the park was just over a month away from starting to use it.

Some inner canyon trails reopened in late October, including the South Kaibab Trail below the Tipoff and the River Trail.

But the Black Bridge, the Silver Bridge, Phantom Ranch and the entire North Kaibab Trail remained closed, and the park warned that water would stay off at Mile-and-a-Half and Three-Mile Resthouses and at Havasupai Gardens for the rest of the winter.

Hikers must carry all their water and a way to filter or treat it.

According to recent reports, el Tovar, a National Historic Landmark since 1987, was built from local limestone and Oregon pine for nearly $250,000. The hotel, which has 78 rooms, is once again taking guests.

The park states water conservation remains vital as operations resume, and that the patience of residents, visitors and businesses during the emergency helped it keep essential services running.

The information was obtained from the National Park Service’s releases on the reopening of South Rim lodging, the August 29 flash flood, the recovery plan, the projected water dates, the August 31 hotel closure, the two hikers who died, the second flash flood, the trail reopenings and the December 2025 hotel reopening, its pages on the Transcanyon Waterline and its history, and its page on El Tovar Hotel.

When it comes to keeping your house clean, a reliable vacuum is a must. Vacuums are the quickest and easiest way to tackle dust bunnies, stubborn pet hair, and debris that collect in hidden corners. But not just any vacuum will do.

Finding the right vacuum is often overwhelming when you’re faced with sifting through dozens of upright models, robot vacuums, and more. A vacuum is a big investment, and an uninformed purchase often leads to disappointment if your choice turns out to be too heavy, too cumbersome, or not powerful enough. Plus, you want to pay for features you need without overspending on extras you’ll never use.

In this guide, we considered upright, cordless, canister, and robotic options from trusted brands, and evaluated them based on research and rigorous testing. We broke down key factors related to functionality, features, and maintenance to help you find the best vacuum, whether you need a pet-friendly option, one that’s powerful enough to clean up after kids, or a budget-friendly model.

More Home Appliances: Best Vacuums for Hardwood Floors • Best Dryers • Best Clothes Steamers.

Industry observers note that to find the best vacuums for every home, we first gathered a lineup of models across a range of brands, price points, and features. We deliberately chose a mix of canister, upright, stick, and robot vacuums to help ensure our selections accommodate different living situations, flooring types, and cleaning needs.

We focused on criteria like performance, ease of use, and versatility. For meaningful results, we ran each vacuum through a series of real-world tests to simulate common messes they’d be likely to come across in everyday life. We tried them on multiple surfaces like low-pile carpet, thick shag rugs, hardwood flooring, and bare concrete, seeing how well the vacuum adjusted to different demands. This also helped us assess suction power and how well the brush roll adapted to each surface type.

For debris, we chose materials that mimic typical household spills, like crumbled potato chips, popcorn, coffee, and cereal. The different weights and sizes of rubbish gave us a realistic view of how effectively the vacuum could remove the mess.

Recent findings suggest that we also conducted similar tests with the handheld portions and attachments of these vacuums, using crevice tools and motorized brushes on couch cushions, on upholstery, and in tight corners. We noted how easy the tools were to maneuver, and whether they still packed enough power even when detached from the main unit.

By running each vacuum through comprehensive tests, we were able to get a clear picture of their real-world performance, so we could find dependable models for everyday cleaning.

I love using an upright vacuum for heavy-duty cleaning, and the AZ2002 packs the punch you need for tackling messes on carpets, couches, and floors. This model has two brushes: a soft roller brush and a foam-paddled brush. These work in tandem to increase contact with flooring and rugs, and I think that gives the vacuum a significant boost compared to models with just one traditional brush roll. The AZ2002 successfully picked up cat litter, dirt, and crumbs on a textured area rug.

All the cleaning modes are accessible right on the handle, so I was able to swiftly transition between carpet and laminate flooring without having to stop my cleaning session. The LED headlights brought attention to any dirt and gunk I missed during my initial swipes, too.

Industry observers note that the AZ2002 also easily converts from an upright to a motorized canister vacuum. I especially liked using this functionality with the powered pet brush for cleaning couch cushions, so I didn’t have to haul the entire vacuum around. The hose and stick attachments extend to clean crevices and curtains, which I normally wouldn’t be able to reach.

The vacuum is on the heavier side, weighing a little over 16 pounds, but because it functions as a canister vac, I'm not too upset about sacrificing a little portability.

Full Shark AZ2002 Vertex Powered Lift-Away Upright Vacuum Review.

Recent findings suggest that you don’t get a ton of newly introduced tech with the Rocket, but I’ve found that it performs well on multiple surfaces. It also stores easily, and doesn’t require any hands-on effort emptying a bag or figuring out how to pair the appliance with a compatible app.

Full Shark HV301 Rocket Ultra-Light Corded Stick Vacuum Review.

Sources indicate that the hose is long, which I found helpful because I didn’t have to lug the entire vacuum around as I cleaned. The floor head light helped illuminate dirt better, too.

Sources indicate that another useful feature is the docking station. Once our tester was finished cleaning, he locked the vacuum back onto the base, and it automatically suctioned collected dirt, hair, and dust out of the main dustbin. This doesn’t entirely offset the small dustbin capacity on the vacuum itself, but it’s nice not having to manually empty the receptacle after every clean.

Full Shark PowerDetect Cordless Stick Vacuum Review.

Industry observers note that we have several roundups of vacuums, including cordless stick models and robots. This guide is dedicated to the top overall vacuums we’ve tested, but there are still a few other units worth considering depending on your cleaning needs.

In a recent development, miele Guard L1: This canister vacuum offers convenience and power for cleaning different floor types. The Classic C1 Turbo Team we recommend above comes with a powered carpet brush, while the L1 does not. It does have longer cable reach and an illuminated display, but the C1 is the better, more affordable selection if you have a mix of surface types in your home.

Industry observers note that shark PowerDetect: This is a buy-up version of the Shark PowerDetect Speed we recommend above. It comes with the same flexible hinge for cleaning under furniture and several intuitive features, including automatic suction adjustment and a cleaner head with LED lights for illuminating dirt. With the regular PowerDetect, you get 10 more minutes of run time and one more level of detection (the vacuum can tell when it’s in a corner or up against a wall and ramp up the suction accordingly). But you get more bang for your buck with the Speed.

Many vacuums are available in both corded and cordless models. Corded vacuums offer unlimited run time, but require a nearby outlet. Cordless or battery-powered models are convenient to use, as you can just pick them up and start cleaning, but they have a limited runtime.

The best option for you depends on how you like to clean—do you vacuum your whole house in one go? If so, go for a corded model. Or do you normally clean one room at a time? Then a cordless option might work just fine for your needs.

According to recent reports, different vacuums are better suited for cleaning hard floors or carpeting, and some feature heads that raise or lower to meet the height of the surface you’re vacuuming. If you have a combination of flooring types, you may want to look for a vacuum with multiple heads and attachments, too.

In a recent development, vacuum brush rolls, or “beater bars,” come in several different styles, and each is made for specific cleaning tasks and flooring. The most common types you’ll see are bristle, soft, and tangle-free. Bristle rolls are designed with stiff, nylon bristles that are ideal for thick carpets because they lift dirt effectively. They are less optimal on delicate surfaces as their harsh structure causes scratches or other damage.

For hardwood floors, or homes with a mix of surfaces, a vacuum with a soft roll brush is what you need. They’re gentle yet efficient, picking up fine particles without scattering. Tangle-free is best for pet owners, since they resist hair wrapping and are easier to maintain.

Some of today’s vacuums feature dual brush rolls, or have detachable vacuum heads for adjusting to different situations.

Capacity refers to how much dust, dirt, and grime the vacuum can hold before the dustbin needs emptying. Bigger capacities are better for larger homes or heavy-duty cleaning, while smaller dustbins are better for compact spaces or low-lift tasks. Upright vacuums typically have a dustbin capacity of 0.75 liters or more, while stick vacs only hold a couple of quarts at a time.

Maneuverability determines how easily the vacuum navigates around furniture, corners, and other obstacles. Features like swivel steering, lightweight builds, and sturdy wheels all contribute to better control. Typically, vacuums with bigger capacity are more difficult to maneuver around, usually due to a combination of size and weight. Striking the right balance between capacity and maneuverability will help you find a vacuum that’s both efficient and easy to handle.

The suction power of vacuums is commonly measured in Pascals (Pa), a unit that gauges pressure, but some brands—including Dyson—list airwatts, or the watts used by the vacuum to move a unit of air through its nozzle, instead. Not all vacuums have their suction power listed, but when comparing different models, keep in mind that high Pa or airwatts equates to more suction power.

In a recent development, vacuums vary widely in price ranging from as little as $20 to $1,000 or more. Budget-friendly vacuums tend to have less powerful suction and fewer features, and if it’s a cordless model, its battery life will likely be shorter. Premium vacuums, on the other hand, typically have an ergonomic design that’s more comfortable to operate for longer periods, and their suction power is often noticeably better.

While it’s certainly tempting to give up vacuuming all together, a robot vacuum generally isn’t going to be sufficient to keep your home clean. These vacuums are designed for light-duty cleaning, and they simply can’t match the suction power of a full-size vacuum, especially on carpeting. You might be able to get away with using just a robot vacuum if you have a small home, no pets, and solely hard floors, but I think you’d still find yourself needing another vacuum to clean up occasional messes.

If you have pets, you know that pet hair wreaks havoc on a vacuum. A few passes over a dirty rug, and all of a sudden there’s a wad of hair wrapped around the brush roll, forcing you to stop and untangle it. To avoid problems like this, I highly recommend vacuums designed for pet hair. These models often have anti-tangle brush rolls and good filters, ensuring they capture all the dirt and dander that your furry friends bring into your home.

While often neglected, vacuum cleaner maintenance is key to keeping your machine running properly and ensuring it will last for years to come. You’ll want to make sure you’re emptying the bag or dustbin as often as recommended, as well as washing or replacing filters. Periodically cleaning the brush roll improves suction power, too.

Some vacuums are easier to maintain than others, and you’ll want to be honest with yourself about how much maintenance you’re willing to do—otherwise, your expensive tool might break sooner than expected.

In her free time you can likely find her trading trinkets at an EDM festival, searching for hidden gems at thrift stores, or cuddling with her two cats.

#65791. What to know about kratom and its powerful derivatives

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1282 w)
📖 Baca
