18 Family Resorts That Go Above and Beyond for Those With Babies and Toddlers

📅 13 Apr 2022 | ⏱️ 20 min read (4027 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that I've traveled to some pretty far-flung places, but nothing could have prepared me for the logistical circus of vacationing with a baby.
  • Recent findings suggest that the best resorts for infants and toddlers also understand that keeping littles happy isn’t a one-size-fits-all proposition.
  • Recent findings suggest that that kind of thoughtfulness is what sets the properties on this list apart.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that I've traveled to some pretty far-flung places, but nothing could have prepared me for the logistical circus of vacationing with a baby. Four years and 30 countries later, my son Julian has taught me a thing or two about what makes a resort genuinely welcoming to its littlest guests. For starters, there’s a massive difference between a hotel that hands your kid a coloring book at check-in and one that has anticipated the thousands of little things that can make or break a family vacation.

Recent findings suggest that the best resorts for infants and toddlers also understand that keeping littles happy isn’t a one-size-fits-all proposition. A baby might need a quiet nursery and a reliable nanny; a three-year-old might be thrilled to feed goats on an Austrian farm, explore a Japanese forest, or make plaster casts of lion tracks in the Kalahari. And parents? Sometimes we just want to eat dinner without having to negotiate with a tiny inquisitor.

Recent findings suggest that that kind of thoughtfulness is what sets the properties on this list apart. I’ve seen it firsthand at more than half a dozen of them, where the greatest luxury wasn’t necessarily the thread count or the size of the swimming pool, but getting to enjoy a five-star vacation instead of merely financing one for your offspring. Read on for the best resorts for infants and toddlers.

Location: Savusavu, FijiPrice: From $1,136 per night.

According to recent reports, jet lag aside, this is one of the rare luxury resorts where traveling with a child feels not just doable, but deeply supported. Every family with a child under five is assigned two dedicated nannies—one for daytime adventures, one for evenings—so parents can book a snorkeling trip with the resident marine biologist or linger over a blissfully kid-free dinner. When my son and I arrived in 2024—the first international stop on our 88-day, 14-country trip—it took me all of four minutes to abandon any guilt I had about dropping him off. His nanny was warm, attentive, and completely unfazed by toddlers being toddlers; she whisked him away for glass-bottom boat rides, hermit crab hunts, and splashes in the resort’s “mushroom-cascade” wading pool.

It has been revealed that parents of even younger children will appreciate the made-to-order purées and unlimited milk supply; nurseries stocked with infant cots, toys, and baby baths; and daily laundry service and disposable diapers for sale in the on-site boutique. Following a spring 2026 renovation, the resort now has five two-bedroom bures (a traditional Fijian hut or cabin), giving families more room to spread out. The Bula Club—essentially a resort within a resort—has a sun-safe junior pool with a waterslide, trampoline, and tricycles.

Check Availability at Hotels.com.

Location: Flamands Beach, St. BartsPrice: From $805 per night.

With 61 rooms, suites, and villas, Cheval Blanc is one of the glammest maisons on an island full of glammy maisons. The inn has even partnered with high-end Parisian baby accessories brand Baudou to spoil its style-conscious guests. Cots are dressed in the finest linens, and rooms include a changing table with a diaper basket and baby care products, a rattan high chair with a cushioned seat, baby-friendly crockery, and a hand-stitched bib embroidered with seahorses and stars. Wee beach towels and a selection of beach toys are available for afternoon romps on Flamands, one of the prettiest powder-white beaches in St. Barts. At the new Le Carrousel play space, children ages 3 to 12 can climb aboard an imaginary exploration vessel, tumble into a coconut-themed ball pit, and discover the island’s Arawak history through interactive storytelling. Come mealtime, they can indulge in made-to-order baby purées prepared by the in-house culinary team. Upon request, a professional photographer can be brought to the premises to document your family trip.

Check Availability at Michelin Guide.

Location: West End, AnguillaPrice: From $725 per night.

Industry observers note that toddlers are greeted with custom Anguilla-themed stuffies, pint-sized bathrobes, and slippers at this upscale resort on Anguilla’s West End, where accommodations range from contemporary-chic guest rooms to five-bedroom beachfront villas, some with private pools and kitchens. Wherever you rest your head, expect kids to squeal when they catch a glimpse of the iguanas that freely roam the property. The zero-entry Bamboo Pool has mini loungers for infants; other five-star amenities include complimentary cribs, strollers, car seats, bottle sterilizers, baby tubs, Le Petit Prince toiletries, SlumberPods, and organic puréed baby food on the room service menu. A refreshed splash pad offers another place for little ones to cool off, while children five and under eat free from the kids menu throughout the resort. Also notable: American Airlines operates year-round nonstop flights from Miami, while AnguillAir offers seasonal service from Boston, Newark, and Baltimore, so families no longer have to hitch a ride over from St. Maarten.

Check Availability at Booking.com.

Location: Karatu, TanzaniaPrice: From $518 per adult per night, including full board.

It has been revealed that after a long-haul flight with a toddler, Gibb’s Farm feels like an exhale. Set on 80 acres of organic gardens and coffee groves on the forested outer slopes of the Ngorongoro Crater, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, the property is an ideal place to begin or end a safari. My son was only 20 months old when we stayed here, but we happily spent hours roaming the gardens, chasing chickens, and learning how to milk cows. The farm’s one-bedroom cottages—many decorated with pieces from Gibb’s unique artist-in-residence program—are ideal for families, offering private terraces, outdoor showers, and enough breathing room for mid-tantrum resets.

In a recent development, there’s no kids club, but toddlers are warmly embraced here. The staff arranged a private game drive for us so we could move at Julian’s pace, stopping for snack breaks and diaper changes as needed. In the crater—home to one of the densest populations of large mammals in Africa—we saw lions, hippos, warthogs, wildebeest, and flamingos, but it was the dazzle of zebras milling around our vehicle that most delighted my son. Back on the farm, little ones can collect eggs, feed the pigs, wander among the coffee shrubs, splash in the pool, or learn about the music and customs of the local Iraqw tribe through hands-on cultural activities.

Check Availability at Go2Africa.

Location: Palm Beach, FloridaPrice: From $890 per night.

In a recent development, florida is a perennially popular destination for young families, and no resort rolls out the red carpet for babies better than the Breakers Palm Beach. Founded in 1896, the luxury hotel has a private beach and four oceanfront pools, including a zero-entry one designed specifically for youngsters. There’s also a 4,500-square-foot playground with slides, tunnels, and bridges, plus the latest Seaside Family Entertainment Center, a beachfront hub with a dedicated Toddler Cove, arts and crafts, and interactive games. Cribs, infant baths, bottle warmers, and strollers are available upon request, as is the childproofing of guest rooms, which involves padding perilously edged furniture, covering electrical sockets, and removing trash bags from cans. Bicycles with baby seats and children’s bikes are available to rent, as are private poolside bungalows with a dedicated concierge standing by, ready to fetch popsicles and pool toys at a moment’s notice. Other big wins for tiny visitors: poolside spin art, Build-A-Bear workshops, and daily children’s programming.

Check Availability at Booking.com.

Location: Punta Cana, Dominican RepublicPrice: From $850 per night.

In a recent development, for parents seeking a more home-like environment, the multi-bedroom villas at this secluded Relais & Chateaux property offer spacious living rooms, full kitchens, and private pools. Staff arrange scavenger hunts and arts and crafts hours; for an additional $325, parents can reserve the VIBabies package. This comes with two hours of complimentary babysitting plus a host of handy gear—including a portable crib (with turndown service!), a changing table, diapers, a bottle warmer, a baby monitor, an infant tub, pool alarms, a Baby Einstein play table, a 4moms MamaRoo baby swing, and a basket of kid-approved snacks and juices. For fun in the sun, Eden Roc will throw in a pop-up beach playpen, swim nappies, and sun protection gear (a bucket hat, colored sunglasses, Nivea sun lotion, and aloe vera gel) for use at the sandy beach and artificial lagoon.

Check Availability at Booking.com.

Location: Nuevo Nayarit, MexicoPrice: From $454 per adult per night.

According to recent reports, families vacationing at this AAA Five Diamond resort on the Riviera Nayarit are assigned a baby concierge who coordinates all meals and nanny services. Whatever gear you don’t want to drag from home—crib, stroller, baby tub and toiletries, bottle brush and sterilizer, pacifier, floaties—the team can arrange for on-site, all complimentary. Parents checking in with infants also receive a sleep guide developed with pediatric sleep consultant Rachael Shepard-Ohta of Hey Sleepy Baby, with tips for managing time zone changes and maintaining bedtime routines on the road. The kids club is stocked with books, blocks, and a play kitchen; parents may additionally request a crib mobile, rattle, or teether for use in the room.

Some suites have private plunge pools, but the hotel jewel is the triple-tiered, multi-temperature infinity pool. Mini cabanas await down at the beach, along with hooded baby towels and fresh-squeezed juice. Young spa-goers can opt for a gentle sunrise massage soundtracked by Mozart or a chocolate explosion face mask, then strike a pose with mom or dad during a baby yoga class. Executive chef Guillaume Morancé and his team prepare gourmet purées to challenge young palates (think white fish with celery, leeks, and mushroom) at every meal. The resort even offers a Mi Primer Fiesta package for celebrating a baby's first birthday, complete with piñatas and foam.

Check Availability at Booking.com.

Location: Koh Yao Yai, ThailandPrice: From $308 per night.

Recent findings suggest that set on one of the Andaman’s last unspoiled islands—reachable only by boat and blissfully free of traffic—this resort feels worlds away from the party throngs on Phuket and Krabi. When Julian and I visited in 2024, it was during a vintage sidecar tour through rubber plantations and rice fields that I realized how special this island really is: no honking, no rush, just villagers waving as you pass. The accommodations were a slam dunk too: Family suites with bunk beds and tipi play tents come stocked with baby tubs, bottle warmers, sterilizers, baby chairs, and toys. The Grand Family Suite ups the ante with a chocolate treasure box at check-in, while all families with children receive a treasure map. Ground-floor suites open directly onto the resort’s enormous family pool, while infants and early swimmers have dedicated splash zones and shallow areas. As a bonus, the staff truly adores kids—one affable pool attendant peeled off his socks and shoes and joined my son on the slides when he saw how happy it made him.

In a recent development, pristine beach and pools aside, the resort is home to southern Thailand’s largest kids club, featuring climbing walls, a dance stage, and an epic ball pit. Parents can join kids under six for Junior Explorer activities like kite making, batik painting, and sandcastle building, or arrange a family excursion to go island-hopping by longtail boat. For something even more tailored, little ones can try Muay Thai lessons, aerial yoga, or beach fishing with locals.

Check Availability at Booking.com.

Location: Beaver Creek, ColoradoPrice: From $275 per night.

Recent findings suggest that ask anyone who has ever attempted skiing with a toddler—it takes an act of Congress just to get them into a snowsuit. What saved my sanity at Park Hyatt Beaver Creek was that the slopes were, quite literally, outside our front door. This 189-room, chateau-style property is one of only two true ski-in, ski-out hotels at the base of Beaver Creek Mountain Resort, and that convenience is priceless. I could bundle up my kiddo and hand him off to a private instructor at the Ski and Snowboard School (open to ages three and up) and know that he was in eternally patient hands. After his post-lesson hot chocolates, Julian burned off whatever energy he had left in the family game room and the snowy outdoor playground before splashing around in the heated pool and hot tubs—his preferred après.

Check Availability at Booking.com.

Location: Palm Desert, CaliforniaPrice: From $348 per night, including a $45 daily resort fee.

This 450-acre resort features a 12,000-square-foot arcade—the largest hotel arcade in California. This is great news for kids of all ages who are stoked to play retro video games, test their skills in high-tech simulators, or try their hand at duckpin bowling. Family by JW programming gets the whole gang together with seasonal arts and crafts, fish feedings, movie nights, and more. Tots will also love meeting the property’s flock of Chilean flamingos, practicing their putt-putt on the 18-hole miniature golf course, and ordering off the children’s menus available at all on-site dining outlets. Families can also hop aboard boats departing from the hotel lobby for a cruise along the resort’s waterways.

Check Availability at Booking.com.

Location: Chicago, IllinoisPrice: From $129 per night.

The Loews Loves Families initiative, available at 27 properties throughout North America, is one of the most baby-friendly hotel offerings around. Guest rooms are equipped with mini fridges and kettles for storing and sanitizing bottles; full-size cribs, baby tubs, and night-lights are complimentary. Housekeeping will cover electrical outlets and supply foam bumpers upon request, and kids are given a cute amenity kit with baby lotion, wipes, shampoo, conditioner, and body wash. Board games, coloring books, pool toys, and iPads preloaded with movies and games are available from the concierge desk, as is a family activity guide highlighting the best local options for museums, zoos, and kid-friendly restaurants. There’s even a Bedtime Book Cart to help parents maintain their routine while on the road.

Check Availability at Booking.com.

Location: Sagres, PortugalPrice: From $149 per night.

At Martinhal Sagres, a stylish beachfront resort tucked inside a protected natural park in Portugal’s Algarve, the littlest guests get the VIP treatment. A baby concierge stocks rooms with cribs, bottle sterilizers, high chairs, and other essentials before families arrive—sparing parents the frustration of hauling half the nursery overseas. Even better, the resort’s supervised kids clubs welcome infants as young as six months, with separate programs for crawling babies, curious toddlers, and older children. Accommodations range from contemporary hotel suites to spacious villas with kitchens and washing machines; other perks include five swimming pools, sandy playgrounds, and restaurants offering dedicated baby menus. The Baby's First Holiday package sweetens the deal with a couples massage and romantic dinner—babysitting included.

Check Availability at Booking.com.

Location: Oklahoma City, OklahomaPrice: From $149 per night, inclusive of water park access for two people.

Operated by the Chickasaw Nation, this 404-room property blends substantial-ticket family fun with a strong sense of place. When Julian and I visited, it was the cultural aspect that surprised us most—especially the Chickasaw-curated gallery and easy access to the Smithsonian-affiliated First Americans Museum next door, which recently debuted the fully immersive FAMily Discovery Center. Outside, the 4.5-acre lagoon complex boasts the fourth-largest pool in the country—complete with zip-line plunges, an inflatable obstacle course, and an adults-only swim-up bar for parents who need a moment of respite. Inside, the 100,000-square-foot water park is kept at a blissful 82 degrees and features a low tide pool with pint-sized splash structures that didn’t overwhelm my budding swimmer.

There’s an arcade, mirror maze, and candy store, plus a slew of specialty eateries serving the four main food groups for toddlers: hot dogs, pizza, ice cream, and tacos. On Friday and Saturday evenings, there’s even a storytelling Pajama Hour led by resort staff at the lobby fireplace, with bedtime attire encouraged. Families will appreciate the value here: Children under two stay free, and spacious suites offer bunk beds and semi-private sleeping areas, with cribs available on request.

Location: Puerto Morelos, MexicoPrice: From $420 per night.

As far as resorts for families go, Sensira, an all-inclusive luxury resort on the Riviera Maya, sure knows how to make a kid feel special. The Baby Explorer Club, designed for ages 18 months through 3 years, has indoor slides, bounce houses, and a ball pit, plus supervised sensory activities, music, and storytelling. For families with older kids in tow, there’s a movie theater, miniature golf course, zip line, water park, basketball court, tennis court, climbing wall, gaming stations, indoor trampoline park, and two swimming pools (there's a third pool designated for adults only).

It has been revealed that the hotel can prepare fresh purées on request for infants and toddlers and has a kids corner at the buffet with food displayed at little ones’ eye level. It also supplies all the equipment parents need for a hassle-free stay, including bottle warmers and sterilizers, full-size cribs, and car seats. Babysitting services are available from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. daily, and parents are given a beeper to stay in touch. (If an infant is still breastfeeding, the nanny will fetch a parent for mealtime.) Even the spa takes family well-being into consideration, offering a full slate of all-ages wellness programming, including gentle therapies for children and teens that mirror adult rituals, and purpose-built family treatment cabins.

Location: Crete, GreecePrice: From $199 per night.

According to recent reports, phāea Cretan Malia is one of those rare design hotels that’s as thoughtfully geared toward families with babies and toddlers as it is toward style-hungry adults. The low-rise, modernist buildings sit in lush, shady gardens that keep the grounds cool even in peak summer heat. When Julian and I stayed here in 2024, we spent hours pinballing from the sandy, shallow beach to the swimming pools to the Tiny Explorers’ Club—a padded, sunlit playroom for ages three and under where parents can spend time with their little ones.

Sources indicate that for ages 3–12, the Little Explorers Kids Club has its own kitchen for baking sessions, a mini stage for dance and theater, an environmental play area, an organic garden to tend, and an outdoor playground—a godsend when little ones have energy to burn. Parents can also request the Baby Package, available for an additional charge, which includes babysitting services and toddler gear to cut down on packing. And while the open-air restaurants serve gorgeous Cretan dishes built around local produce, they’re equally prepared for picky palates: think wood-fired pizzas, simple pastas, and fresh fruit. When you’re ready to venture out, Potamos Beach and the Minoan ruins of Malia Palace, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, are an easy walk away.

Location: Southern Kalahari, South AfricaPrice: From around $7,000 per night for two adults, all-inclusive.

Taking a toddler on safari sounds like a terrible idea until you discover Tswalu, South Africa’s largest privately protected conservation area, in the malaria-free Kalahari. At Loapi, six stand-alone safari homes with one or two bedrooms have private plunge pools, chefs, house managers, and dedicated guides, trackers, and vehicles—meaning no one cares if your child talks incessantly through a lion sighting. (Mine certainly did.).

It has been revealed that when we visited in August 2026, Julian raced our guide and tracker through the red dunes, dictated his pasta preferences to the chef, and played catch with his child minder while I squeezed in some work. The flexibility is extraordinary: Game drives can be tailored around naps and short attention spans while older siblings can learn archery and animal tracking through the Junior Ranger program. Other highlights include close-up encounters with habituated meerkats and some of the best stargazing I've experienced anywhere. We also spotted black-maned lions, cheetahs, wild dogs, and desert black rhinos, but some of Julian’s happiest moments were spent chasing a ball with the staff. For families seeking a (slightly) less extravagant safari, Tswalu’s Motse camp offers one- and two-bedroom suites and shared facilities; its five-bedroom Tarkuni homestead is another option for multigenerational groups of up to 10.

Location: Atami, Shizuoka Prefecture, JapanPrice: From $238 per night.

Recent findings suggest that less than an hour by bullet train from Tokyo, Risonare Atami sits high above a Japanese seaside town famous for its hot springs and fireworks festivals. All 81 rooms overlook Sagami Bay, with some offering front-row views of the town’s fireworks displays. The resort’s Baby-Friendly Stay Blueprint outfits spacious rooms with cribs and other infant necessities, while the restaurants serve complimentary rice porridge and vegetable purées. Parents can even hand off children as young as six months to an in-house nursery for up to 150 minutes of complimentary childcare while they tuck into a multicourse kaiseki dinner at the hotel’s restaurant, Hanabi.

According to recent reports, little ones have a heated indoor pool with a shallow splash zone and an ocean-view playroom with a ball pit and toddler-friendly climbing wall. Outdoors, Kusu Kusu centers on a tree house built into a 300-year-old camphor tree, with forest treasure hunts for children ages two and up and a treetop obstacle course for older kids. Parents can also steal away to the resort's semi-open-air onsen overlooking the bay.

Location: Grossarl, AustriaPrice: From $669 per night, including full board and childcare.

Recent findings suggest that part luxury Alpine retreat, part working organic farm, Moar Gut is a five-star family resort where children can feed goats, cuddle rabbits, and even “adopt” an animal to care for during their stay. Set on a sprawling car-free estate in Austria’s Grossarl Valley, the 46-suite property takes its back-to-nature philosophy seriously. Its 10,000-square-foot kids club is built from natural materials like wood, linen, and sheep’s wool, with a painting studio, woodworking workshops, and guided forest adventures. Even babies get the full Alpine treatment: The separate nursery, offering supervised care from 30 days old, has Swiss stone pine cribs, organic bedding, and hay-covered walls. At the Lillee Baby Spa, parents can book guided infant massage, yoga, or floating sessions starting at three weeks old. Older children can ride ponies, forage for alpine herbs, and bake traditional Austrian treats, while parents have an adults-only spa and six-course farm-to-table dinners to look forward to. There's even a dedicated organic baby buffet with fresh purées and formula.

What is the best destination to travel to with an infant and/or toddler?

For a first trip with a baby or toddler, destinations with manageable flight times, reliable medical care, and resorts that minimize the logistical headaches of traveling with little ones are ideal. Florida, Mexico, and the Caribbean are excellent starting points, with direct flights from many US cities, and resorts that cater specifically to young children. Four Seasons Resort and Residences Anguilla is one standout, offering complimentary baby equipment, a zero-entry family pool, and a splash pad. For families ready to venture farther, Portugal's Algarve is another excellent choice, especially Martinhal Sagres, where supervised childcare starts at six months. In the Austrian Alps, Moar Gut goes a step further, welcoming infants as young as 30 days into its professionally staffed nursery.

Are there any good all-inclusive resorts for infants and toddlers?

Sources indicate that absolutely. Jean-Michel Cousteau Resort in Fiji is particularly impressive, with meals, activities, and dedicated nanny care included in the rate. Children under six are assigned two nannies who work opposite shifts, providing personalized care throughout the day and evening, while older children are paired with Fijian companions who guide them through age-appropriate activities. Closer to home, Grand Velas Riviera Nayarit in Mexico features gourmet dining, a baby concierge who arranges infant equipment and coordinates meals and childcare, and specialty purées for its youngest guests (babysitting costs extra).

What resort in the US is best for families with infants and toddlers?

It has been revealed that the Breakers Palm Beach in Florida is hard to beat. Its private beach and zero-entry family pool are ideal for little swimmers, while a 4,500-square-foot playground and the Seaside Family Entertainment Center—with its dedicated Toddler Cove—give youngsters room to burn off energy. The hotel can also supply cribs, strollers, and bottle warmers, as well as childproof guest rooms upon request. Parents, meanwhile, get the restaurants, spa, and old-school Palm Beach glamour that have made The Breakers a fixture on luxury travel lists for generations.

#65780. Latest Update: Brain scans reveal where fractions fit on the mental number line

Latest Update: Brain scans reveal where fractions fit on the mental number line

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1079 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Brain scans show that adults use a shared mental number line to compare fractions and whole numbers, even as the brain distinguishes between them.
  • Industry observers note that A quarter looks more like four on the page, but its value is much closer to zero.
  • As adults compared fractions and whole numbers, brain activity followed a shared number line.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Brain scans show that adults use a shared mental number line to compare fractions and whole numbers, even as the brain distinguishes between them.

Industry observers note that A quarter looks more like four on the page, but its value is much closer to zero. In a new brain scan study, that difference mattered.

As adults compared fractions and whole numbers, brain activity followed a shared number line.

The patterns still distinguished fractions from whole numbers, but numbers close in value tended to produce more similar patterns.

One idea about how the brain handles abstract concepts is that it files related concepts close together, so that similar ideas produce similar patterns of activity.

Numbers are a good way to test that, because everyone agrees on their order.

Daniela Valério and Stanislas Dehaene of the Inserm-CEA Cognitive Neuroimaging Unit, known as Unicog, led the study at the NeuroSpin center outside Paris.

In a recent development, people have long been known to carry a number line in their heads for whole numbers. The team wanted to know whether fractions, which children learn after years of schooling, get added to the same line.

Twenty-two adults took part, all right-handed native French speakers between 19 and 39 who had finished high school with a science track.

Two were excluded, one for a cyst found on the scan and one who had a panic attack in the scanner.

That left 20 participants in the brain scan analysis. A faulty response button reduced the number to 19 for the analysis of speed and accuracy.

According to recent reports, each person lay in a high-field MRI scanner run by the French research agency CEA. The numbers 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 and the fractions 1/4, 1/3, 1/2, 2/3, 3/2, and 5/2 flashed up one at a time, each for one second.

For every number, the person pressed a button to say whether it was bigger or smaller than the one before.

Sources indicate that each run lasted just under ten minutes, and every number followed every other number exactly once. The fractions were built from the same digits as the whole numbers on purpose.

That let the team tell whether the brain was reading 1/4 as a quarter or as a 1 next to a 4.

Fractions slowed people down. A comparison between two fractions took about 1.2 seconds on average, against 0.8 seconds between two whole numbers.

People also got 9.5 percent of fraction pairs wrong, compared with 3.7 percent of whole number pairs.

In an interview with Earth.com, Valério noted fractions are harder for a few reasons.

Whole numbers follow a simple counting sequence, so 3 is followed by 4, while there is always another fraction between any two different numbers.

Industry observers note that the size of a fraction is also not always easy to judge from the numbers in it. “For example, although 5 is greater than 3, 1/5 is smaller than 1/3,” Valério said.

Numbers that were close together were also harder than numbers far apart, whichever kind they were. The closer two numbers were, the slower and less accurate people got, and the effect was strongest when both were fractions.

Psychologists have known this distance effect for whole numbers for decades, and here it held for fractions too.

Sources indicate that the team then laid out the speed and error data as a map. The 12 numbers fell along a single curved line in order of size, with the fractions among the whole numbers where their values belonged.

The scans revealed the same thing. Across the brain regions that handle math, the pattern of activity for each number varied along two main directions.

One separated fractions from whole numbers. The other ordered all 12 numbers by size, from small to large, and ignored whether they were fractions.

The size ordering was strongest in the intraparietal sulcus, a fold near the top and back of the brain that has long been tied to math.

Sources indicate that researchers have also linked this region to the ability to estimate quantities. In the upcoming study, patterns of activity in the hippocampus also reflected how close numbers were in value.

Then the team looked at single points on the cortex.

Within the front part of that parietal fold, many spots responded most to one particular number and less to its neighbors. The spots formed a map, with small numbers at the front and larger numbers farther back.

Sources indicate that the map for fractions matched the map for whole numbers. Spots that preferred 0 also responded to 1/4, 1/3, and 1/2, and 1/4 ended up far from 4.

Valério said that when people compare numbers, they have to focus on magnitude, meaning how large or small each one is.

“Our study shows that the brain organizes this information into a shared map, much like a mental number line, “Valerio told Earth.com.

“This map brings whole numbers, such as 1 and 2, and fractions, such as 1/2 and 2/3, into the same system, according to their values.”.

It has been revealed that the size map highlighted up in only 14 or 15 of the 20 participants, depending on the number type. The fractions also stopped at 5/2, short of the range the whole numbers covered.

Fractions and whole numbers were mixed in one stream, so people may have had to build a single line to keep up.

Sources indicate that the authors wrote that if the two kinds had been shown in separate sessions, each might still have run from small to large. The two lines might not have lined up, though.

It has been revealed that valério remarked the study was not designed to explain why fractions are harder to learn or to find the best way to teach them. Other studies in her lab are working on that.

Her next step is to see how the shared map differs across people with different mathematical backgrounds and levels of education, and whether those differences go with mathematical ability.

How the brain represents fractions in children who are still learning them remains an open question.

The team has posted its data and code on the Open Science Framework. It wrote that longer scanning sessions could extend the map to more kinds of math.

The full study was published in the journal PLOS Biology.

Hawaii’s 90-foot Hōlei Sea Arch was carved from lava that flowed about 550 years ago, and in late September it fell into the Pacific

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (793 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The 90-foot Hōlei Sea Arch in Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park collapsed in late September 2026.
  • For years, visitors who drove to the end of Chain of Craters Road in Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park could walk a short distance and see a 90-foot arch of lava rock reaching out from the cliffs into the Pacific Ocean.
  • The Hōlei Sea Arch was still standing on Wednesday, September 23, 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The 90-foot Hōlei Sea Arch in Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park collapsed in late September 2026. Here is how it formed and why sea arches eventually fall.

For years, visitors who drove to the end of Chain of Craters Road in Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park could walk a short distance and see a 90-foot arch of lava rock reaching out from the cliffs into the Pacific Ocean.

That view is gone. The Hōlei Sea Arch was still standing on Wednesday, September 23, 2026. By the night of Sunday, September 27, it had collapsed into the ocean, the National Park Service announced on October 1.

The exact time of the collapse is unknown. According to the park, it could have happened while the park was temporarily closed during Tropical Storm Nolo.

The arch stood about 90 feet (27.4 meters) high and extended from steep sea cliffs into the ocean along the park’s southern coast, on the Island of Hawaiʻi.

It was carved into the cliff of an ancient lava flow from about 550 years ago, according to the park. The arch took shape through what geologists call differential erosion: some layers of lava are harder than others, so the sea wears them away at different speeds.

Visitors could see it by walking a short distance from the end of Chain of Craters Road, which the park described in 2020 as a 19-mile drive through some of the most spectacular scenery in the park.

The park’s own page on the arch was clear about one thing. The formation was beautiful but temporary, with a limited life span, and it would eventually crumble into the sea.

Sources indicate that sea arches like Hōlei can be found along a wide stretch of Hawaiʻi’s southern coast. They are remnants of once-continuous sea cliffs, built where lava met the sea and added to the size of the island.

Lava meeting the sea can even build whole latest land, as it did when a new island rose from the sea off Iceland in 1963.

The moment that latest lava cooled and turned to rock, it began to erode, the park explains. The seas on the island’s southern edge are known for rough water and violent surf, and the waves slowly break apart the rock and carve sea caves into the cliffs.

Sources indicate that when waves hit the back wall of a sea cave, the water bounces back and starts to erode the cave’s headland. Over time, that forms an arch.

Recent findings suggest that the erosion does not stop there. Given enough time, the waves cause the remaining bridge of rock to collapse, leaving behind a pile of rocks known as a sea stack.

Volcanic coastlines are constantly being remade, and on the same island, Kīlauea has produced 55 lava fountains since December 2024.

The coastline around the arch had shown signs of instability for years.

In a recent development, earthquakes during the 2018 Kīlauea eruption and summit collapse damaged the cliffs near the arch. In January 2020, fresh cracks and instability led the park to close the original viewing area and the short trail to it.

“This newly introduced development reminds us that Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park is an ever-changing volcanic landscape,” Rhonda Loh, then the park’s acting superintendent, stated in January 2020.

A safer viewing area opened in March 2020, about 1,000 feet past the gate at the end of Chain of Craters Road and set back from the cliff edge.

Later that year, massive surf from Tropical Storm Darby broke off a chunk of rock from the lower part of the arch.

The park is urging visitors to stay back from the unstable cliffs, which drop vertically into the ocean and present a serious risk of falling.

After the collapse, photos on social media showed people entering the closed area near where the arch once stood.

According to the park, that puts both the visitors and first responders at great risk of falling and drowning off the rough, wave-swept coast.

Visitors are required to stay out of closed areas and away from cliff edges, which can collapse without warning.

The park describes individual sea arches as an ephemeral feature of the island’s constantly shifting coastline.

In a recent development, as the cliff slowly migrates inland, other arches will form and replace Hōlei, the park says. The park notes that erosion does not stop once an arch has formed.

The information was obtained from the National Park Service’s announcement of the collapse, its pages on Hōlei Sea Arch and how sea arches form, and its 2020 releases on the closure of the overlook and the upcoming viewing area.

Bipartisan process for picking GAO chief breaks down

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., speaks during a Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee business meeting on Sept.
  • Republican leaders have skipped a bipartisan deliberative process for recommending the next comptroller general to head the Government Accountability Office, as lawmakers prepare to consider a nomination for the post from President Donald Trump.
  • Sources remarked Trump is planning to nominate Eric Ueland, who right now serves as deputy director for management at the Office of Management and Budget.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., speaks during a Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee business meeting on Sept. 23. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Republican leaders have skipped a bipartisan deliberative process for recommending the next comptroller general to head the Government Accountability Office, as lawmakers prepare to consider a nomination for the post from President Donald Trump.

Sources remarked Trump is planning to nominate Eric Ueland, who right now serves as deputy director for management at the Office of Management and Budget. The White House submitted ethics paperwork on Ueland — required for nominations — to the GAO, according to a source.

In a recent development, senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., on Thursday posted notice of a committee hearing Nov. 19 to examine more than a dozen presidential nominees for executive and judicial offices, including “a nominee to be Comptroller General.”.

According to recent reports, the post identifies by name all of the nominees except the candidate for comptroller general. The post has been filled by an acting comptroller general, Orice Williams Brown, since Gene L. Dodaro completed his 15-year term at the end of last year.

It has been revealed that the move by Paul to short-circuit the convening of a legislative commission to recommend candidates infuriated top Democrats, who excoriated the chairman in a joint statement Wednesday night. A special bipartisan, bicameral legislative commission is supposed to recommend at least three candidates for comptroller general to the president, according to statute.

Recent findings suggest that homeland Security Committee GOP staff solicited recommendations for a comptroller general from some Democratic congressional offices Wednesday afternoon, imposing a deadline of 8 a.m. Thursday, according to Democratic aides.

The president nominates the head of the GAO, the investigative arm of Congress, with the advice and consent of the Senate.

Recent findings suggest that paul pushed back on the criticism Thursday, saying, “Democrats have known about this for months and months and months.” He remarked the last time the special commission made recommendations for the office, when Barack Obama was president, “Democrats submitted their own list, Republicans submitted their own list. So they can complain all they want but they just need to make their list and submit it.”.

In the past, however, the special commission convened, sought applications for the position, interviewed candidates and deliberated before sending recommendations to the president.

A 1980 law states that when there is a vacancy in the comptroller general position, “there is established a commission to recommend individuals to the President for appointment to the vacant office,” and that the commission must submit at least three names.

Under the statute, the commission includes the speaker, Senate majority and minority leaders, House majority and minority leaders, chairs and ranking members of the Senate Homeland Security and House Oversight and Government Reform committees, and the Senate president pro tempore.

According to recent reports, in 1981, for example, after the law took effect, the two congressional leaders, Speaker Thomas P. “Tip” O’Neill Jr., D-Mass., and Senate Majority Leader Howard H. Baker, R-Tenn., sent a letter to President Ronald Reagan saying the special commission had met and voted to recommend eight candidates to succeed Comptroller General Elmer Staats.

“The members of the Commission have taken their statutory responsibility seriously,” they wrote.

Recent findings suggest that reagan nominated Charles A. Bowsher, who was on the list, and he was confirmed.

Sources indicate that after Bowsher’s term ended in 1996, the commission eventually formed, interviewed multiple candidates, and deliberated for several months. Republicans controlled both chambers, and Bill Clinton was president. The members of the commission could not reach agreement, and as a result, the Republicans on the committee submitted their list to Clinton, and the Democrats on the panel submitted theirs.

According to recent reports, clinton also had his own list. Clinton nominated David M. Walker, who was on all three lists, and he was confirmed by the Senate more than two years after Bowsher’s departure. Walker argued Thursday against short-circuiting the commission process.

Industry observers note that “The position is of critical importance and the related statutory Commission process should not be circumvented," Walker noted. "Doing so would undercut the credibility of the person and the effectiveness of the GAO.”.

Walker resigned in March of 2008, when George W. Bush was still president. He appointed Dodaro as acting comptroller general when he left. The commission got going several months later, creating a website with application instructions and candidate questions.

Over the next two years, the commission interviewed some 20 candidates. Democrats and Republicans on the panel were unable to reach agreement, and Democrats, who had a majority on the commission, submitted their own list to Obama in 2010. Republicans followed up with their list.

“The Commission has been working in earnest on this undertaking for more than one year and has dedicated considerable time and effort to present you with highly qualified candidates for this crucial position,” then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., and then-Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, D-Nev., along with other Democratic leaders, wrote to Obama when they submitted the Democrats’ list.

Sources indicate that the Democrats’ move drew a rebuke from Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, who was ranking member of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee at the time.

It has been revealed that collins said in a statement she was “extremely disappointed” that Democrats “abruptly ended the selection process for the next Comptroller General without a bipartisan agreement” on the recommendations. “We have had several exceptionally qualified individuals apply to be the next leader of the GAO, and it should have been possible to come up with a consensus list.”.

Obama nominated and the Senate confirmed Dodaro, who was one of four recommendations from the Democrats.

Cracks in public health grew in 2026

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3200 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • Industry observers note that it’s tough to tally the injuries or deaths that don’t happen thanks to seat belts, lead testing, smoking bans and vaccines.
  • But when disaster strikes — say, an outbreak or a pandemic — people take notice.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Public health is invisible — until it’s not.

Industry observers note that it’s tough to tally the injuries or deaths that don’t happen thanks to seat belts, lead testing, smoking bans and vaccines. “It is the invisibility paradox,” notes Georges Benjamin, CEO of the American Public Health Association in Washington, D.C. “We are invisible because when our best work is done, nothing happens.”.

But when disaster strikes — say, an outbreak or a pandemic — people take notice. This year’s outbreaks of measles, Ebola, hantavirus and cyclosporiasis brought recent federal reductions into focus — and exposed cracks in a system that aims to keep people healthy. For years, that system functioned “reasonably well” despite chronic underfunding, Benjamin claims. “But since the Trump administration has come on board, they have really made the system at all levels much more dysfunctional.”.

In 2025, the second Trump administration instituted sweeping federal funding cuts and layoffs, dismantled the global health–focused U.S. Agency for International Development and withdrew the United States from the World Health Organization. Officials reversed some of those changes in the wake of lawsuits and public backlash. But the damage persists.

Two stalwarts of U.S. public health — the Food and Drug Administration and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — have lost between 20 and 30 percent of their staff, due largely to layoffs and early retirements. They have had to scale back, pause or cancel crucial disease-tracking programs at home and abroad. Some CDC divisions don’t have enough staff to function. And both agencies have cut funding to the local governments and nonprofits that shoulder much of the nation’s public health work.

Combined with deep cuts to international aid, that has stymied efforts to contain infectious disease outbreaks around the world, with Ebola in particular going undetected for months, public health experts say.

Domestically, 2026 saw a record-breaking measles outbreak, with some 5,412 confirmed cases as of November 12. That’s more than double last year’s count, and it is the highest number of annual cases since 1991. In mid November, the Pan American Health Organization determined that measles is again endemic to the United States and has stripped the country of its elimination status.

According to recent reports, against a backdrop of shifting federal vaccine guidance, fewer children are receiving the MMR shot that prevents measles. Roughly 92 percent of kindergartners across the United States had gotten the vaccine in the 2025–2026 school year, down from 95 percent in the 2019–2020 school year, according to the CDC. At least 95 percent of people in a community need to be vaccinated to prevent the measles virus from sparking an outbreak.

“The fact that we are spending so much time and energy [on measles] when we have a reliable vaccine is very disconcerting,” says Lori Handy, a pediatric infectious diseases physician and associate director of the Vaccine Education Center at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia.

The CDC has not responded to Science News requests for an interview.

It has been revealed that such issues do not bode well for the future. Public health is tested during times of crisis, and the world will eventually face another pandemic, says Michael Osterholm, director of the Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy at the University of Minnesota in Minneapolis. “We’ve not responded [to the 2026 outbreaks] in a way that would give me confidence that the public health system … is prepared for what’s coming down the pike.”.

On the heels of multiple 2025 outbreaks, measles continued to wallop parts of the United States this year. Communities in South Carolina, Utah and Wisconsin have been among the hardest hit, with sporadic outbreaks also popping up in other states. Until August, however, none of this year’s outbreaks had turned deadly. That all changed in Pennsylvania.

According to recent reports, about a quarter of this year’s cases stem from an outbreak in central Pennsylvania, where the virus has spread widely in communities with low vaccination rates. Since April, seven people in the state have died, including two infants too young to be vaccinated. The CDC has so far attributed just six deaths to measles, despite the insistence of Pennsylvania state public health officials. Three children died of measles in November in Upcoming York and Wisconsin.

As of November 12, U.S. health officials recorded 5,412 measles cases for 2026. The last time this many cases were recorded was 1991, nearly a decade before the disease was eliminated from the country.

Measles spreads like wildfire, and one sick person can infect more than a dozen others in an unvaccinated community. While milder symptoms include fever and a hallmark full-body rash, infection can lead to pneumonia, brain swelling and even death. Statistically, the virus kills one to three out of every 1,000 infected people.

It has been revealed that the United States eliminated measles in 2000, thanks to the MMR vaccine. “Elimination” means the virus was not spreading widely, and any outbreaks were controlled within a year. But dropping vaccination rates have reestablished the conditions to sustain multiple outbreaks — and may have done so as early as 2022, researchers reported in August in Nature Medicine.

According to recent reports, in the wake of losing measles elimination status in November, beating back the the virus again “will take a true change in the public’s trust of health care,” Handy says. That means figuring out how to get people vaccinated — and to encourage them to work with public health officials on testing and contact tracing after exposure.

During the 2009–2010 school year, 20 states had MMR vaccination rates equal to or above 95 percent among kindergartners. Just 10 states hit that threshold for 2025–2026, and 18 states had vaccination rates below 90 percent.

It has been more than three decades since measles caused widespread outbreaks in the United States, and many have never experienced the devastation it can cause. When one community hears about an outbreak halfway across the country, “it still feels very foreign,” Handy indicates. When the threat feels far away, people are not likely to line up to get a vaccine. Yet measles is so contagious that one unvaccinated traveler can bring the virus back home and spark an outbreak in their own community.

It has been revealed that even with the recent spike in cases, there is hope vaccination rates can catch up, says Cornell University epidemiologist Ana Bento. She points to California and Fresh York, which experienced outbreaks in 2015 and 2018; they ended non-medical exemptions for school vaccinations shortly thereafter. Both states now have vaccination rates above 95 percent in kindergartners. “This is not a tipping point where there’s no coming back,” Bento says.

If measles exposed the consequences of long-simmering vaccine hesitancy, then this summer’s cyclosporiasis outbreak was a quick lesson in food safety screening.

In a recent development, in June, Michigan detected its first cases of the foodborne illness. By August 31, contaminated lettuce had caused the largest outbreak of explosive diarrhea ever in the United States, with 12,883 cases reported across 21 states. By the time the CDC declared the outbreak over on September 11, some 570 people had been hospitalized and two had died. Another 8,113 cyclosporiasis infections have not been traced back to any source. “[This] was one of those events where you felt like the cracks highlighted,” Handy indicates.

But it isn’t easy to track the origins of foodborne illness. Typically, local and state public health officials report cases to the CDC — and investigate the outbreak, with the agency lending support as needed. If patient interviews reveal the culprit to be produce, dairy or packaged food, the CDC contacts the FDA, which identifies the producer and the distribution area — and coordinates recalls. The FDA also conducts on-the-ground investigations at the farms and processing facilities that supplied the food.

It can take weeks to identify which contaminated foods are behind a foodborne illness outbreak. Each outbreak is different and timing can depend on the pathogen, laboratory evidence and availability of records, an FDA spokesperson told Science News. After Michigan health officials notified CDC that something was amiss on June 25, it was another 21 days before federal officials announced a possible culprit: shredded lettuce ultimately traced to a Taylor Farms processing facility in Mexico.

Of more than 20,000 cyclosporiasis cases reported this year, nearly 13,000 occurred across 21 states, with the preponderance of them in the Midwest.

According to recent reports, the FDA aims to complete investigations as soon as possible. But delays in agency reporting early in the investigation led to unnecessary confusion about which foods to avoid in which states, said Sarah Sorscher, director of regulatory affairs at the Washington, D.C.–based Center for Science in the Public Interest, at a July 16 news briefing. “It’s a perfect storm for viral news. A lot of people have been posting on social media about avoiding fruits and vegetables, which is not good public health messaging.”.

Sorscher applauded the dedication of public servants working to contain the outbreak. But she stated they were working with inadequate support. “These programs are completely overwhelmed by the scale and scope of the work of solving and communicating these novel emerging outbreaks with a dwindling set of resources.”.

Due in part to funding squeezes, in 2025 the CDC stopped mandatory surveillance of six foodborne pathogens, including the single-celled parasite that causes cyclosporiasis, Cyclospora. Speaking at the July 16 news briefing, epidemiologist Barbara Kowalcyk of George Washington University’s Institute for Food Safety and Nutrition Security in Washington, D.C., noted that half of CDC’s food safety budget goes to states to support surveillance and other programs. Yet that budget has remained flat for nearly a decade.

FDA investigations have also been impacted, with foreign food inspections at historical lows. In the case of cyclosporiasis, delays gathering testing supplies and getting clearance from the Mexican government meant it took nearly a month for FDA investigators to arrive in Mexico once the source of the outbreak was identified, according to the Upcoming York Times. Once there, inspectors found the parasite in a wastewater tank at a Taylor Farms processing plant — and in a drainage ditch at a farm that supplied the lettuce. Since Cyclospora infects only humans, the probable contaminant was sewage from a source that has yet to be identified.

Sources indicate that without knowing the source of the contamination, it’s hard to know how to stop the parasite from reaching produce in the future, states Francisco Diez-Gonzalez, a food microbiologist at the University of Georgia in Athens. “It leaves us with the feeling that we most likely are going to have something similar next year.”.

Starting in 2027, FDA plans to increase surveillance of produce historically associated with Cyclospora and boost laboratory capacity in Mexico to speed up investigations.

Outbreaks of other foodborne pathogens — including Salmonella, Listeria and E. coli — have popped up this year, but not at a rate that’s out of the ordinary, notes Diez-Gonzalez, who served on the U.S. National Advisory Committee on Microbiological Criteria for Foods before the Trump administration disbanded it in 2025. That suggests the sky isn’t falling, though he and others are concerned about our future ability to rapidly contain outbreaks.

It has been revealed that “We may see [fewer] cases, but it’s not that they are disappearing,” Diez-Gonzalez says. “We will not be able to detect them because we don’t have the resources.”.

When the WHO unveiled in May that an Ebola outbreak had erupted in the Democratic Republic of Congo, the virus had been simmering for months. People in the mining town of Mongbwalu, where the outbreak was first detected, began falling ill in January or earlier, according to reporting from Science. Armed conflict in the region has made the outbreak response difficult, says the WHO, and some aid workers and health facilities have been attacked.

Sources indicate that confirmed Ebola cases as of November 15, 2026. To date, 5,593 people have died, and 3,109 have recovered.

As cases and death counts soared in May, health officials scrambled to test a backlog of patient samples for Bundibugyo virus, the species behind what has become the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak ever recorded. As of November 15, there were 11,432 confirmed cases and 5,593 deaths. Roughly 3,109 people have recovered. Cases have also been detected in France, Uganda, Kenya and Nigeria.

Before the outbreak, the United States significantly scaled back international aid that once flowed from USAID and the CDC. Such cuts may have hampered Ebola monitoring before the outbreak was declared — and affected infection control measures such as contact tracing, says infectious disease physician Krutika Kuppalli of UT Southwestern Medical Center in Dallas.

Industry observers note that kuppalli led an Ebola treatment unit in Sierra Leone during the 2014–2016 outbreak, the largest ever recorded. At the time, the CDC sent 1,450 physicians, epidemiologists and other experts to help out in affected areas. So far around 500 CDC employees stationed in the United States and abroad have responded to the current outbreak.

It has been revealed that by September, the U.S. State Department pledged $887 million toward the purchase of personal protective equipment and the building of fresh Ebola treatment units. That’s roughly a third of the total amount sent during the 2014–2016 outbreak. Still, earlier investments in public health could have saved lives and helped minimize transmission, Kuppalli says.

Information-sharing has also been a huge problem, Kuppalli says. Prior to the second Trump administration, U.S. health officials were in constant contact with WHO teams that shared information about cases and contact-tracing efforts. After the United States withdrew from the WHO in January 2025, CDC officials had to coordinate with other groups such as UNICEF, the United Nations Children’s Fund.

In a recent development, nevertheless, there has been some progress toward developing treatments and vaccines. Researchers in Congo are testing whether antivirals and engineered antibodies can stave off severe disease and death in people infected with Bundibugyo virus, and whether those treatments can protect people after exposure. In October, a large clinical trial began testing a vaccine that is already approved against the species that caused the 2014–2016 outbreak. Kuppalli and colleagues argued in September in the Lancet Infectious Diseases that the vaccine’s potential for cross-protection merited its use in high-risk situations.

Two Bundibugyo-specific vaccines are poised to join the fresh trial after early evidence in animals and people showed the shots are safe — and suggested they may be protective.

According to recent reports, conditions have improved in some parts of Congo, according to the WHO. But there are still hundreds of new cases per week, and other countries should be prepared to respond rapidly if the virus crosses borders. “The longer this outbreak continues, the more opportunities the virus has to reach new communities,” Kuppalli notes.

It has been revealed that the M.V. Hondius was in for a rough voyage the moment it set off from Ushuaia, Argentina, on April 1. A passenger on the small ship had contracted Andes hantavirus, a rodent-borne disease that can cause severe respiratory illness and death. By the time the outbreak was contained, 13 people were infected and three people had died. Public health experts say a lagging U.S. response let other countries take the lead — and suggests the country is not prepared for future epidemics.

According to recent reports, it’s unclear how the first patient, who died on April 11, was infected. Another patient died on the ship, and a third — who was allowed to board a plane — died in South Africa.

Recent findings suggest that more than 300 high-risk contacts, including people who spent more than 15 minutes with an infected individual, were quarantined and monitored across 33 countries and territories. None of them got sick. Nor did another 336 low-risk contacts who had brief encounters with someone who fell ill, and who monitored themselves for symptoms.

According to recent reports, the United States’ severed relationship with the WHO “in many ways hampered the [country’s] hantavirus outbreak response,” notes Benjamin, of the American Public Health Association. Before 2025, U.S. experts frequently received information about emerging health threats from the organization. But confusion over who government officials could talk to likely resulted in knowledge gaps and communication delays, Benjamin says. “CDC was not engaged as early on as they needed to be on that outbreak.”.

Instead, other countries including Spain, South Africa, Argentina and Chile played leading roles. After scientists in South Africa determined that Andes hantavirus was behind the outbreak on May 2, passengers disembarked in mid-May in Tenerife, Spain, where health officials screened for symptoms and helped people travel home.

“Outbreak response depends on the knowledge and the relationships that already exist.”.

In a recent development, the CDC didn’t set up a response team until after May 2, according to the Fresh York Times. And controversy erupted over uneven U.S. quarantine practices, with some people forced to remain for weeks in quarantine units in Omaha, Neb., while others remained at home. “There was nothing standard” about the protocols, Osterholm says. “Almost everybody got a different approach.”.

The outbreak, which ended July 2, was swiftly contained in part because Andes hantavirus isn’t very contagious. Of more than 50 known hantaviruses, Andes hantavirus is the only one known to spread from person to person. Although some rare superspreaders transmit the virus to others through casual contact, transmission typically happens through close contact, such as spending long periods of time together or kissing. It would have been harder to stop a pathogen that spreads easily through the air, Osterholm says. “By the time that they recognized what was going on, transmission would have already occurred.”.

It has been revealed that the international collaboration had some successes, notes virologist Gustavo Palacios of the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in Fresh York City. Experts in South Africa “kept digging when everything was negative,” he says, until they finally identified Andes hantavirus as the cause.

Hantavirus infections are also relatively rare in the Americas, for now. Studies suggest climate change will increase the likelihood that hantaviruses — and other zoonotic illnesses like Ebola — will make the jump from animals to humans. Dense cities can make it easier for diseases to spread. And such threats don’t disappear when funding for studying them dries up.

“The strongest lesson [from the M.V. Hondius] is that outbreak response depends on the knowledge and the relationships that already exist before the event,” Palacios says. Of the billions of viruses on Earth, just a few hundred pose threats to people. With enough resources, researchers can work together to learn as much as possible about those pathogens and be better prepared when a upcoming one emerges — just as previous work on coronaviruses made the rollout of COVID-19 vaccines possible within a year of the pandemic’s start.

Recent findings suggest that “We will not always know in advance which [pathogens] will become key,” Palacios says. But by not tracking rare threats that could one day become larger problems, “we are shooting ourselves in the foot.”.

#65775. Tech Report: Inside NYC’s Pool Scene, the City’s Great Equalizer

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1812 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cntraveler ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Inside NYC’s Pool Scene, the City’s Great Equalizer

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1812 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Just when we thought Fresh York had seen it all, I caught wind that the first-ever five-borough pool tournament—in the city’s history—was about to kick off.
  • It was all thanks to Dan Tran, the brains behind the Five Boro Break.
  • Dan Tran, the brains behind the Five Boro Break, has been shooting pool across the city for more than a decade.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Just when we thought Fresh York had seen it all, I caught wind that the first-ever five-borough pool tournament—in the city’s history—was about to kick off.

It was all thanks to Dan Tran, the brains behind the Five Boro Break. Tran has been shooting pool across the city for more than a decade and has played on more than 130 tables out of the 400 to 500 he estimates are in NYC (he even catalogs them out of his own goodwill for other New Yorkers, on Pool Tables NYC). He’s just that guy: an absolute force of nature with a heavy case of do-the-impossible syndrome. One day over summer, at a league night with fellow pool-playing regulars, he wondered if there was a way to get folks like these together for one big game—to unite New York’s pool-playing dive bar families and play as one.

Dan Tran, the brains behind the Five Boro Break, has been shooting pool across the city for more than a decade.

The idea was a tournament “built by pool players, run by pool players,” says Tran, who you’ll most often find playing at George & Jacks in Williamsburg. “No money changing hands, no ulterior motive.” Just bringing together this community, which Tran is the first to admit existed long before he stepped on the scene.

According to recent reports, so this powerhouse did it: 256 players, 16 venues, all five boroughs, over two days in early November. When I caught up with Tran the week before the tournament, he still couldn’t believe he was bringing the idea to life. “I was like, 'What am I signing up to do once I post this?' But then I posted it, and it just took off—like completely took off. And everybody was like, 'Yeah, we can totally do this.'”.

I rode the wave of Tran’s infectious energy and spent an entire weekend hopping between dives watching the tournament’s pool players do what they do best.

The audience at NYC bar Sugar Mouse applauds Five Boro Break creator Dan Tran at the finals.

Recent findings suggest that on Saturday, November 7, you could feel it in the air. There was something electric about knowing the grittiest corners of New York City were locked in on the same game. That distinct four o’clock autumn sunlight was shining on Bushwick Ice House, one of the 16 venues, when I walked in with Traveler’s Julia Abbonizio and Skyli Alvarez, who were ready to photograph the scene. Gathered around a red-felt table were a dozen or so players who shot us “what’s up” nods as we entered; the bartender moseyed over with “what’s it gonna be?” eyes. Without a word exchanged, we were already part of the bar’s family.

Industry observers note that the crowd around us was dressed in their dive-bar best (jeans), and glowing under the neon-red Budweiser lights. The energy in the room matched the game unfolding. One moment, the place roared with Miller High Life clinks and friends catching up. The next it would go pin-drop silent as someone bent over and lined up a shot. More often than not, we’d hear a “nice” before the cue even struck, or a congratulatory clap before someone sank the 8-ball, because everyone knew the game well enough to see exactly what was coming.

Will Pay, a Bushwick Ice House regular, designed the tournament's felt-green shirts.

Satoe Onizuka plays Netta Rawner (left) at Bushwick Ice House.

Will Pay, a Bushwick resident and the creative mind behind the tournament’s T-shirt and site design—dark green, like a pool table’s felt, and featuring a solid orange 5-ball to nod to the boroughs—was running the show. He jokingly told me he’s something of a pool scout around the city, sniffing out the best shooters to join his league. Pay attested that, when Tran initially announced the tournament, interest at his local dive Bushwick Ice House was immediate. Within 10 minutes of the link being live, the waitlist to play at the venue had passed 100.

Recent findings suggest that while Satoe Onizuka, the stealthiest star of the regulars, shook another hand after winning yet another round, I snuck outside of Bushwick Ice House to chat with Pay, who was wearing the Five Boro Break shirt he designed. We got into the type of conversation you do at a dive bar or around a pool table. The love of the game. The importance of dives as sacred spaces. The alluring seediness of it all. Pay knows how we got here: “The game itself is called billiards, but it got casualized to ‘pool’ because people used to throw a ton of money on the table—pool their money—and gamble,” Pay stated. “Obviously, that’s gone out the window because everyone’s super chill these days, but what’s cool is that it still has that air of danger, of being something a bit forbidden.” Will’s right: it’s never corny to shoot pool. No matter who you are, it makes you feel like the slickest person in the room.

In a recent development, there’s also that sense that you’re part of something bigger. Back inside, Pay gestured around the room. “Look at this place,” he stated in admiration. “There’s literally no real estate for this table. But it’s here. And without it, this place would simply not be what it is. These people would probably not be here in this bar. I don’t even think this bar would exist.”.

The enthusiasm at Bushwick Ice House reminded me of how this tournament could only have happened because NYC dive bars already operate as tight-knit communities of their own. They’re the ultimate third places, the spots that aren’t home or work—and the pool table is, in fact, their beating heart.

By 9 p.m. on Saturday, when we stumbled into LES’ Sadie’s Ward, '80s dance-pop shook the walls. Drinks were flowing, the room glowed disco-lit, and everyone was having such a good time you had to shout to be heard by the person next to you. A group of hodge-podge regulars stood two and three deep around the pool table, watching the small, curly-haired Amanda Andries, one of the bar’s most beloved shooters, sink her way toward Sunday’s finals.

Andries is one of the Ladies of Sadie’s, a magnetic group of female regulars at this bar, who were gassing each other up and out-shooting all the 6-foot-something men in flannels that dared to play them. For all the history that tables at bars like Sadie’s have absorbed, it’s the people gathered around them who make the pool scene so captivating—and at this bar, the social fabric is very tightly knit.

East Williamsburg's Anchored Inn was one of the 16 bars that hosted Five Boro Break games.

We sat in the small hideaway across from the bar as the games rolled on, reflecting on the players we’d met throughout the tournament so far: soft-spoken, sharp-shooting Audrey Jones at Anchored Inn over loaded Carmen fries; Allegra “Legz” Fierro outside the graffied, mirrorless bathroom at Blue Ruin Bar; and Elvin Estevez, a polite killer on the table, in the leather booths at Twins Lounge. I’d asked each to tell me their golden rule of playing pool in this city, but it all came back to one recurring theme: be a good person. There’s a camaraderie in wanting to keep NYC’s pool scene a sacred place.

According to recent reports, it’s easy not to suck, though. Sam Shumway of Pool Table Archive mentioned to me by phone in the days following the event. Five years ago, he started posting photos of the pool tables he’d played on in cities across the US, but his hobby grew into a living record of pool culture.

It has been revealed that “Pool tables are special because they’re a snapshot of a time and a place in a bar,” he told me. “A lot of these tables are older than you are. Like, that’s a 40-year-old table. Imagine how much life it’s seen around it.” You can picture a montage of scenes immediately: 4 a.m. closings, birthday toasts, latest friendships, awkward first dates, breakups, and more than a few questionable decisions. Maybe a win in the first-ever cross-city tournament.

Allegra “Legz” Fierro in Hell's Kitchen's Blue Ruin Bar, just before a match.

Come Sunday, we walked into a jam-packed, purple-lit Sugar Mouse for the finals. The winners from each of the 16 bars would go head-to-head across two pool tables. A live dad rock band jammed in the corner, and all I saw were familiar faces from Saturday’s hijinks, smiling, watching respectfully, nodding when a friend nailed a shot, and hugging and shaking hands when one missed. As the field dwindled to four semifinalists, then just two, the crowd drew tighter around the remaining table. Two large projectors cast a live feed onto the wall, as former WPBA No. 1 Jennifer Barretta commented and Hall of Famer John Leyman refereed with a stern eye.

According to recent reports, we were all there for the moment Brennan Brooks of the BCA Brooklyn Travel League took the inaugural win, cementing his right to take home that iconic sign. But as I took in the room around me, what stood out most was seeing people packed in like sardines to watch their fellow dive bar regulars take the stage. It was a kaleidoscope of communities, each representing their local with love. The Five Boro Break was never just about winning; it was about creating a space where everyone could be part of something.

A triumphant moment at Sadie's Ward on the Lower East Side.

The East Village's Sugar Mouse hosted the tournament final.

Recent findings suggest that it was a fresh alternative to life on a screen—maybe that’s part of why so many people revealed up. “People are craving human connection again; people are craving something to do with their hands,” Shumway had mentioned. And though it might look too cool, or intimidating, everyone has a place if they want it. “Pool brings together people who would normally have nothing in common. And there are no pre-qualifications for putting your name on a chalkboard. You might get beat, and that’s okay.”.

Industry observers note that at the end of the Finals night, all of us riding a collective high, Tran stood next to the championship table to thank everyone who helped bring his vision to life. He couldn’t get a word out before the room burst into applause. Thirty seconds of it, and it showed no signs of letting up. Humble as he is, he just smiled.

Tran rattled off the bars, businesses, and people who stepped up to make the tournament possible, shaking his head happily. “This is what pool does,” he said. “It brings people together rather than pushes people apart.”.

Or as Shumway likes to put it: “Pool is the great equalizer.”.
