  • According to recent reports, more U.S.
  • According to recent reports, monthly dispensing of hormone therapy for women aged 40 to 74 more than doubled since 2023, growing from 2 million to 4.9 million, researchers report November 19 in JAMA.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

According to recent reports, more U.S. women are taking menopause hormone therapy, new prescription data suggest.

According to recent reports, monthly dispensing of hormone therapy for women aged 40 to 74 more than doubled since 2023, growing from 2 million to 4.9 million, researchers report November 19 in JAMA. The analysis of U.S. pharmacy dispensing data revealed that this increase began in 2024. The rise continued in 2025, before and after the Food and Drug Administration’s November removal of the black box warning from packaging, and into 2026.

Although the data in the fresh study are aggregate, the researchers used population data to estimate the dispensing rate for this age group, which jumped from 28 prescriptions per 1,000 women to 67 prescriptions per 1,000 over the period studied.

The upcoming study wasn’t designed to determine what’s behind the increase. It’s possible that the evidence regarding hormone therapy’s safety and effectiveness for the treatment of menopause symptoms, such as hot flashes, is reaching more women. Medical groups such as the Menopause Society have recommended menopause hormone therapy for women with symptoms who are younger than 60 or within 10 years of the start of menopause, absent certain risk factors including prior breast cancer and stroke.

According to recent reports, “Greater attention to women’s health, updated medical guidance supporting individualized menopause hormone therapy and social media may all be contributing to increased interest,” says Dana Sarnak, who studies sexual and reproductive health at Johns Hopkins School of Medicine. Anecdotally, her clinician colleagues report more patients seeking menopause care, she says.

Many women and physicians turned away from hormone therapy in the early 2000s after a large study called the Women’s Health Initiative raised safety concerns, which were later considered overblown. Research since then has provided a more nuanced understanding of the benefits and risks of menopause hormone therapy at different ages.

There are safer formulations, including patches and gels, of estrogen today then at the time of the Women’s Health Initiative, for which participants took a pill. The fresh study found that product use increased for transdermal and vaginal estrogen and for progesterone products — women who have their uterus need to take progesterone along with estrogen. The use of oral formulations remained stable. There has been a shortage of estrogen patches in the United States this year, which the U.S. Food and Drug Administration attributes to increasing demand.

  • Sources indicate that on December 18, 2026, Denis Villeneuve’s Dune: Part Three arrives, overcoming the hurdles that had tripped up its predecessors and capping off the decade-in-the-making trilogy in an explosive finale.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favorite films, television shows, and more. This time, we take a look at Dune: Part Three.

The celestial saga that is Frank Herbert’s Dune was practically made for cinema. And yet, for so long, adapting the breathtakingly expansive space opera seemed like something of a curse. David Lynch called his turn at the franchise “a huge, gigantic sadness” in his life, and for Alejandro Jodorowsky, his psychedelically expensive vision for Dune never escaped development hell.

Sources indicate that on December 18, 2026, Denis Villeneuve’s Dune: Part Three arrives, overcoming the hurdles that had tripped up its predecessors and capping off the decade-in-the-making trilogy in an explosive finale. Key to the creation of the trilogy’s universe was keeping it as grounded as possible in ours, with otherworldly planets raised from the volcanic shores of Iceland’s beaches and the banded dunes of the United Arab Emirates’ Liwa Desert. By this point, fans of the first two installments are well-acquainted with settings like the desert planet of Arrakis, but Villeneuve's latest offering delves deeper than ever into their intricate textures. Condé Nast Traveler spoke with production designer Patrice Vermette, location manager Duncan Broadfoot, and director of photography Linus Sandgren to learn how this much-anticipated conclusion was crafted.

According to recent reports, dune: Part Three opens with Fremen forces landing on Enfeil, a wetland planet that stuns the soldiers—used to desert and drought—with its rain. After the battle concludes, the Fremen forces run to the black sand shores of the planet and wade into the sea. This sequence was filmed in Iceland, specifically at Ingólfshöfði Beach, a nearly 250-foot-tall cape and nature reserve. “Denis [Villeneuve] always envisioned a black surface going on for forever, a super flat surface with those low clouds and a band of light, just the sun piercing through the horizon," noted Vermette, “Because of the black sand, we thought, obviously, Iceland. We also looked to see if it was possible to shoot in the Canary Islands.” At the end of the day, Iceland won the booking, leading the team to spearhead an unprecedented film shoot. “When we scouted Iceland, there were multiple options,” said Broadfoot, “but this particular beach that we ended up on is part of a nature reserve, and actually during the summer, you can book puffin tours, but it's never been shot on before, so that was also an appealing aspect.”.

According to recent reports, twenty different locations across the UAE's Liwa Desert were stitched together to comprise Arrakis. Across all three films, the Liwa Desert has been used as a stand-in for the desert planet at the center of it all. “There's a reward to travel to the Liwa Desert, which is close to the border of Saudi Arabia, and the dunes there are like the kind you've seen in Lawrence of Arabia,” said Sandgren, “it's magical just to be there; they're beautiful and contain copper sand and beige sand, and the mix of the two creates these incredible patterns of ripples from the wind each night, and every morning, you see new patterns.” While Sandgren arrived at the desert for the first time to film for Part Three, for Broadfoot and Vermette, returning to the region was like a homecoming for the crew. “Denis [Villenueve] and Patrice [Vermette] are always very keen to find something new that we haven't filmed on before, so that was always the challenge," said Broadfoot, “specifically for Part Three, we had to go deeper and further into the desert than we had done in Part Two.” Filming in the ever-shifting landscape with temperatures peaking at a boiling 120 degrees Fahrenheit posed significant challenges to the shoot, especially as the crew based themselves even deeper into the desert, but getting comfortable was almost counter to the brief. “We love making movies because we thrive on challenges, you know?," said Vermette, "If it was easy, I don't think we'd want to make them.”.

While nearly all of the Arrakis scenes were shot in the Liwa Desert, select sequences were set in Al Ain, the UAE's “Garden City.” Though scenes shot in Al Ain didn't take up as much screen time as those shot in the desert, they span a considerable range as the area served as the setting for Alia Atreides's personal Golgotha—the site where Paul's sadistic younger sister crucifies traitors to the regime—as well as where Chani plays with her young children. “It's an incredible area that is still very unknown,” remarked Vermette. “We shot on a mountain called Jebel Hafeet, the only real mountain in the area,” said Broadfoot, “we scouted the entire mountain and found a plateau up high, which gave you this sort of scale and rocky, craggy environment that's very different than the desert which we were filming in. It was a blank canvas for Patrice [Vermette] to take over and create his beautiful set.”.

Industry observers note that to enhance all the footage that was shot on location, several landscapes from Part Three were recreated using a combination of practical and digital effects across four facilities in Budapest: NFI Studios, HungExpo Budapest Congress and Exhibition Centre, Korda Studios, and Waberer. Much of the battle scene on Enfeil was shot in Budapest. “Most of it was in the back lot of Waberer,” said Vermette, “the amazingly technical thing achieved by Denis [Villeneuve] and Linus [Sandgren] was that they erected a 65-foot-tall by 470-something-foot-long LED screen wall, which was the biggest wall of that sort ever built." The sheer scale of the shoot even required the crew to break out cranes to navigate the airspace around production to move props and equipment around.

Sources indicate that atreides home planet Caladan has made an appearance in all three films of the trilogy. The visual opposite of Arrakis, Caladan was shot on the northwestern Kråkenes region of Norway. The agrestic shoreline is hugged by verdant cliffs and the frosty Norwegian Sea. Caladan's cameos in Part Three come as brief flashes, but Vermette also winks to the filming location in an Easter egg on Arrakis. “In the movie, in the interior courts of Alia's meditation room, there's a tree,” claims Vermette, “I had the idea of putting a pine tree, a Norwegian pine tree there, because it's the roots of their family; it's something that anchors their family. The only pine tree in all of Arrakis is right there.”.

Industry News: What satellites leave behind

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3255 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Astronomy

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It was the lithium that gave it away, indicates Daniel Murphy, an atmospheric chemist at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
  • It was early 2023, in Fairbanks, Alaska, in the deep blue of winter, and Murphy and his colleagues had just sent a plane through the stratosphere, the atmospheric stratum 6 to 31 miles (10 to 50 kilometers) above Earth’s surface where the protective ozone layer lies.
  • Their experiment came as interest was growing in controversial proposals to cool the planet by injecting certain aerosols into the atmosphere — a form of geoengineering.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It was the lithium that gave it away, indicates Daniel Murphy, an atmospheric chemist at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.

It was early 2023, in Fairbanks, Alaska, in the deep blue of winter, and Murphy and his colleagues had just sent a plane through the stratosphere, the atmospheric stratum 6 to 31 miles (10 to 50 kilometers) above Earth’s surface where the protective ozone layer lies.

Their experiment came as interest was growing in controversial proposals to cool the planet by injecting certain aerosols into the atmosphere — a form of geoengineering. The team hoped to get a baseline measurement of the chemistry of the upper atmosphere, before any geoengineering experiments altered the hard-to-reach atmospheric layer.

The lithium showed they were too late.

The team expected to find trace amounts of metals naturally deposited by meteoroids, which constantly bombard and burn up in Earth’s atmosphere. But their data showed way more lithium in stratospheric particles than is typically present in meteoroids.

Recent findings suggest that “That’s what led us to the other metals,” Murphy notes. Analyzing their samples, they also found higher than expected levels of aluminum, plus significant amounts of other metals like copper and lead that are scarcely found in meteoroids and must have come from some other source. Then there were the more exotic metals like niobium and hafnium, which appeared in their samples in the same ratio as in an alloy used to manufacture rocket engine nozzles.

Recent findings suggest that the data pointed to an obvious culprit: human-made objects such as satellites and spent rocket stages that fall back to Earth from orbit and reenter the atmosphere. On the way down, they wear away and disintegrate under the heat of friction — a process known as ablation.

Later that year in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), Murphy and his colleagues reported that 10% of stratospheric aerosol particles carried metals from spacecraft.

The number was shocking, but not altogether surprising. Reentries have been rising sharply in recent years as corporations and countries began launching megaconstellations of thousands of satellites, like SpaceX’s Starlink. And all those satellites will inevitably deorbit.

Recent findings suggest that since Murphy and his colleagues’ 2023 report, it’s become clear that human-made satellites are now dumping more of certain metals into the upper atmosphere than meteoroids naturally do. This influx has raised concerns that the metals might catalyze chemical reactions that destroy ozone, alter cloud formation, or boost or buffer the greenhouse effect.

According to recent reports, researchers say it’s too soon to know for sure if the metals are a serious environmental problem. But megaconstellations are growing faster than our ability to close these knowledge gaps.

Recent findings suggest that at the same time, the uncertainty over whether regulators might have to act presents a significant risk to the space industry, says Martin Ross of the Aerospace Corporation, a research and development nonprofit based in El Segundo, California, and a co-author of the 2023 study. “We would call it an enterprise risk,” says Ross, “in that the longer we wait to see if there is something going on, the bigger the mitigation will be — if there needs to be any mitigation — down the line.”.

From our vantage point on Earth, space may be incomprehensibly vast, but the orbital environment is not.

Six years ago, according to the U.S. Space Force’s public catalog, there were some 13,700 trackable objects circling in low Earth orbit; last year, the number had climbed to nearly 25,000. Disposing of satellites in the atmosphere reduces overcrowding and the risk of uncontrolled objects crashing into each other — and potentially setting off a chain of collisions that wipe out key space-based technologies or turn Earth orbit into an impenetrable debris field.

RELATED: Our increasingly cluttered skies.

“Reentry is the only sustainable, short-term way of cleaning up the orbital environment,” says José Pedro Ferreira, a doctoral candidate in astronautical engineering at the University of Southern California (USC) in Los Angeles, who left an industry job for academia in the early 2020s when it became clear that reentry could have unintended consequences. “We need to do it, otherwise we may undermine our capability of accessing orbit.”.

But operators are also typically held responsible by their national regulators for any damages their spacecraft cause on the ground, and for decades the industry has designed spacecraft to burn up as much as possible in the atmosphere to minimize the risk to lives and infrastructure on the ground, a principle known as design for demise.

Recent findings suggest that as a result, the space industry has long perceived its impacts to Earth as minimal. But in the age of megaconstellations, that’s no longer the case.

“As with everything, we live in a closed system,” states Ferreira, “and things do not disappear.”.

Industry observers note that spaceX introduced its first 60 satellites into orbit in May 2019 to bring internet to even remote regions of the globe; less than a decade later, Starlink’s constellation is more than 10,000 satellites strong. Starlink already comprises roughly two-thirds of active satellites, and SpaceX prepares to grow it to as many as 42,000. Other countries and corporations are not far behind: Amazon Leo is authorized by the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to operate roughly 7,700 satellites; China has plans to deploy some 28,000.

Not only are we launching more than ever, but we’re also bringing spacecraft back down faster than ever before.

Sources indicate that for decades, spacecraft have been designed to burn up as much as possible upon reentry to minimize risks to those on the ground. As a result, the space industry has long perceived its impacts to Earth as minimal. But in the age of megaconstellations, that’s no longer the case.

Historically, satellite operators had what Ferreira calls a “gentleman’s agreement” to deorbit their spacecraft within 25 years of mission termination to prevent orbital clutter. Recently, some national authorities have begun enforcing even tighter timelines. The FCC, for example, now enforces a five-year window.

“If you have 50,000 satellites in orbit, which is almost surely going to be reached in the not too distant future, with a design lifetime of five years,” Murphy states, “that would mean a satellite would be reentering and burning up in the atmosphere on average more than once an hour.”.

It has been revealed that operators of megaconstellations may use even shorter timelines for deorbiting satellites, according to Ferreira, bringing them down at the first sign of malfunction. “Which is great from a standpoint of orbital sustainability,” he indicates, “but it starts raising the question more and more about what the impacts are in the atmosphere.”.

There are reasons to be concerned.

Recent findings suggest that aluminum, for example, which makes up the bulk of most spacecraft, may form aluminum oxides as it breaks down during ablation, which can kick-start a chain of chemical reactions that eat away at ozone, Earth’s main shield against UV radiation. Some atmospheric models suggest that metals from spacecraft in stratospheric particles could seed polar stratospheric clouds, further accelerating ozone depletion.

Injecting aluminum into the upper atmosphere is also the basis of many controversial geoengineering aims. Aluminum compounds would block radiation from the Sun, which could cool down our warming planet. But they might also entrap radiation reflected off the surface of the ocean, which could increase surface temperatures. Opposition to geoengineering has so far stymied any field experiments, but with the number of reentries rising from a few hundred to many thousands per year, an uncontrolled geoengineering experiment on a grand scale may have already begun.

“The metals are at the same altitude range as the ozone layer, so we have to be concerned about what they would do,” Murphy says. “We don’t know it’s bad, but we don’t know it isn’t bad either.”.

Recent findings suggest that one reason it’s so difficult to predict the impacts of ablation is that we don’t yet understand what happens to spacecraft during ablation. “We reenter things all the time and we have been since the moment we started launching spacecraft,” says Stijn Lemmens, a space debris mitigation analyst at the European Space Agency (ESA). “It’s fascinating, for something which is so ubiquitous, how little we actually know about it, and how little we used to care about it.”.

Operators have long been incentivized to design spacecraft to burn up as much as possible in the atmosphere, and decades of this design for demise ethos has given the space industry a solid idea of how much material — or how little — will make it to the ground when objects burn through the atmosphere.

But in terms of that material that is ablated, “we’re really in the dark,” claims Ross. Previous studies have suggested that around 90% of the bodies of orbiting satellites and spent upper stages could be vaporized, later condensing into the nanosized particles the team detected. But, says Ross, “we really don’t understand how these vehicles melt, how they break apart, how they form smoke trails.”.

Recent findings suggest that to quantify the impacts on the atmosphere, researchers start with atmospheric models and then add ablated material, examining how those particles interact with the natural stratospheric background via complex chemical reactions and physical processes like mixing. But the outputs of the atmospheric models are at the moment held back by our limited understanding of the fiery, complex process of ablation — details like what compounds are being emitted and what size particles are being formed. “We’re basically guessing at this point,” Ross notes. “And we’re getting to the limit of what we can do with guessing.”.

To do better, scientists are developing upcoming models of the physics and chemistry of ablation itself. At USC, Ferreira and his colleagues model how ablation produces aluminum oxides in the upper atmosphere, providing atmospheric researchers with inputs for both emissions and particle size. In a 2024 study in Geophysical Research Letters, the team reported that a 550-pound (250 kilograms) satellite — about the size of your average megaconstellation satellite — could deposit some 66 pounds (30 kg) of aluminum oxide nanoparticles in the upper atmosphere. Such particles could remain aloft for upwards of 30 years, potentially catalyzing ozone-destroying reactions as they settle throughout the stratosphere for decades after reentry.

Sources indicate that but state-of-the-art ablation models don’t always agree on what products are being formed, according to Ross. A model from researchers at the University of Leeds in the U.K. suggests that aluminum hydroxide, rather than aluminum oxide, may be the main byproduct.

To validate ablation models and get more useful data from atmospheric models, we need more measurements from reentries. How an object breaks apart as it tumbles through the air is a messy process — a product of astrophysics, fluid mechanics, materials science, and engineering. “You cannot reproduce it on Earth,” Lemmens states. “There is no facility large enough to, in one assessment, combine all the effects.”.

That means scientists need to measure ablation where it’s actually taking place — “take instruments and put them on airplanes and go out and watch these things reenter,” Ross says.

In a recent development, since the beginning of the Space Age, these kinds of measurements have only been taken a handful of times. Observing space objects from an airplane as they streak through the atmosphere is difficult work — and potentially dangerous. Most reentering objects are uncontrolled, making it hard to predict exactly where the object will hit the atmosphere and how much of it will burn up in the process. Researchers need a degree of certainty to avoid sending a plane full of scientists and sensors up into a debris field. “These types of reentries, which are destructive and still predictable so that you can get close, are extremely rare,” Lemmens notes.

It has been revealed that but in 2024, ESA got lucky. The first of four Cluster II satellites — rolled out in 2000 to study Earth’s magnetosphere — was poised to reenter the atmosphere, and the agency had a pretty good idea of exactly where and when it would break up over the southern Pacific Ocean.

According to recent reports, “We could get close,” Lemmens says. “The drawback is it was in broad daylight, which had not been attempted before on this level of detail.”.

It has been revealed that in daytime, the team would have no visual confirmation of reentry, and it would be harder to get clean data than at night. The team had to trust they were pointing their instruments at the right spot, and then look at their data after the fact to see if they caught it. “In the end, it’s a leap of faith,” Lemmens indicates. “You predict as well as you can, you fly the plane as well as you can, but in the end, you do it all in the blind,” he says.

In a recent development, on Sept. 8, a team of scientists took off from Easter Island on a modified Dassault Falcon 900 business jet packed with instruments, and pointed their cameras just above the bright blue horizon roughly 500 miles (800 km) away.

According to recent reports, the team used spectroscopic instruments to identify which vapors were coming from the ablating satellite. Since the team knew the material makeup of the satellite, they could gauge its surface temperatures during reentry, as the appearance of specific ions would indicate a certain material had reached its melting point.

Altogether, they captured about 20 seconds of the reentry. Two more satellites from the same cluster were set to reenter within 24 hours of each other on Aug. 31 and Sept. 1, 2026, giving ESA another opportunity to capture more of the reentry process and to fully reconstruct the breakup.

For researchers, one upside to the rapid and unmitigated increase in satellite reentries is more opportunities to capture the process in action.

According to recent reports, some of the best data yet to come will be collected by ESA’s Draco mission, in which the agency plans to build and launch a satellite with the “sole purpose of falling apart again,” states Lemmens. Draco will launch in 2027 with an indestructible capsule that will survive reentry, protecting the data collected from the surface of the satellite as it’s torn apart by the atmosphere.

Industry observers note that researchers will be able to combine these onboard data with remote observations, using them to improve or validate existing models of ablation. “That means we, for the first time, will actually have the full story without any ambiguities,” Lemmens claims.

Once a scientific consensus is reached, then mitigation measures, whether technological or regulatory, can be deployed.

Sources indicate that if research confirms that one material or another in spacecraft is particularly damaging to the atmosphere, for example, space operators can remove and replace it. “That was the basis of the success of the Montreal Protocol,” states Ross.

After scientists discovered a hole in the ozone layer in the 1980s, every country in the world signed on to the Montreal Protocol, an international agreement to control the ozone-depleting substances humans were emitting into the atmosphere. The hole has been shrinking ever since. Signed in 1987, the agreement is widely considered one of the most successful environmental treaties to date. Since then, however, other global climate agreements have not fared as well.

According to recent reports, still, many remain optimistic, including Ross. He points to the commercial space industry’s track record of working with regulators and astronomers to reduce space debris and light pollution. “There is some current flowing in those lines,” he says.

RELATED: Can robots save Earth orbit?

Industry observers note that some operators have already expressed a commitment to acting on whatever guidelines come out of research on the atmospheric risks. “The difficulty that I have as a responsible operator is, in this particular case, I don’t know what to do,” Vijay Thakur, a technical authority at French satellite corporation Eutelsat, said at an October 2025 panel at the Secure World Foundation’s 7th Summit for Space Sustainability in Paris. There are clear brightness limits he can follow to mitigate impacts to the astronomical community, he noted, but no such guidelines exist yet for atmospheric impacts.

“I want to put the right technical requirements, for me as the operator customer, onto industry so they can build what I need to operate and take it up and bring it back down without damaging anything from 0 kilometers to the von Kármán line,” Thakur said, referring to the commonly accepted boundary of outer space at 62 miles high (100 km). “Help.”.

There are some design tweaks currently available that could reduce emissions and help more of each spacecraft survive reentry, including non-ablative heat shields and inflatable aerodynamic decelerators, according to Adam Mitchell, a materials and processes evaluation engineer at ESA.

Sources indicate that of course, the more of a spacecraft that survives reentry, the greater the risk on the ground during uncontrolled reentries — and most reentries are uncontrolled. “There is this balance between sustainability and safety, but when it comes to human safety, there is no compromise at all,” Chris Young, space sustainability senior lead at the U.K. Space Agency, remarked at the same Secure World Foundation panel. “Design for demise has to take priority.”.

In a recent development, satellite builders could also consider replacing problematic metals — but that comes with its own trade-offs. In 2024, the world’s first wooden satellite, LignoSat, launched to orbit in a partnership between Kyoto University and Japanese logging firm Sumitomo Forestry. A cube of magnolia wood panels, LignoSat will give researchers insights into how well wood holds up in the space environment, and how cleanly it burns up in the atmosphere. Carbon fiber is another material of interest, according to Ferreira. But these organic materials may release black carbon into the upper atmosphere, which may absorb sunlight or reflect it, depending on the structure the carbon takes.

Recent findings suggest that ross thinks we can close the remaining knowledge gaps in short order — and that those lessons can be applied almost immediately. “We can do that before the next generation of satellites comes along,” he states, “but we just need the resources.”.

A cultural revolution is coming for the industry, regardless of what’s discovered about the impacts to the atmosphere. “The one-use, nonrecyclable culture that we have in space, of, ‘We’ll launch something to space with rare Earth minerals that are of limited supply and then burn them all up in the atmosphere after one use,’ that is unsustainable,” mentioned Young.

A sustainable future — one that balances both Earth and space sustainability — will involve creating something we haven’t quite nailed yet in our earthbound industries. “We need to move beyond the single-use mindset that at the moment defines much of spacecraft design and accelerate the transition toward an in-space circular economy,” Mitchell says.

According to recent reports, can we do in space what we’ve failed to do on Earth? Right now, researchers are gathering data as fast as they can, as fast as resourcing allows, to inform models of ablation and atmospheric processes that will eventually be validated by measurements taken during reentry.

Then, equipped with actionable data, we can act.

Kate Wheeling is a freelance journalist based in Santa Barbara, California. She writes about the environment and humans’ relationship with the natural world. Her work has appeared in The Atlantic, Smithsonian magazine, The Daily Beast, and Mother Jones.

The Sky This Week from November 20 to 27: Uranus at opposition

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2049 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Astronomy

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, friday, November 20The Moon passes 5° north of Neptune at 8 A.M.
  • In a recent development, in the northeast, Auriga the Charioteer is above the horizon by 7 P.M.
  • Recent findings suggest that why are these called the Kids?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, friday, November 20The Moon passes 5° north of Neptune at 8 A.M. EST, then passes 7° north of Saturn at 8 P.M. EST. They remain visible all evening, forming a triangle in southern Pisces and northern Cetus. The Moon and Saturn are visible to the naked eye, but Neptune will be invisible without binoculars or a telescope. Check out last week’s column for more details on how to view the celestial trio.

In a recent development, in the northeast, Auriga the Charioteer is above the horizon by 7 P.M. local time. Its brightest star is Capella, which shines at magnitude 0.1 and sits some 43 light-years away. Just southeast of this star, you’ll find another triangle in the sky tonight. This small shape is an asterism about 2.7° long, known as the Kids. It consists of Epsilon (ε), Zeta (ζ), and Eta (η) Aurigae, which range from 3rd (Epsilon and Eta) to 4th (Zeta) magnitude.

Recent findings suggest that why are these called the Kids? Capella’s name essentially means “She-Goat,” according to the late stellar expert Jim Kaler. These fainter stars cluster close by the brighter star like goat kids around their mother.

Mercury reaches greatest western elongation (20°) at 7 P.M. EST; it will be visible before dawn tomorrow morning, so keep reading for more details.

Sources indicate that sunrise: 6:51 A.M. Sunset: 4:40 P.M. Moonrise: 2:04 P.M. Moonset: 2:12 A.M. Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (84%) *Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

Recent findings suggest that saturday, November 21If you’ve got a viewing site with a clear eastern horizon, this morning offers a great opportunity to spot the solar system’s innermost planet. Look for Mercury about an hour before sunrise, when it reaches 7° high and shines at magnitude –0.5. The planet reached its greatest western elongation from our Sun yesterday evening, and is now 20° west of our star in the sky.

Located in Libra, the tiny world sits to the far lower left of bright Venus, higher in the sky. Venus is in the constellation Virgo, standing just north (to the upper left) of the bright star Spica. Another bright star, Arcturus in Boötes, hangs to that pair’s far upper left.

Pull out a telescope to check out the size and phase of each planet. Start with Venus, whose disk spans a hefty 46” — right now larger than Jupiter’s apparent size in our sky. Despite its impressive width, however, the disk of Venus appears as just a sliver, only 19% lit. Slide down to Mercury for comparison, and see that its phase is much larger — 62% — while the planet’s overall apparent width is much smaller, just 7”.

If you’re able, keep watching Mercury day by day in the morning sky. Its gibbous phase will continue growing, reaching 84% lit by the end of the month.

Industry observers note that sunrise: 6:52 A.M. Sunset: 4:39 P.M. Moonrise: 2:29 P.M. Moonset: 3:22 A.M. Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (92%).

In a recent development, sunday, November 22With the Moon not far from Full, its western limb is now coming into view as the Sun rises across the lunar landscape. The large, flat-floored crater Schickard is prominent in the southwest, near the small, circular Mare Humorum. Because the nearly Full Moon is so bright, you may want to use a Moon filter before you turn your telescope toward our satellite tonight for a closer look.

Zoom in on Schickard to discover that its dark floor isn’t perfectly smooth, but pockmarked by smaller craters that came after the initial, larger crater’s formation. Its outer walls are shallow and beaten down, also showing off their age. Look closely at Schickard’s western wall to see how it has slumped, particularly compared to the eastern side of the crater rim. Also compare the texture of the southwestern portion of the crater floor, which appears quite rough, to the rest of the crater, which is smoother. The difference arises because most of the crater was flooded by lava, which didn’t quite reach its southwestern regions.

It has been revealed that stretching about 130 miles (210 kilometers) across, Schickard is roughly 4 billion years old and was formed by a giant impact. Because it sits so near the limb of the Moon, it often looks oblong from our vantage point on Earth — but from above, orbiters have shown it is really quite circular in shape.

In a recent development, sunrise: 6:53 A.M. Sunset: 4:39 P.M. Moonrise: 2:59 P.M. Moonset: 4:34 A.M. Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (97%).

Sources indicate that monday, November 23A few hours after sunset, the house-shaped constellation Cepheus stands on the point of its roof in the northern sky, above the Little Dipper. Cepheus is home to several lovely double stars, including Xi (ξ) Cephei, also known as Kurhah.

Glowing at magnitude 4.3, Kurhah is not one of the stars in the house’s outline, but lies within the boxy base. You can find it about midway between Alderamin (Alpha [α] Cep) and Iota (ι) Cep, the western and eastern points in the house’s box, respectively. Kurhah’s two components are separated by just under 8” — once you find the star in binoculars or your finder scope, any telescope will split them. The pair consists of a brighter magnitude 4.4 primary, which glows white, and a fainter magnitude 6.5 secondary, which appears to many observers as yellow.

Recent findings suggest that if you happen to have a large telescope, you may want to give a nearby deep-sky treasure a try: planetary nebula NGC 7139 sits just 2° west-southwest of Kurhah, but it requires a large scope (8 inches at least) to spot, as this bubble of gas glows at magnitude 13.3. If available, an Oxygen-III filter will help bring it out by dimming the nearby stars.

Sources indicate that sunrise: 6:54 A.M. Sunset: 4:38 P.M. Moonrise: 3:37 P.M. Moonset: 5:52 A.M. Moon Phase: Full.

Tuesday, November 24Full Moon occurs at 9:54 A.M. EST, bringing us our second Super Moon of the year. A Super Moon occurs when the Moon reaches Full phase close to perigee, its closest point to Earth, making our satellite appear larger and brighter than average. The November Full Moon is also called the Beaver Moon.

A few hours earlier, before dawn, the Full Moon passes through the Pleiades star cluster (M45) in Taurus, occulting several of its bright stars. This is an easy event to watch, visible to the naked eye — or you can get a closer view with binoculars or a telescope (just note that you may want a Moon filter if available, as our satellite is so big and bright). The timing of the event will depend heavily on your location; note that it begins right around sunrise along the East Coast, so observers there may only see the Moon approaching the famous group of stars.

The 5th-magnitude star Celaeno (16 Tauri) disappears behind the Moon’s leading edge just moments before 6 A.M. CST, followed minutes later by 4th-magnitude Taygeta (19 Tau). Next to vanish is 4th-magnitude Maia (20 Tau) just before 6:20 A.M. CST, followed rapidly by Sterope (21 Tau) a few minutes later. The latter two may be difficult to catch from the Midwest without optical aid, as sunrise is fast approaching. If you are using binoculars or a telescope in this region, make sure to put them away several minutes ahead of sunrise from your location. Celaeno reappears around 6:40 A.M. CST, 15 minutes or so before sunrise.

For specific timings from your location, visit the International Occultation Timing Association at http://www.lunar-occultations.com/bobgraze/index.html.

The Moon then passes 5° north of Uranus (also in Taurus) at 2 P.M. EST. Over in the constellation Leo, Mars passes 1.8° north of Regulus at 5 P.M. EST.

Sunrise: 6:55 A.M. Sunset: 4:38 P.M. Moonrise: 4:24 P.M. Moonset: 7:10 A.M. Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (99%).

Wednesday, November 25The Moon reaches perigee, the closest point to Earth in its orbit, at 4:01 P.M. EST. At that time, our satellite will stand 223,288 miles (359,347 km) away.

Recent findings suggest that the distant ice giant Uranus reaches opposition tonight at 6 P.M. EST. Opposition is the best time to view a planet in our sky, and it’s visible roughly from dusk until dawn. Because Uranus is faint — magnitude 5.6 — you’ll want to give it a few hours after sunset to climb away from both light pollution and turbulent air near the horizon. Around 10 P.M. local time, you’ll find Uranus midway between the bright star Aldebaran and the Pleiades star cluster in Taurus the Bull, about 60° above the southeastern horizon. It sits some 1.5° south of 4th-magnitude 37 Tauri.

Although Uranus can be visible to the naked eye under clear, dark conditions, the bright waning Moon is nearby, so pull out binoculars or a telescope to view the far-off planet tonight. Once you land on its location, look for a “flat,” grayish-colored star. Uranus’ disk spans 4”, so you will likely be able to tell it is circular, rather than a pinpoint of light like any background stars.

Sunrise: 6:56 A.M. Sunset: 4:37 P.M. Moonrise: 5:24 P.M. Moonset: 8:26 A.M. Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (96%).

Thursday, November 26Celebrate Thanksgiving with a celestial turkey: The famous Orion Nebula (M42) is also playfully known as the Turkey Nebula because it looks to some like a turkey, particularly in deep astrophotos. But whether you’re a photographer or not, this bright deep-sky treat is easy to enjoy tonight while dinner digests.

It has been revealed that by about 9 P.M. local time, Orion the Hunter has risen above the eastern horizon, his recognizable three-star belt standing in a vertical line. The lowest star in that line is Alnitak (Zeta [ζ] Orionis), and the Orion Nebula lies just 3.7° south-southwest of this star, to its lower right on the sky this evening. You might be able to spot its glow without optical aid, although the bright Moon nearby may make that difficult. Binoculars or any telescope will easily show it.

At 4th magnitude and spanning some 85’ by 60’, the Orion Nebula is a huge and bright star-forming region that sits roughly 1,350 light-years from Earth. In the brightest portion of the nebula lies a small grouping of young stars called the Trapezium Cluster. Take your time with this gorgeous sight, scanning around the region to pick out detail in the nebulosity. And if you are an astrophotographer, consider turning the view into a Thanksgiving memory to share for years to come.

Industry observers note that sunrise: 6:58 A.M. Sunset: 4:37 P.M. Moonrise: 6:35 P.M. Moonset: 9:33 A.M. Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (91%).

Industry observers note that friday, November 27The Moon-free window for observing Comet 161P/Hartley-IRAS reopens tonight, the same day the comet reaches perihelion, the closest point to the Sun in its 21½-year orbit. It has been a fairly stable 10th to 11th magnitude, and although it has no appreciable tail, the nucleus’ green glow has been notable in recent astrophotos.

It has been revealed that you’ll find Hartley-IRAS in the west a few hours after sunset. Around 7 P.M. local time it is still 30° high, well above the turbulent air near the ground that can muddy astronomical views. Tonight the comet is in western Sagitta, about 6.3° north-northeast of 3rd-magnitude Zeta (ζ) Aquilae. Even a small (4-inch) scope will net you a view, but larger apertures will show more detail around the nucleus, allowing you to look for features such as a sharpened southern flank as it flies into the solar headwind.

While you’re in this region, make sure to sweep just 2.1° northeast of the comet’s location to spot the famous Coathanger asterism in Vulpecula. This 1°-long grouping of stars looks just like its namesake, with the hook on the southern side of the hanger’s arms.

According to recent reports, sunrise: 6:59 A.M. Sunset: 4:36 P.M. Moonrise: 7:53 P.M. Moonset: 10:26 A.M. Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (82%).

Alison Klesman is senior editor of Astronomy magazine. She holds a Ph.D. in astronomy and has studied a variety of topics, from minor planets to supermassive black holes.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • “When children and adolescents have access to sufficient, high-quality food, they grow taller, within the constraints of genetic factors,” Manon Stephan, an economic historian at Germany’s University of Tübingen, said in a statement.
  • Sources indicate that to test that idea, Stephan and colleagues at Tübingen and the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology examined 18,457 bones from 783 sites in 45 countries.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the dairy industry’s “Milk. It does a body good” slogan has some historical backing, at least in Europe. That’s one of the more surprising takeaways from a large study that used ancient skeletons to track how well people lived across Europe and Asia over the past 7,000 years. The researchers based their analysis on one telling measurement: human height.

“When children and adolescents have access to sufficient, high-quality food, they grow taller, within the constraints of genetic factors,” Manon Stephan, an economic historian at Germany’s University of Tübingen, said in a statement. “Therefore, height enables us to draw conclusions about living standards.”.

Sources indicate that to test that idea, Stephan and colleagues at Tübingen and the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology examined 18,457 bones from 783 sites in 45 countries. In the study, published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, the team estimated people’s heights from their long bones. They then tracked how average height changed in each region and compared those changes with shifts in population density and technology.

Industry observers note that in China, men were taller 7,000 years ago, averaging 5 feet 10 inches. Over time, however, their height steadily declined, reaching a low of just 5 feet 3 inches on average in the 19th century. Chinese women’s height also declined, though less drastically, falling from an average of 5 feet 2 inches 7,000 years ago to 4 feet 10 inches in more recent times.

According to recent reports, trends like these would be nearly impossible to trace through written records alone. “In many parts of the world, any written sources that would allow us to draw conclusions about economic development appear quite late on our timeline and are patchy in their distribution,” Stephan said. “That’s why we rely on bones.” The bones in question came from 22 Asian and 23 European countries and were taken from the graves of commoners in both densely populated and rural regions.

In Europe, by contrast, the trends went in a different direction. Around 5,000 years ago, men in northern Europe averaged just 5 feet 4 inches. However, the study authors wrote, as pastoralist peoples migrated from the steppes of Eastern Europe and western Siberia, they brought with them more advanced dairy farming and the genetic trait of lactose tolerance. This led to greater consumption of dairy products, which the study identifies as a leading factor in increased height. Average heights in northern Europe continued to climb into the early Middle Ages, but sometime between 500 and 1000 C.E., they began to decline, a trend that lasted until the end of the 19th century.

Women’s heights followed a similar pattern. China and Japan experienced the steepest declines, while Europe saw a rise, though a less steep one than among men.

The authors wrote that “human stature is a valuable indicator of nutritional status and health.” Reconstructing this indicator offers insight into which societies provided better health and nutrition to their people. Surprisingly, technological progress did not prove to be a major factor in improving either.

It has been revealed that “Our study also confirmed that technological progress does not automatically lead to greater height,” said Jörg Baten, a professor of economic history at the University of Tübingen. “In China, for example, fresh, higher-yielding rice varieties and other innovations were introduced in the 11th century [C.E.]. While the higher yields enabled the empire to remain the dominant power, they did not subsequently lead to a better standard of living for the general population. Instead, population density increased: People had more children because this was seen as a form of security in old age. This meant, however, that each individual had not more to eat, but less. And importantly the quality declined, for example, in terms of high-quality protein.”.

Europe’s findings on technology mirrored Asia’s. Improved technology helped support denser populations, but it didn’t increase average height or necessarily improve the nutritional value of food.

Going forward, the authors hope to link more of these changes in height to shifts in social conditions or developments in agriculture. “This requires further research,” said Mark Hudson, an archaeologist at the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology. “However, the statistical data reveal trends and provide clues as to when these changes occurred.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • WASHINGTON — A part of the brain famous for listening is key for talking, too.
  • It has been revealed that data collected from people as they listen and try to talk show that this brain region, a small spot inside a larger area called Wernicke’s area, has a more expansive job than researchers thought when it comes to communicating.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

WASHINGTON — A part of the brain famous for listening is key for talking, too.

It has been revealed that data collected from people as they listen and try to talk show that this brain region, a small spot inside a larger area called Wernicke’s area, has a more expansive job than researchers thought when it comes to communicating. The results may help efforts to restore people’s voices. The results presented November 15 at the annual meeting of the Society for Neuroscience and published November 19 in Science.The study provides convincing evidence that this brain spot is critical for speech production, says neurologist and language researcher Jeffrey Binder of the Medical College of Wisconsin in Milwaukee. “My hope is that this study will help scientists and clinicians accept a more accurate interpretation of this focal area” as an early stop on the pathway to saying a word.

A small part of the brain, just above the left ear, was first described in 1874 by a neurologist Carl Wernicke as necessary for making sense of speech. People with damage there had trouble comprehending words. But some people also had trouble producing them. “Sounds were swapped, words were replaced with near misses,” Edward Chang of the University of California, San Francisco, stated in a news briefing. “The basic question has been, ‘Why would damage to a hearing area of the brain break the ability to speak?’ That question has been open for 150 years.”The new research offers an answer: A small bit of Wernicke’s area (to be extremely specific, the left posterior superior temporal gyrus or lpSTG ) becomes active just before a word is spoken. “Every word that you have said today began in that small part above your left ear about a quarter of a second before you said it,” Chang said.

The finding adds to growing evidence that brain areas are more complex than people have appreciated, indicates neuroscientist Leigh Hochberg at Brown University in Providence, R.I. “I believe that one of the things we are going to learn over the next five, 10 years of this research, is that each part of the brain that, we were taught as a med student or a grad student, does this, probably does that and a whole lot more.”.

Sources indicate that scientists measured brain activity in 28 people before they had surgery for epilepsy or tumors. They were able to see that this brain region kicked on as a person listened to words, and also just before they attempted to speak. Cells there had preferences for certain sorts of words, long ones, for instance. “It’s more active when you’re about to say the word caterpillar than when you’re about to say the word cat,” said Matthew Leonard, a cognitive neuroscientist at UCSF.

Sources indicate that electrical stimulation to this small bit of brain also interfered with people’s ability to talk. “What we found was that stimulation, really only in this lpSTG area, disrupted this speech production when it was delivered just prior to speaking,” stated UCSF bioengineer Alexander Silva.

Some efforts to make implanted devices that can help restore speech to people who no longer talk focus on the motor cortex, a part of the brain that controls the movements required for speech. This bit of Wernicke’s area offers an additional spot to consider, Silva said. “What if you could target a single brain region and gain access to the full spectrum of speech, from listening all the way up to speech production?”.

Experimental brain implants in two volunteers with paralysis were able to detect both what they heard and what they were trying to say, the researchers report in the study.

The discovery may help scientists better understand situations that involve both hearing and speaking, such as speech or comprehension differences in people with autism, or how children first begin learning to talk, Chang said.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The best cruise lines for families with kids and teens are likely more diverse than you realize. Many are the substantial-ship brands you see in ads, tricked out with waterslides, dazzling reveals, and an abundance of onboard restaurants to satisfy picky toddlers and ravenous teens alike. Yet other family-friendly cruise lines let mom and dad get the taste of luxury they crave or provide the entire crew with adventure and active pursuits around the globe.

According to recent reports, I’ve sailed on more than 80 cruises, sometimes with my kids, often surrounded by everyone else’s. I can tell you that the best family cruises won’t make bedtime any easier, but they will do their best to make sure no one in your crew ever feels the need to cry, “I’m so bored!”.

A cruise line that devotes a day to all things LEGO and offers a special baby laundry service gets top marks in my list of the best cruises for kids and teens. MSC Cruises is a European significant-ship cruise line that’s making waves in the US with its family-friendly mega-ships.

Five kids clubs for babies, preschoolers, kids, tweens, and teens target activities to different age groups. MSC is constantly developing new family programs, including family discos, original game demonstrates, drone races for teens, MasterChef at Sea cooking challenges, and obstacle course competitions.

World Class ships feature the top-deck Family Aventura District with an outdoor adventure area (including an overwater swing ride), water park, and an indoor space for rollerskating and bumper cars. Select ships offer arcades with a Formula 1 simulator and virtual reality attractions or the Robotron robotic-arm thrill ride. The line’s US–based ships also feature connecting cabins and family-friendly dining (the pizza and gelato are superb).

Families looking for an exclusive hideaway can book rooms in The Yacht Club, with access to a private restaurant, lounge, sun deck, and pool—all ages welcome.

Standout itinerary: 7-night Caribbean and Bahamas cruise on MSC World America sailing round-trip from Miami.

Royal Caribbean operates the world’s largest, most activity-laden ships, and its calling card is high-energy fun for all ages.

Families can rock climb, zip-line, ice skate, splash down waterslides, solve escape room challenges, and enjoy entertainment ranging from musical performances to acrobatic high-dive dance indicates without leaving the ship. The enormous Icon Class ships even have a dedicated family deck called Surfside, where kid-friendly restaurants, splash playgrounds, and a carousel are surrounded by cabins and suites designed to accommodate families.

On all ships, parents can steal away for adults-only fun when they drop the littlest cruisers at onboard nurseries run by professional caregivers. Kids can make crafts, play games, and do science experiments at onboard camps operating morning until late in spacious, tech-enhanced multipurpose spaces. Teens have their own hip hangouts for foosball, video games, and evening parties with latest friends. The whole family can later reunite to share the day’s fun over Johnny Rockets burgers and shakes or perhaps a teppanyaki dinner with showman chefs.

Standout itinerary: 7-night Perfect Day CocoCay and Caribbean cruise on Icon of the Seas sailing round-trip from Miami.

According to recent reports, disney’s rapidly expanding cruise ship segment isn’t just for preschoolers reveling in their Frozen era. Its itineraries across the Caribbean, Alaska, and Europe offer family fun for a wide range of ages, including adults. Plus, its short itineraries pair nicely with a theme park visit.

Entertainment is a highlight, from live on-stage productions of classics like Moana and Beauty and the Beast to mealtime shows themed around the Marvel universe and Coco. The ships’ movie theaters screen first-run flicks across the Disney-owned studios (not just animated classics), and the once-a-cruise Pirate Night is the only time you’ll ever see fireworks rolled out from a cruise ship.

According to recent reports, disney Cruise Line’s enormous youth facilities, also with nurseries and teen clubs, offer activities themed to Disney IP. Kids can design a superhero suit or theme park ride, pilot the Millennium Falcon, and join Olaf for virtual snowball fights. The line also treats adults very well with pools, sun decks, fine-dining restaurants (including ones by Michelin-starred chefs), bars themed around The Haunted Mansion and Star Wars, and cafés exclusive to travelers ages 18+.

In a recent development, disney supports traveling families in less flashy ways, as well. Cabins feature extra berths for kids, split bathrooms with a toilet in one room and a sink in the other, and room-dividing curtains so grownups won’t distract would-be nappers. Waiters will purée baby food and cut up your kid’s dinner all while cracking silly jokes and performing magic tricks. When the travel logistics are handled, families can focus more on having fun.

Standout itinerary: 4-night Bahamas cruise on Disney Wish sailing round-trip from Port Canaveral.

Retirees rule the world of river cruising, but AmaWaterways has teamed up with Adventures by Disney (Disney’s escorted travel arm) to offer select Rhine and Danube cruises to families.

Sources indicate that disney’s onboard Adventure Guides handle all the logistics in port, from escorting tours in every destination to managing dietary restrictions and directing guests to the best restaurants and local treats. On board, they host movie evenings and kids-only dinners so parents can enjoy a leisurely meal with adult conversation.

Adventures by Disney swaps the history- and culture-focused walking tours typical of river cruise excursions for alpine coasters, amusement parks, river kayaking, and visits to chocolate factories. A selection of winery visits and slower-paced tours appeal to multigenerational families willing to split up childcare responsibilities ashore.

AmaWaterways, in turn, has specially built ships with more third-berth and connecting cabins than the typical river ship. It supplements its regional cuisine with kid favorites, while introducing the whole family to specialties like French macarons and German sausages.

Standout itinerary: 7-night Rhine River cruise from Basel, Switzerland, to Amsterdam, Netherlands.

Industry observers note that A family cruise can be a nature-filled adventure to places like Alaska, the Galápagos, Baja California, Iceland, Greenland, and even Antarctica. For active families with curious kids and teens (and parents!), National Geographic-Lindblad Expeditions is a top choice.

The cruise line’s ships carry under 200 guests, so families can focus on each other without those massive-ship distractions. Though small, the ships do offer connecting cabins to accommodate groups and casual dining with plentiful options to suit all tastes.

In a recent development, on a National Geographic cruise, the destination is the draw, and family-friendly activities range from snorkeling and kayaking to hiking and biking. On select voyages, the cruise line offers its National Geographic Explorers-in-Training program for kids and teenagers, led by certified field instructors. The program focuses on nature, science, and storytelling, with activities like practicing smartphone photography in Alaska with a photo instructor, collecting and then observing plankton under a microscope in Baja California, and learning to drive a Zodiac.

Standout itinerary: 7-night Galápagos Escape cruise from Quito, Ecuador.

Luxury cruise ships aren’t built for kids, but select cruise lines make an effort to entertain junior cruisers during holiday and summer sailings in places like Alaska and the Caribbean. Regent Seven Seas Cruises’ ships might not offer a dedicated kids club on board, but the line’s longstanding Club Mariner Youth Program welcomes children ages 5 to 17 with a schedule of onboard activities.

Industry observers note that trained counselors make use of the ships’ public spaces to keep kids busy with mini-golf games, dessert decorating, karaoke parties, and movie nights. In Alaska, programming is destination-themed, and a youth-oriented enrichment speaker engages kids in learning about Alaska’s nature and wildlife.

Recent findings suggest that don’t underestimate your family’s ability to find fun on an adult-oriented ship. On Regent, kids can enjoy swimming in the onboard pool, joining a team for trivia, and playing board or card games in the library. Afternoon tea and evening reveals may also become family attractions. You might find that complimentary room service from the main dining room menu coupled with movies on-demand in your suite is the perfect family activity to end your day.

Standout itinerary: 7-night Alaska cruise on Seven Seas Explorer from Vancouver, Canada, to Whittier, Alaska.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • From the gibbous Moon, drop down first to check out Saturn through a telescope, including its lovely ring system and brightest moon, Titan.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

November 19: Mercury moves into Libra.

The Moon passes 5° north of Neptune at 8 A.M. EST; 12 hours later, our satellite passes 7° north of Saturn at 8 P.M. EST. The trio is visible in the southeastern sky two hours after sunset, forming a triangle with the Moon to the upper left of Saturn, and Neptune to Saturn’s right. Only the Moon and Saturn are visible to the naked eye, while Neptune will require optical aid.

From the gibbous Moon, drop down first to check out Saturn through a telescope, including its lovely ring system and brightest moon, Titan. Saturn is the brightest object in this part of the sky after the Moon, so you don’t have to worry about misidentifying it. After passing south of the ringed world earlier this week, Titan now sits about 3.2’ to Saturn’s west, in line with the rings. Fainter moons Tethys, Rhea, and Dione may be visible clustered closer to the planet, but the bright moonlight might also make them challenging for visual observation.

From Saturn, scan 6.6° west-southwest to land on Neptune. If you have a go-to scope, it may take you right to the outermost planet, which glows at magnitude 7.7 and offers up a tiny, 2”-wide disk. It may look like a “flat,” bluish-gray star, rather than a bright pinprick of white light. Look for a large parallelogram of 4th- and 5th-magnitude stars just over 9° to Saturn’s southwest if you need a closer stepping stone. The star at the northeastern point of that shape is 5th-magnitude 29 Piscium, and it lies about 2.6° southwest of Neptune.

Traditional thermostats only require power through the four classic wires while smart thermostats typically require low- voltage power all day in order to run the display screen and some basic functions. This low-voltage power comes from an additional fifth wire called the “common” wire or C-Wire. The biggest potential issue you may have with installation is if your home lacks this wire.

Industry observers note that if this is the case, it’s probably time to step away from your weekend home project and call an HVAC technician. While installing a common wire isn’t an incredibly difficult undertaking if you’re somewhat handy, it’s one that likely requires the expertise of a trained professional.

According to recent reports, along with scheduling heating or cooling programs from the convenience of your phone, there are a handful of features that set smart thermostats apart from their traditional counterparts. Most smart models automatically adjust the temperature based on peak usage and some automatically respond to outdoor temperatures and set ideal temperatures indoors.

Other models use geofencing, or virtual fencing technology. This creates a radius around your home and detects how close or far away your smartphone is from it. With this, the smart thermostat eases energy use when you aren’t home, and ramps back up as you reenter the virtual boundary.

According to recent reports, several smart thermostats we cover use external sensors to expand the reach of temperature readings. Setup is typically no more complicated than placing the sensors around the house and syncing them up with the rest of the system.

They’re great for maintaining different temperatures in rooms, like keeping bedrooms and bathrooms warm and offices and laundry rooms cool. Smart thermostats that include sensors as part of their systems often come with one, though some models require purchasing sensors separately.

Dan Bartlett from June Lake, California.

Asteroid 6993 (1995 BJ4), a small body 7 miles (11 kilometers) across, orbits in the main belt between Mars and Jupiter. In August 2026, astronomers spotted a faint tail, making it candidate for the largest known main-belt comet. However, the tail has been gradually fading through 2026, which hints at it being caused by debris from a one-time impact rather than ongoing outgassing, astronomers reported last month in a paper accepted in The Astrophysical Journal Letters. In this image, the tail spans more than 35′, or wider than the Full Moon.

Sources indicate that former Rep. Jim McDermott, D-Wash., is seen in a vineyard near his cottage in Civrac-en-Médoc, France, on March 20, 2024. (Ariel Cohen/CQ Roll Call).

It has been revealed that former Rep. Jim McDermott, D-Wash., a fierce advocate for universal health care and outspoken war critic who served 28 years in Congress, died Thursday at the age of 89, his family confirmed.

In a roughly 50-year career in state and federal office, the salty-tongued, liberal lawmaker from Seattle won both praise and criticism for pushing an aggressive agenda focused on expanding health care to all Americans.

As the top Democrat on the House Ways and Means Health Subcommittee, McDermott defended the 2010 Affordable Care Act that expanded health insurance to millions of Americans, while critics complained it did little to control costs.

In a recent development, “Jim was one of the first and most powerful voices fighting to fix our broken health care system in Congress,” Sen. Patty Murray, D-Wash., wrote on X. “He was passionate and fearless — and left a tremendous legacy on WA state and its people. My thoughts are with Congressman McDermott’s family and loved ones during this difficult time.”.

When McDermott announced his retirement from Congress in 2016, then-President Barack Obama praised him in a statement as “a much-needed voice for his most vulnerable constituents.”.

Sources indicate that born and raised in Illinois, McDermott came from a poor, conservative and deeply religious family. His father, a bond underwriter, and his mother, a telephone operator and homemaker, started a church in the garage of their two-bedroom home. His three siblings slept in one bedroom; his parents in the other. McDermott, the oldest child, had the couch.

Sources indicate that he attended the conservative evangelical Wheaton College. His bend toward liberalism began during medical school at the University of Illinois, when he voted for John F. Kennedy in the 1960 presidential election. After a stint in the U.S. Navy Medical Corps from 1968-1970, McDermott won his first seat in the Washington state House in 1970 running on an anti-war platform.

Industry observers note that he continued his anti-war stances in Congress, voting against the 2002 resolution authorizing the use of military force in Iraq. In 2013, he opposed U.S. intervention in Syria and was one of only 20 House members to vote against fresh sanctions on Iran.

Shortly after he retired from Congress, McDermott settled on a newly introduced life for himself by moving to a small town in southwestern France, where he admired some of the public policies he had fought hard to deliver in Washington with mixed success.

Recent findings suggest that “I spent 16 years in the Washington state legislature trying to get single-payer health care,” he recalled in a 2024 interview with CQ Roll Call at his home about 90 minutes outside of Bourdeaux. “Then I spent nearly 30 years in Congress trying to get single-payer. Then I came to France and in three months I had single-payer. Was that mind-blowing? You bet.”.

As he stated, McDermott dedicated much time in the Washington state legislature to trying to create a single-payer system. When that didn’t work out, he developed the Washington State Basic Health Program, a health coverage system for the unemployed and working poor — the first state program of its kind.

Sources indicate that then, once he got to Washington, he tried to work with then-First Lady Hillary Clinton to hatch a federal single-payer program, but that effort came to naught. He later backed the Affordable Care Act and tried to pass his own legislation in 2015 for comprehensive health care coverage.

“The only way to truly ensure that access to quality health care is a right enjoyed by every American is through a single-payer system,” he mentioned in a statement at the time.

Sources indicate that mcDermott will also be remembered for some of the attacks he leveled against Republicans. In the most notorious incident, he was ordered to pay then-Rep. John A. Boehner of Ohio — who later became speaker — nearly $1.1 million in 2008 after releasing a recording of a 1996 cell phone call between Boehner and then-Speaker Newt Gingrich. McDermott maintained it was worth the fight, and the cost of the settlement, to protect free speech.

“Jim McDermott was as significant as it gets in Washington state politics,” Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., wrote on Facebook. “Smart, funny, and Irish, Jim McDermott will be missed.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

It was a hot, dry day in the Kalahari Desert, and Mathilde Martin was running after a meerkat.

Recent findings suggest that the animal wore a GPS tracker around its neck and bolted between shelters, like an action hero running for cover, indicates Martin, a biologist at the University of Zurich. She and her colleagues had captured the meerkat earlier that morning, driven it 1.5 kilometers from its pack and then released it into the desert. They were trying to find out how well individual meerkats could find their way back home.

The answer was quite well, the researchers reported November 19 in the Journal of Experimental Biology. The results suggest that meerkats can navigate expertly on their own, perhaps relying on mental maps charted early in life. “They all seem to be very, very good,” Martin says. It’s a surprise finding for a species known for its group cooperation.

In a recent development, meerkats (Suricata suricatta), which live in southern Africa, form tight-knit family groups of up to 50 members. These social animals cooperate in many aspects of life, including by babysitting each other’s pups and watching for predators while traveling along foraging paths. Martin and her colleagues thought meerkats might also rely on one another for navigating. Some pack members, perhaps those who’ve had more opportunity to explore solo, might have spatial knowledge of their territory and lead the rest, she indicates. But that’s not what the team discovered.

In separate catch and release experiments with 20 individual meerkats, 18 made a beeline back home, back to their group or back to the site where they were captured. (The other two may have been too stressed to get moving, Martin says.).

It has been revealed that neither age nor individual experience, which researchers had been tracking, seemed to factor into the meerkats’ homing skills. Nearly all of them knew where to go, Martin says. She thinks these crackerjack navigators relied on visual cues to orient themselves. They’d pop up on their hind legs and scan the landscape before scampering off in a direct line to their target.

It’s likely that scent played a role, too, though distant scent marks may have faded by the time the meerkats were released. The researchers dropped the animals off in territory they hadn’t visited for at least 30 days. “Otherwise,” she claims, “it would have been a bit too easy for them to find their way back,” she says.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the phenomenon of a Full Moon arises when our planet, Earth, is precisely sandwiched between the Sun and the Moon. This alignment ensures the entire side of the Moon that faces us gleams under sunlight. Thanks to the Moon’s orbit around Earth, the angle of sunlight hitting the lunar surface and being reflected back to our planet changes. That creates different lunar phases.

The next Full Moon will be the November Beaver Moon, which occurs at 9:54 a.m. EST on Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026. It will also be a Super Moon.

We’ll patch this article multiple times each week with the latest moonrise, moonset, Full Moon schedule, and some of what you can see in the sky each week.

Here’s the complete list of Full Moons this year and their traditional names.

(All times Eastern; * denotes a Super Moon.).

According to recent reports, the images below show the day-by-day phases of the Moon in November. The Full Moon this month will be on Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026.

The times below for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location. All other times are Eastern unless otherwise specified. For more details on upcoming sky events, check out our full Sky This Week column.

Friday, November 20The Moon passes 5° north of Neptune at 8 A.M. EST; 12 hours later, our satellite passes 7° north of Saturn at 8 P.M. EST. The trio is visible in the southeastern sky two hours after sunset, forming a triangle with the Moon to the upper left of Saturn, and Neptune to Saturn’s right. Only the Moon and Saturn are visible to the naked eye, while Neptune will require optical aid.

Sunrise: 6:51 A.M.Sunset: 4:40 P.M.Moonrise: 2:04 P.M.Moonset: 2:12 A.M.Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (84%).

Sunrise: 6:52 A.M.Sunset: 4:39 P.M.Moonrise: 2:29 P.M.Moonset: 3:22 A.M.Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (92%).

Sunday, November 22With the Moon not far from Full, its western limb is now coming into view as the Sun rises across the lunar landscape. The large, flat-floored crater Schickard is prominent in the southwest, near the small, circular Mare Humorum.

In a recent development, stretching about 130 miles (210 kilometers) across, Schickard is roughly 4 billion years old and was formed by a giant impact. Because it sits so near the limb of the Moon, it often looks oblong from our vantage point on Earth — but from above, orbiters have shown it is really quite circular in shape.

Sunrise: 6:53 A.M.Sunset: 4:39 P.M.Moonrise: 2:59 P.M.Moonset: 4:34 A.M.Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (97%).

Sunrise: 6:54 A.M.Sunset: 4:38 P.M.Moonrise: 3:37 P.M.Moonset: 5:52 A.M.Moon Phase: Full.

Tuesday, November 24Full Moon occurs at 9:54 A.M. EST, bringing us our second Super Moon of the year. The November Full Moon is also called the Beaver Moon.

Sources indicate that A few hours earlier, before dawn, the Full Moon passes through the Pleiades star cluster (M45) in Taurus, occulting several of its bright stars. This is an easy event to watch, visible to the naked eye — or you can get a closer view with binoculars or a telescope. The timing of the event will depend heavily on your location; note that it begins right around sunrise along the East Coast, so observers there may only see the Moon approaching the famous group of stars.

The 5th-magnitude star Celaeno (16 Tauri) disappears behind the Moon’s leading edge just moments before 6 A.M. CST, followed minutes later by 4th-magnitude Taygeta (19 Tau). Next to vanish is 4th-magnitude Maia (20 Tau) just before 6:20 A.M. CST, followed swiftly by Sterope (21 Tau) a few minutes later. Celaeno reappears around 6:40 A.M. CST, 15 minutes or so before sunrise.

For specific timings from your location, visit the International Occultation Timing Association at http://www.lunar-occultations.com/bobgraze/index.html.
